## PREFACE
### To the
# READER.

Since <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: *Chymie*; in the 17th century, this term was used interchangeably for both practical chemical science and the older traditions of alchemy.</note> is rightfully one of the oldest arts, it is by no means the least: for it investigates all powers and the interconnectedness of things, not only in plants and animals, but it even penetrates to the innermost core of metals and minerals, decomposing them and joining them back together again. *Tubal-cain* <note>A biblical figure from Genesis 4:22, described as an "instructor of every artificer in brass and iron"; he was historically regarded by early modern scientists as the legendary founder of metallurgy and chemistry.</note> seems to have laid the first stone regarding copper and iron, since he could not easily forge...

<summary>The author introduces chemistry as one of the most ancient and vital sciences, capable of revealing the inner nature of plants, animals, and minerals through analysis and synthesis. He cites the biblical figure Tubal-cain as the historical originator of metalworking.</summary>

# P R E F A C E .

And since the discourse on **Metals** has been described by many either very obscurely or deceptively, I have added a continuation to it. All of this was either worked upon by *Sir K. Digby* <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665) was a famous English courtier and natural philosopher whose "chemical secrets" became bestsellers in the 17th century.</note> with his own hands, or presented to him by many trustworthy gentlemen throughout all of *Europe*, and published in English by *George Hartman* <note>George Hartman was Digby's laboratory assistant who published Digby's posthumous papers.</note>. He had these writings partly in his own keeping, or they were found in that great library—which was sold for ten thousand crowns after his death—in various languages such as Latin, French, Italian, and High German, and were translated into English by the same *Hartman*; in this way, his secrets have come to light.

Now, dear reader, accept this *Theatrum Chimicum* <note>original Latin: "Chemical Theater"; a title used for books that aimed to put the "spectacle" of chemical secrets on display for the reader.</note> as something rare and extraordinary. I have named it thus because it is a theater <note>original: *schouw-toneel*; literally a "show-stage" or public spectacle.</note> and an open door,

->Or<-

->Of all<-

### *Chemical Mysteries.* <note>original: *Chymische Verborgentheden*; in the 17th century, "mysteries" or "secrets" often referred to specific recipes, hidden properties of matter, or the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note>

->First of<-

## CHEMISTRY in GENERAL.

### CHAPTER I.

### On the definition of Chemistry.

<margin>I.</margin> Chemistry can be defined in many different ways, but since they all carry the same meaning, it is best defined as *a decomposition of substances through fire.* <note>The author uses the word "bodies" (*lighamen*), which in early modern science referred to any physical matter or material substance being analyzed in a laboratory.</note>

<margin>II.</margin> The word *Chemia* <note>The Latinized form of Chemistry.</note> is originally an Arabic word, and was written *Chamâ*, from the

<summary>This title page and opening chapter introduce the work as the "Chemical Theatre" and provide the foundational definition of chemistry as the analysis or breaking down of substances using fire. The author also begins to explore the Arabic etymology of the word "Chemia."</summary>

<keywords>Chemistry, definition of chemistry, decomposition, fire, etymology, Arabic, Chemical Theatre</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the etymological discussion of the word "Chemistry" from the previous page, specifically linking it to Arabic and Greek roots, before moving into the classification of matter (the Three Kingdoms).</meta>

root-word *Zymiâ*, which means hidden or concealed; *Chemistry* is thus named because it is a hidden art, which the Masters of the Art have intentionally kept secret, either because of its presence or for the profit they derived from it; for it can also transform base metals into noble ones, and base stones into precious ones. There are some Greek writers who believe that *Egypt* was formerly called *Chymia*, and that this art was called *Aegypta* <note>Original: *Ægypta*.</note>, which the Egyptians are said to have discovered first, or at least practiced more than others.

III. The *subject of Chemistry consists of all bodies*, both simple and compound; the former insofar as simple substances are extracted from them; and the latter insofar as they constitute compound bodies. Nevertheless, compound and mixed things are the *subject of Chemistry*, and these are divided into three kingdoms: the *mineral*, the *vegetable*, and the *animal*.

IV. The *kingdom of minerals encompasses metals, stones, and earths.*

V. *Metals* are those minerals which can be melted and forged, of which there are seven, according to the number of the planets: for gold is called *Sol* <note>The Sun.</note>; silver *Luna* <note>The Moon.</note>; iron *Mars*; copper *Venus*; tin *Jupiter*; lead *Saturn*; and quicksilver *Mercury*.

VI. *Stones* are said to be minerals which can indeed be melted by fire, but are nevertheless not malleable; and these are either noble, such as diamonds; or base, such as pebbles.

VII. The *Earths* are also called minerals; these cannot be forged, but can be melted; they can easily be rubbed into pieces, and are either salts, such as <term>rock salt</term> <note>original: *sal gemmæ*; a pure, crystalline form of salt.</note>, saltpeter, sea salt, alum, or vitriol <note>A group of chemicals consisting of hydrated sulfates, often used in making acids.</note>;

It specifically details the mineral kingdom, categorizing metals by their planetary associations and distinguishing stones and earths by their physical properties.</summary>

VIII. The vegetable kingdom encompasses plants and their juices, such as wine, oil, vinegar, resins, fruits, white milky substances, etc.

IX. The animal kingdom includes all types of living creatures, whether they be beasts or humans, and their various parts, such as excretions, flesh, bones, fat, urine, blood, etc.

X. The defining term of Chemistry is decomposition or <term>anatomy</term> <note>In this context, "anatomy" refers to the chemical process of taking a substance apart into its basic elements.</note>, which is nothing other than a separation of compound bodies into their primary principles; these are then water, earth, spirit, salt, acid, oil, etc.

XI. The water, otherwise called <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *plegma*; the tasteless, watery byproduct of distillation.</note>, is the watery moisture that is tasteless and not very volatile, unless it is driven by a moderate fire.

XII. The earth is a thick and dry body, which after distillation is commonly called a <term>dead head</term> <note>original: *caput mortuum*.</note> or <term>condemned earth</term> <note>original: *Terra damnata*; the useless residue left in a flask after all the spirits and oils have been boiled away.</note>; it is from this that bodies derive most of their solidity.

XIII. The spirit is called **Mercury** by the Chemists because of its resemblance to fine volatility, being very penetrating and mobile, such as <term>alcohol of wine</term> <note>original: *alcoholvini*.</note>, or the **spirits** of wormwood, grain, roses, etc. <note>original: *spiritus absinthii, frumenti, rosarum*.</note>, being made from fermented and processed things. One must then call everything "spirit" that is highly volatile, for its identification consists in that quality.

XIV. The salt is a solid substance, yet one that easily melts in moisture. It is of two kinds: namely fixed and volatile <note>original: *fixum* and *volatile*.</note>; both are named thus in relation to fire. For the fixed salt can constantly withstand the second, third, and fourth <term>degrees of fire</term> <note>Early chemists used four "degrees" of heat, ranging from the warmth of a brooding hen to the intense heat of a furnace.</note>

Among the **fixed salts** are those which are leached out of burnt ashes, such as **salt of tartar** <note>original: *sal tartari*; a salt derived from the residue of wine casks</note>, **potash** <note>original: *cinerum clavellatorum*</note>, **wormwood** <note>original: *absinthii*</note>, etc. Among the **volatile salts** <note>original: *vlugge*</note>, one has **salt of hartshorn** <note>original: *sal cornu cervi*; an early form of ammonia</note>, **flowers of sal ammoniac** <note>original: *flores salis armoniaci*</note>, etc. There is also a salt that has an affinity with acid, such as **vitriol** <note>original: *vitriolum*</note>, **common salt** <note>original: *sal commune*</note>, **saltpeter** <note>original: *nitrum*</note>, **essential salt of herbs** <note>original: *sal essenziale herbarum*</note>, etc. Minerals give fixed salt; animals give volatile salts; and herbs give fixed, volatile, and mixed salts.

XV. The **acid** is a substance always acting and fermenting upon the salt; it is fluid if it stands on its own, and sharp and biting in taste, such as the **spirit of nitre** <note>original: *spiritus nitri*; nitric acid</note>, **spirit of sulfur** <note>original: *salis sulphuris*; sulfuric acid</note>, etc., which are called **spirits** <note>original: *spiritus*</note> by the Chemists, but they are not actually such <note>The author suggests that despite the name "spirit," these acids are distinct from the volatile "spirit" described earlier.</note>. Among these, one has some that are mixed with other fixed parts, such as **crystals of tartar** <note>original: *crystalli tartari*</note>, **vitriol**, **common salt**, etc.; these are obtained from minerals and plants.

XVI. To this is added the **oil**, which one calls **sulfur** <note>original: *sulpher*</note> or **brimstone** <note>original: *swavel*</note>, being everything that is combustible: this has, according to its various mixtures, also various tastes and smells, such as bitter, sweet, stinking, pleasant, etc.

XVII. Of these, some are easily moved and others are difficult to move, especially the **earth**, since it consists of coarser parts than the others. And notwithstanding that these bodies are called "simple" <note>In the sense of being basic elements or "principles."</note>, they are nevertheless so entwined with others that they cannot be separated by any art.

This [composition] is said to occur when many and various bodies are brought together into one body, which happens in many ways: through **precipitations** <note>original: *precipitatien*; the process where a solid settles out of a liquid solution</note>, **congelation** <note>original: *congelatie*; the thickening or solidifying of a substance</note>, **cohobation** <note>original: *cohobatie*; the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid over its own solid residue to increase its potency</note>, **reduction** <note>original: *reductie*; returning a metal to its metallic state from an oxide or ore</note>, **digestion** <note>original: *digeſtie*; the application of gentle, consistent heat over a long period, similar to a stomach’s warmth</note>, **coction** <note>original: *coctie*; boiling or "cooking" a substance</note>, and **exhalation** <note>original: *exſalatie*; the release of vapors</note>.

XIX. Fire is indeed the most important tool in chemistry, yet it is not the only one; for water, air, and earth also serve this purpose.

XX. The end or goal of chemistry is not always the same. Sometimes one seeks certain physical truths, in which case the goal is the knowledge or science of the structure of bodies. At other times, it is the **transmutation of metals** <note>The alchemical process of turning "base" metals like lead or iron into "noble" metals like gold or silver</note>, when the base metals are transformed into noble ones. Thirdly, it is practiced to seek proper medicines, which is the subject we shall mostly deal with in the future.

## II. CHAPTER.

->*Of the Instruments which must be used in Chemistry, and the degrees of fire.*<-

I. All of chemistry, with respect to its means and its ends, is divided into three parts: namely, instruments, operations, and effects.

II. The instruments or tools are many and varied; the most important are fire, **separating-liquids** <note>original: *schey-vochten*; strong solvents or acids like aqua fortis used to separate metals</note>, and vessels.

III. The **furnaces** <note>original: *ovens*</note>, in terms of their operations, have various forms, such as round, square, low, high, small, large, closed, open, single, compound, separate, joined together, and **reverberatory-** <note>A reverberatory furnace is one where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof onto the material being heated, preventing direct contact with the fuel.</note>

VI. The **first degree** of fire is the gentlest of all, and is called **digestive**, **circular**, or **putrefactive**; it is the warmth of a bath at the beginning, which is equal to the warmth of **horse manure** <note>original: *paardemist*; decaying manure was used in alchemy as a source of steady, low-level heat for fermentation</note>, which the finger of the most delicate person can endure, also corresponding to freshly shed blood or fresh urine.

XX. The **vessels** <note>original: *Vaten*</note> required for chemistry differ in material, shape, and size.

XXI. Regarding the **material** <note>original: *ſtoffe*</note>, these are made of glass, earthenware, copper, tin, iron, lead, etc.

XXII. Regarding the **shape** <note>original: *figuur*</note>, they are round, square, curved, beaked, hollow, bulbous, long, flat, etc.

XXIII. Regarding the **size**, they are low or high, and can hold much or little liquid, etc.

XXIV. They are either flasks or pots.

XXV. The flasks include the **cucurbit** <note>original: *kolf*</note>, **pelican** <note>a circulatory vessel with two "arms" feeding back into the body</note>, **vial-glass**, **receiver** <note>the vessel that catches the distilled liquid</note>, **philosopher’s egg** <note>an oval-shaped glass vessel used for long digestion</note>, etc.

XXVI. A kolf or **cucurbit** <note>original: *cucurbita*; a gourd-shaped boiling vessel</note>, if it has a crooked neck, is called a **retort** <note>original: *retorta*</note>; there are also straight cucurbits, separating-glasses, etc. If the vessel is made of copper, it is called a **vesica** <note>original Latin: *Vesica*; literally "bladder," referring to its shape</note> or bladder.

XXVII. That which is used to cover the cucurbit is called a **helmet** <note>original: *helm*</note> or **alembic** <note>original: *Alembicum*; the cap or "head" of a still where vapors condense</note>. This is either turret-shaped or formed like a human skullcap, with or without an inner rim, and with a beak <note>spout</note> or "blind" <note>without an outlet</note>.

XXVIII. Pots are either made of earthenware with a flat bottom, or **cupels** <note>original: *capellen*; small porous bowls used in assaying</note>, or oval, or flat and square. Some rise from an oval base like a beaker, tapering upwards in a triangular fashion; others are broad for the purpose of **calcination** <note>original: *calcineren*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile parts or reduce it to powder</note>, and are either glazed or unglazed. However, since a student cannot easily grasp the nature of ovens and vessels from descriptions alone, we shall set some down here and illustrate them with figures.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Of Chemical Operations.*<-

I. **CHEMICAL** operations, considered in general, are of two kinds: namely *Dissolving* and *Coagulating*, which nevertheless include many varieties under them.
II. *Solution* <note>the process of dissolving or breaking down a substance</note> occurs through *Calcination*, *Extraction*, or *Purification*.
III. *Calcination* <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve oxidation or reduce it to powder</term> occurs in six different ways, and its purpose is achieved by heat or primarily by a mineral powder.
IV. The first type of calcining occurs by means of **Mercury**, and is specific to all metals except iron; it is commonly called *Amalgamation*, which seems to mean "bringing into a single mass." The second occurs through some acidic **spirit** <note>a "spirit" refers to a volatile liquid obtained by distillation</note>, such as through **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fortis" (nitric acid)</note>, **spirit of Vitriol** <note>original: "spiritus Vitrioli" (sulfuric acid)</note>, **vinegar** <note>original: "acetti"</note>, **saltpeter** <note>original: "nitri"</note>, **alum** <note>original: "aluminis"</note>, or **salt** <note>original: "salis" (hydrochloric acid)</note>, and is commonly given the name *precipitation*. The third type occurs by

<summary>This page concludes the description of a complex distillation apparatus and begins a theoretical discussion on the primary chemical operations: dissolution and coagulation.</summary>
<keywords>distillation, phlegm, calcination, solution, amalgamation, mercury, acids, aqua fortis, precipitation</keywords>

--- Page 69 ---
<meta>This page continues the classification of chemical operations begun in Chapter III, specifically concluding the six methods of calcination before moving on to extraction, purification, and coagulation.</meta>

# Chemical Theater. <note>original: "Theatrum Chemicum"</note>

...by a corrosive powder put into action, such as by **sulfur**, **nitre** <note>original: "nitrum" (saltpeter)</note>, **vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolum" (sulfate minerals)</note>, **common salt**, **salt of tartar** <note>original: "sal tartari" (potassium carbonate)</note>, which is called *stratification* or *cementation* <term>cementation: a process of surrounding a solid metal with a powder and heating it to change its properties</term>. The *fourth* is performed by a sharp fuming of **quicksilver** <note>original: "Quiksilver" (mercury)</note>, arsenic <note>original: "afijn" likely referring to arsenic or a refining agent</note>, strong water <note>original: "sterk water" (nitric acid)</note>, likewise by the vapor of some distilled water of **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini" (ethanol)</note>, and that is called *fumigation*. The *fifth* occurs by the bare fire, and is called *incineration* <note>the process of reducing something to ashes</note>. The sixth is performed by a reverberatory furnace <term>reverberatory furnace: a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material being heated</term>, and is called *reverberation*.

V. *Extraction* resolves bodies into various parts, and occurs first through an extraction "in kind" so to speak, being specific to tinctures and essences; a *Tincture* is a certain transparent color, containing some powers of the whole within itself, which, when the *menstruum* <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract active principles from a substance</term> is drawn off from it, is called an *extract*. But an *essence* includes all the powers of the whole within itself. Secondly, by *putrefaction*, which is followed by *Separation*. Thirdly, by distillation, which is *sideways* <note>original: "Sydelinx" (distillation *per latus*, usually using a retort)</note>, in matters which give off heavy smoke; or by descending, when the vapors are very heavy, and this is called *by descent* <note>original: "per descensum"</note>. Or by ascending, if the vapors are very light. Fourthly, by *sublimation* <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note>. Fifthly, by *filtration*; sixthly, by *deliquescence* <note>original: "deliquium"; the process of a salt absorbing moisture from the air until it dissolves</note>; seventhly by *rectification* <note>purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</note>. Eighthly by *cohobation* <term>cohobation: a process where the distilled liquid is poured back onto the remaining solid residue and re-distilled</term>, and ninthly by *digestion* <note>heating a substance gently over a long period</note>.

VIII. *Purification* removes all uselessness and foreign matter, and occurs through a manifold solution in water and filtration; or by burning, as in salts, bones, horns, etc.

# Chemical Theater <note>original: "Theatrum Chemicum"</note>

...ways occurs, through *precipitation*, *reduction*, *concretion*, *digestion*, and *cohobation*.

X. *Precipitation* is when a certain precipitating liquid is poured onto a body that has been dissolved by a *menstruum* <term>menstruum: a solvent used to dissolve a solid substance</term>. This liquid incorporates itself into the *menstruum* and pushes the dissolved body—which hangs with its smallest particles in the pores <note>original: "pijpjes" (little pipes); a reference to the 17th-century belief that liquids contained microscopic channels</note> of the *menstruum*—downward to the bottom. This process requires three things: the dissolved body, the *menstruum*, and the precipitating liquid.

XI. *Reduction* is the term used when a body is brought back to its previous form. It applies almost exclusively to metals and is performed with a smelting fire using a retort, or through evaporation—specifically by precipitating with *salt of tartar* <note>original: "sal Tartari" (potassium carbonate)</note>. In this way, one makes *Calx of Saturn* <note>original: "Calx Saturni" (lead oxide)</note>, and in this manner, *oil of tartar by deliquescence* <note>original: "oleum tartari per deliquium"</note> <term>oil of tartar per deliquium: a concentrated liquid made by allowing potassium carbonate to absorb moisture from the air</term> precipitates corals <note>likely referring to "vegetable" or "mineral" trees—crystalline structures that resemble coral</note>.

XII. *Concretion* is when salts are turned into crystals by water. This occurs because the salt particles approach one another closely and embrace each other, through which various types of corals <note>crystalline growths</note> are formed.

XIII. Through *digestion* and *circulation*, the parts of a liquid are united; this is performed using the first degree of fire <note>the gentlest level of heat, roughly equivalent to the warmth of the sun or a brooding hen</note>.

XIV. *Cohobation* is when the liquid that has been distilled off is poured back onto the material from which it was distilled. This is done so that the power—which could not be separated during the first or second attempt—may be separated on the third time and united with the distilled liquid. It also frequently happens that what passes over is united with what remains behind.

XV. *Immutation* is said to occur when certain accidents... <note>original: "toevallen" (a philosophical term referring to the external properties or qualities of a substance, rather than its essence)</note>

# CHAPTER IV.
## *On the kinds of Chemistry in general.*

I. The species or kind in **Chemistry** refers to that which is produced through certain operations with proper instruments, such as **spirit of vitriol** <note>original: "spiritus vitrioli"</note> <term>spirit of vitriol: a historical name for sulfuric acid</term>, **spirit of alum** <note>original: "Spiritus aluminis"</note>, etc.

II. This is either simple or composite.

III. Simple is either a Magistery, or an extract, or something that has been separated.

IV. **Magisteries** <note>original: "Magisterien"</note> <term>magistery: a preparation where a substance is purified or transformed into a new form without losing its essential components</term> are a kind in chemistry prepared entirely without extraction, with the external impurities removed: to this belong, 1. **oil of tartar by deliquescence** <note>original: "oleum tartari per deliquium"</note>, **potable gold** <note>original: "Aurum potabile"</note> <term>potable gold: a legendary medicinal liquid believed to contain gold and possess life-prolonging properties</term>, etc. 2. those commonly called magisteries, such as of corals or pearls, as well as **emetic vitriols** <note>original: "Vitriola vomitiva"</note> <term>emetic: a substance that induces vomiting</term>, **powders and calxes of metals** <note>original: "pulveres en calces metallorum"</note> <term>calx: the powdery oxide or "ash" left after a metal or mineral has been burned</term>, **golden sulfur of antimony** <note>original: "Sulpher auratum antimonii"</note>, **crocus of Mars** <note>original: "crocus martis"</note> <term>crocus of Mars: a red powder made from iron (Mars) used in medicine and pigments</term>, and the **flowers** <note>original: "flores"</note> <term>flowers: fine powders created through sublimation, where a solid is vaporized and then collected as it cools</term> of other metals, the **sublimates of precipitated mercury** <note>original: "sublimata mercurij precipitati"</note>, **mineral Bezoar** <note>original: "Bezoardicum minerale"</note> <term>mineral Bezoar: an antimony-based powder named after bezoar stones for its supposed detoxifying properties</term>, **diaphoretic antimony** <note>original: "antimonium diaphoreticum"</note> <term>diaphoretic: a medicine used to induce sweating</term>, etc.

### IX. Vaporous Calcination of Gold, with the Crocus <note>original: "Auri Calcinatio Vaporosa"; in alchemy, "crocus" refers to a fine metallic powder or oxide, named for its resemblance to the color of the saffron spice</note>

This is achieved through vapors that rise from some corrosive moisture.
Take a gold plate and hang it over **child’s urine** <note>a common source of ammonia in early chemistry</note> that has been mixed with the skins of pressed grapes, and do this within an **aludel** <term>aludel: a pear-shaped ceramic vessel used in sublimation and vapor-based reactions</term> that is quite spacious and well-sealed. Place it for 14 days in the warm skins of the grapes; thus, the **Crocus** shall hang upon the gold, which one shall wipe off with a **hare’s foot** <note>the soft fur of a hare's foot was used as a delicate brush to collect fine powders without scratching the metal</note>.

### X. Amalgamatory Calcination of Gold, or Gold Amalgam <note>original: "Calcinatio Auri Amalgamatoria"</note>

Take six parts of pure, raw **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> to one part of a gold plate; make an **amalgam** <term>amalgam: a mixture or alloy of mercury with another metal, which results in a soft or liquid substance</term> from this. Namely, let your gold plate (heated, if you please) be mixed with the mercury, which has been heated by the fire until it smokes. Having been mixed together, pour the mixture into water so that the mixture is uniform throughout.
Then rub it with twice as much **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"</note>, stirring constantly over a gentle fire until it is **calcined** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder (calx)</term>, until the mercury and the sulfur have evaporated without melting or solidifying, and the **calx of gold** remains behind like a **marigold** <note>original: "gouds-bloem"; referring to the bright yellow-orange color of the gold oxide</note>.
Before it is burned with sulfur, one can amalgamate the mercury with the gold and draw it off via the **retort** <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids or separating mercury from metals</term> as many times as needed until they can no longer hold together,

## XI. Cement-like Calcination of Gold <note>original: "Auri calcinatio cementatoria"</note>

This occurs when the gold has been stratified <term>stratified: arranged in alternating layers of different substances</term> either with sulfur or with **common salt** <note>original: "sal comm." / "sal commune"</note>, and placed in the reverberatory fire; if it does not melt, it allows itself to be finely pulverized.

Or, if one rubs the gold filings very diligently with eight times as much **calcined hartshorn** <note>original: "gebrande harts-hoorn"; deer antlers burned to a white ash, primarily calcium phosphate, used as a dry medium to prevent the metal from fusing</note>, then reverberates it (which can well happen in a potter's kiln) until it achieves a **flesh-colored** <note>original: "incarnate"; a pale pink or reddish hue typical of certain gold preparations</note> color.

Administer it in doses of three to four grains <term>grain: a tiny unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams</term> in many illnesses.

### XIII. Reverberatory Calcination of Gold <note>original: "Auri Calcinatio Reverberatio"</note>

It is said that the gold <note>original: "sout" (salt); likely a printer's error for "gout" (gold) given the context of the chapter</note> is reverberated when it is changed into a very purple, light, and fine powder. Repeated calcinations of the gold can substitute for continuous reverberation, whether this is done through amalgamation or through **royal water** <note>original: "aqua regia"; a highly corrosive mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids, so named because it can dissolve "noble" metals like gold</note>.

### XIV. Spiritualized Gold <note>original: "Aurum Spiritualisatum"</note>

The volatilization <term>volatilization: the process of turning a solid substance into a vapor or "spirit"</term> of gold is the term used when it is distilled through an **alembic** <note>original: "Alembicum"; a two-part distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling pot and a cooling cap</note>, whereby the gold becomes like a spirit. This is achieved through a volatile **solvent** <note>original: "Menstruum"; a liquid used to dissolve a solid body</note>: namely, when the solvent is **cohobated** <term>cohobated: a process of repeated distillation where the liquid is poured back onto the remaining residue to extract more "virtue"</term> from the dissolved gold so many times that it carries the gold with it in a liquid form. The most suitable substances for this are **royal water**, **glacial oil of antimony** <note>original: "oleum antimonii glaceale"; likely antimony trichloride, which has a buttery or oily consistency</note>, **bezoardic spirit of nitre** <note>original: "spir. nitri besoard."</note>, and **rectified spirit of common salt** <note>original: "spir. sal comm. rectif."; a purified form of hydrochloric acid</note>; in place of which one can also use the **spirit** of a vegetable salt, such as **blessed thistle** <note>original: "carduus benedictus"; a plant traditionally used in medicine and alchemy</note>.

## XV. **Potable Gold**, or **Tincture of the Sun**. <note>original: "Aurum Potabile, oft Tinctura Solis"; in alchemy, the Sun (Sol) is the symbol for Gold.</note>

Take the calx <term>calx: the fine powder remaining after a metal has been "burnt" or chemically broken down</term> of gold, made by **royal water** <note>original: "aqua regia"; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, and brought to a state of great porosity and purplish color through reverberation <term>reverberation: heating a substance in a furnace where the flames are reflected back onto the material</term>. Pour upon it the **spirit of wine of the microcosm** <note>original: "spir. vini microcosmi"; likely referring to a spirit distilled from urine (the "microcosm" being man), which alchemists believed contained a powerful solvent for gold</note>. Digest this with a gentle fire for one month in a Hermetically sealed glass <note>original: "Hermetisch toegesloten"; an airtight seal, often made by melting the glass neck of the vessel shut</note>, until the tincture becomes blood-red. Then decant it, and pour new solvent <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract the essence of a substance</term> upon it, and repeat this as often as necessary. Then gather all the solutions together and digest them for twelve days. Afterward, draw off the solvent in a **water bath** <note>original: "B. M." or Balneum Mariae; a vessel of hot water used to provide gentle, even heat</note> (to save for the same use later). Thus the tincture will remain at the bottom like a very red oil, which is soluble in all liquids and may be used as **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; literally "drinkable gold," believed by alchemists to be a universal medicine or panacea</note>.

If one distills the same solution in sand <note>using a sand-bath for higher heat than a water-bath</note> through a flask or retort, then the Tincture of the Sun will finally pass over as well, being blood-red in color, while a sour, black, and spongy earth remains at the bottom of the distilling vessel. Once the tincture has been drawn off from its solvent in a lukewarm bath, it can be further exalted <term>exalted: purified or increased in potency</term> if it is frequently dissolved in **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritu vini"; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note> and the same spirit is then drawn off from the tincture.

It is administered in doses of three to eight grains.

### XXI. Another **Potable Gold** <note>original: "Aurum Potabile"</note> by the **Oil of Saturn**. <note>original: "Oleum Saturni"; in alchemy, Saturn is the symbol for lead. This "oil" was typically a concentrated solution of lead acetate</note>

### XXXVI. Flowers of the Sun. <note>original: "Flores Solis"; a term for a gold sublimate or fine gold powder</note>

Take one part Gold that has been well **calcined** <term>calcined: reduced to a powder through heat and chemical action</term> by the **spirit of common salt** <note>original: "spir. sal. comm."; hydrochloric acid</note>. You shall wash these "flowers" <note>the powdery substance that collects at the top of the vessel during sublimation</note> to remove the sal ammoniac and then dry them; these are administered in doses of six to nine **grains** <note>a small unit of weight used by apothecaries</note>.
For this purpose, one makes a special instrument of silver or copper that can be opened and closed like a box, consisting of an upper and lower part. This instrument must have a pipe on the sides through which one can cast in the **fulminating powder** <note>original: "donderend poeder"; gold fulminate, a highly explosive compound used here to create a fine gold coating</note> (and doing so with as little at a time as possible). This pipe is then immediately closed, and thus the Gold lifts itself upward and hangs at the top of the **vault** <note>original: "welffel"; the interior ceiling of the vessel</note>.

## XLI. Paracelsus’s Mercury of the Sun.

### XLVII. *Glass of Gold, or Greuling’s Ruby.*

It causes gentle purging.

### *XLVIII. Potable Gold of Joel Langelot.*
<note>Joelis Langelotii: Joel Langelot (1617–1685) was a German physician to the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp, known for his mechanical approach to alchemy, specifically using grinding machines.</note>

The gold was beaten into plates as thin as possible, and thereafter cut with scissors into the smallest pieces manageable; then, without allowing any impurities to fall in, it is placed in a mill (the first figure of which can be seen in the first table) made of very high-quality steel; this he then has a laborer grind from morning until evening for an entire month without ceasing. When it has been ground into the finest possible powder, he places it into a glass retort <term>retorta: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term>, which is set in a sand bath, with a receiver attached to its neck. Then the fire is stoked by degrees: gentle at first, and thereafter extremely hot. In this way, some red drops will emerge, which can be digested <term>digestio: the process of exposing a substance to steady, gentle heat</term> on their own, or mixed with **spirit of wine treated with tartar** <term>spiritum vini tartarisatum: alcohol distilled with potassium carbonate to purify it and increase its solvent power</term>. Thus it transforms into a **Potable Gold** <term>Aurum Potabile: "drinkable gold," a legendary alchemical medicine believed to cure all ailments and grant longevity</term>.

That which has remained in the retort is then ground and distilled once again, whereby one obtains drops as before, so that eventually the whole is transformed into a liquor, provided that the grinding and distillation are continually repeated.

### *XLIX. Solar Composite Bezoardic.*
<note>Bezoardicum Compositum Solare: a complex gold-based medicine; "Bezoardic" refers to its properties as a restorative or antidote, similar to a bezoar stone.</note>

Take **butter of antimony** <term>butyrum antimonii: a thick, oily liquid (antimony trichloride)</term> made from **Regulus of Mars** <term>Regulus Martis: metallic antimony produced by reducing the ore with iron, the metal associated with Mars</term> and sublimate, two drachms; and **spirit of nitre** <term>spiritus nitri: nitric acid</term> in sufficient quantity. Mix these together, adding the spirit drop by drop, until the bubbling ceases and it becomes like the cream of milk.

Then take **refined gold** <term>aurum obrysum: exceptionally pure gold</term> that has been washed in an antimony bath <note>A process where gold is melted with antimony to remove base metal impurities</note>, having first been beaten into plates; then

### L. *Essence of the Sun.*

### LI. Another *Essence of the Sun.*

Furthermore, **spirit of wine** <note>original: spiritus vini; high-proof alcohol</note>, which has been exalted <note>purified or heightened in potency</note> with the **volatile salt of urine** <note>original: sal uriæ volatilis</note> and **salt of Tartar** <term>sal Tartari: potassium carbonate, used as a powerful purifying agent and solvent</term>, until it stands six fingers high above it.

## LII. *Essence or Elixir of the Sun.*
<note>original title: Effentia ofte Elixir solis. Sol (the Sun) is the alchemical name for Gold.</note>

Take a booklet of beaten Gold <note>gold leaf</note>, and one ounce of angular candy sugar, whether white or yellow. 
Place them in a small vial-glass in a gentle heat; stir them with a small wooden stick. In this way, the Gold will be calcined <term>calcineren: to reduce a metal to a fine powder through heat or chemical reaction</term> by the acidic **spirit of the sugar**. One removes it from there with a small wooden spatula, and the red mass will immediately congeal. Let the same be finely ground.

Then take two ounces of this powder and **spirit of wine** <note>original: spir. Vini</note> exalted <term>exaltatie: the process of increasing the potency or purity of a substance</term> with the salt of urine and **hartshorn** <note>original: C.C. (Cornu Cervi), the horn of a stag, used as a source of ammonia</note>. In this way, with a gentle heat, one will draw a yellow tincture, which is then poured off. 
Once the evaporation is done by half, save the remainder, of which one administers up to half a scruple <note>approximately 0.6 grams</note> in some lemon balm water <note>original: melisse water</note>.

## LIII. *Alcahestine Essence of the Sun.*
<note>original title: Effentia solis Alcahestina</note>

Take one part of the purple calx of Gold <note>a fine purple powder produced by dissolving gold in aqua regia and precipitating it</note>, and ten parts of the **metallic alcahest liquor** <term>Alcahest: the "universal solvent" sought by alchemists, capable of dissolving any substance into its primary matter</term>. 

Once the digestion has been performed in a gentle heat, pour upon it the **spirit of wine of tartar** <term>spiritus Vini tartar: a spirit distilled from wine that has been purified using cream of tartar</term>; in this way, the essence of the gold will leave the alcahest and attach itself to the **spirit of wine**, which one then gently pours off and preserves.

### LIV. *Solar Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar.*
<note>original title: Magisterium tartari vitriolati solare. A "Magistery" is a high-level alchemical preparation intended to concentrate the "virtue" of a substance.</note>

Take one part of **fulminating gold** <term>blixement goud: also known as aurum fulminans, an explosive gold compound that "flashes" (blixemt) or detonates when heated</term>, made in the common manner.
Take three parts of **Vitriolated Tartar** <term>Tartari Vitriolati: potassium sulfate</term>.
Once pulverized, mix them well together, then place them in a crucible, which is set in a wind furnace; let them warm together gently, and calcine <term>calcineren: to reduce a substance to powder through prolonged heating</term>.

The **fulminating gold** does not "flash" <note>original: blixemt; meaning it does not explode</note> because of the acidity that is in the Vitriolated Tartar. The mass then being taken out of the crucible, you have a red Magistery.

### LVI. *Solar Regulus.*

This Regulus is made from one drachm of cupelled gold <note>gold refined in a shallow vessel called a cupel to remove impurities</note> and one ounce of **Regulus of Antimony** <note>original: Regulus Antimonii; the metallic form of antimony</note>, which are put together in a crucible and melted.

### LVII. *Crocus or Solar Sulfur, and Tincture of Gold.*

Let the pounded salts first be well rubbed together on a marble stone, gradually adding the gold leaves to them; then put them in a new glazed pot that is spacious and large enough: then pour five or six fingers' width of rainwater onto it. Boil it first with a moderate fire, which is then made somewhat stronger, until it reaches the thickness of a thick pap <note>a thick paste or porridge-like consistency</note>; thus the gold shall completely melt <note>original: smelten; in this context, it refers to the gold being dissolved into the saline solution</note>. But before this substance comes to dry completely, pour plain water on it again, as much as is needed for dissolution; after it has boiled up two or three times, one shall filter the solution and precipitate <note>to cause a solid to settle out of the liquid</note> it with **Oil of Tartar** <term>Oleum tartari: a concentrated, oily solution of potassium carbonate</term>, for which a good quantity is required. The sunken powder is gray, which shall be separated from the salt water by filtering again, and then sweetened <note>original: afzoeten; the alchemical process of washing a precipitate with fresh water until all traces of salts or acids are removed</note> many times: the remaining powder is dried

## LXII. *Riverius’s Gilded Prep*, or *Glass of Gold*.
<note>original: Aureatum Riverii, oft Vitrum Auri. Lazare Rivière (Riverius) was a famous 17th-century physician whose formulas were widely copied.</note>

Take one ounce of leaf gold and four ounces of raw Antimony, mix them together, and put them in a small crucible; place them in the fire in such a way that they do not flow <note>melt too rapidly</note> and the *Regulus* <note>the metallic heart or purest part of the antimony</note> does not separate. When it has melted, let everything become cold and pound it fine; then calcine it <note>heat it to a powder without melting</note> again with a gentle fire, just as when one makes glass, stirring constantly with a small iron rod. The calcination is finished when the gold and antimony have become very white and no longer stick together at all, and give off no more smoke when placed upon the coals; then, according to the art, make a glass of it, which is the *Gilded Preparation* or *glass*.

It causes vomiting and softens the belly <note>acts as a laxative</note>; given in doses of two to five grains.

## LXIII. *Riverius’s Universal Liquid Panacea*.
<note>original: Panacæa Liquida Universalis Reverii. A 'panacea' is a substance claimed to be a cure-all for every ailment.</note>

Take one ounce of leaf gold and calcine it for eight hours in a circulating fire, adding *sulfur* <note>the alchemical principle of combustibility and soul</note> to it four times: then dilute it with warm water, dry it, and mix it with the *oil of antimony* <note>original: oleum antimonii; a caustic liquid made from antimony</note>, made in this manner.

Take **Regulus of Antimony** <note>original: Regulus Antimonii; the pure metallic heart of the antimony ore</note> and **Sublimated Mercury** <note>original: Mercurius sublimatus; mercury(II) chloride, a common alchemical reagent</note>, four ounces of each; mix them together in a mortar and distill them through a retort like an oil or **Butter of Antimony** <note>original: butyrum van Antimonie; antimony trichloride, which has a thick, buttery consistency</note>. Filter all these tinted spirits through blotting paper and distill them gently in a sand bath <note>original: in assche; literally "in ash," used for steady, gentle heating</note> until four ounces of tincture remain at the bottom of the retort.

## CHAPTER II.

## About SILVER.

### 1. The Purification of Silver from other Metals.

Through **immersion** <note>original: *immersie*</note>, one dissolves the silver in **strong water** <note>original: *sterk water*; nitric acid, which has the power to dissolve silver while leaving gold and other substances untouched</note>, which dissolves only the silver, while the other metals remain unaffected.

Through **fusion** <note>original: *Fusie*</note> or melting with **Saturn** <note>original: *Saturnus*; the alchemical name for lead</note>, one places the lead in a glowing **crucible** <note>original: *smelt-kroes*</note> so that it melts. Once it is molten, throw your silver upon it, maintaining the fire until the imperfect metals, together with the lead, partly evaporate into smoke through the power of the fire and partly remain as **dross** <note>original: *scorien*; waste matter or slag</note>, leaving only the silver at the bottom.

This requires a strong fire, for which a **blast furnace** <note>original: *wind-oven*; a furnace designed to reach high temperatures using a natural or forced draft of air</note> is necessary.

The lead, having now become a foam along with the residues of the silver, is called **litharge** <note>original: *Lithargirie*; lead(II) oxide, a byproduct of the refining process</note>.

One can also purify silver with **niter** <note>original: *Nitrum*; saltpeter</note> by melting the silver and then throwing the niter upon it in turns; in this way, the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver</note> shall be purified.

## II. *Calcination of Silver in various ways.*
<note>Calcination is the process of reducing a metal to a fine powder (a "calx") by heating or chemical action, often changing its chemical state.</note>

Through **immersion** <note>original: *Immersie*</note>, one dissolves the silver plates in a corrosive liquid, then causes it to thicken <note>original: *impisseren*</note> or precipitate, and finally washes it <note>original: *edulcoreren*; literally "to sweeten," meaning to wash away salts or acids with water until the residue is neutral</note>. The dissolved **Silver** <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver, associated with the moon</note> is precipitated by means of brine or salt water, or by throwing a small piece of copper into the solution.

This corrosive liquid is either **Royal Water** <note>original: *Aqua regia*; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, or **Spirit of Nitre** <note>original: *Spir. nitri*; nitric acid</note>, or some similar liquid. For this process, one may use three, four, six, or more parts of the liquid.

If one wishes to crystallize the solution in the common manner, one obtains the **crystals** or **Vitriol of the Moon** <note>original: *Vitriolum Lunæ*; silver nitrate crystals</note>.

The calcination through **Amalgamation** <note>original: *Amalgamatie*</note> is performed with pure **Silver** and **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> in equal parts. Take these and amalgamate them, mixing in a fourth part of **common salt** <note>original: *sal comm.*</note> or **vitriol** <note>sulfate minerals</note>; then let the mercury evaporate <note>original: *avoleren*; to fly away</note> through the action of the fire, and wash what remains.

Through **cementation** <note>a process of heating a solid metal with powdered chemicals to change its properties without melting it</note>, the work is done with **Vitriolated Tartar** <note>original: *Tartarus Vitriolatus*; potassium sulfate</note>, with **Rock Salt** <note>original: *Sal gemmæ*</note>, **Mercury**, **Common Salt**, etc.; and this must be worked without **fusion** <note>original: *fusie*; melting</note>.

### *By Way of Example.*

Take one part of silver plates and two parts of **sublimated mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius subblim.*; corrosive sublimate or mercury(II) chloride</note>. Let the mercury evaporate through the fire, and the **Silver** will remain behind like a **Resin** <note>original: *Resina*; referring to the sticky or waxy appearance of the resulting silver chloride or residue</note>.

In the same way, silver is cemented for 4, 5, 6, 7, or 8 hours with twice as much **Rock Salt**, or with four times as much **Common Salt**.

## III. *Another Way.*

Take filed **Silver** <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver</note>, one part, **flowers of sulfur** <note>original: *Flor. sulph.*; a fine powder of purified sulfur</note> two parts, **common salt** <note>original: *Salis comm.*</note> half a part. **Mix them.** <note>original: *Misce*</note> Sublimate this up to seven times, always adding the sublimated material back to the remaining substance; on the last time, discard the sublimate and wash the residue with water.

The **calcination of silver by cementation** <note>original: *Calcinatio Lunae cementatoria*; cementation is a process of heating a metal in a dry powder of other chemicals to change its properties</note> is also performed as mentioned above regarding **Potable Gold** <note>original: *Aurum Potabile*; a medicinal preparation of gold thought to have life-extending properties</note> with **spirit of salt of tartar** <note>original: *Spir. salis tartari*; a solution of potassium carbonate</note>.

When one desires to prepare it through **reverberation** <note>original: *reverberatie*; a process where a furnace reflects heat back onto the substance being heated</note>, do as follows: because **Silver** obeys the fire and calcination more easily than **Gold** <note>original: *Sol*; the alchemical name for gold</note>, it does not require further laborious reverberation. However, if one so chooses, he may further elaborate upon the calcined **Silver** and cement it several times at his own discretion with **sulfur** or **rock salt** <note>original: *sal gemmae*</note>, or with both sulfur and rock salt together, or with common salt and **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sal armoniak*; ammonium chloride</note> &c., and then free it of its saltiness by washing.

### *By way of example.*

Take silver calx <note>the powder resulting from calcination</note> made by **nitric acid** <note>original: *aqua fortis*</note>, one ounce; **common salt**, two ounces; **sal ammoniac**, two drachms. **Mix them**, and reverberate it for eight days.

### V. *Another [Way] using Tartarized Spirit of Wine.*

Take reverberated **Silver Calx** <note>original: *Calx Lunæ*; silver reduced to a fine powder through heat</note> (burnt with **Flowers of Sulfur** <note>original: *Flores Sulph.*; a purified powdered form of sulfur</note>); add to it the best **Tartarized Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Sp. Vini opt. Tartaris.*; alcohol distilled with potassium tartrate to increase its purity and strength</note>. Distill it off with seven **cohobations** <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its solid residue and re-distilling it</note>, so that the **Silver** melts; circulate for one month in a **water bath** <note>original: *B.M.* or *Balneum Mariae*; a gentle heating method using a vessel placed in boiling water</note>. Thus you have a **Tincture of Silver** that is blue.

### VI. *Another [Way] using Vitriolated Spirit of Wine.*

Take **calcined Silver**; as much as you wish. Extract a blue tincture with **Vitriolated Spirit of Wine** <note>alcohol treated with sulfuric acid or vitriol</note> (see under "wine"); decant and distill off. 
This is better than the others for **Epilepsy**.

### VII. *Basilian Tincture of Silver.*

Take **Common Salt** calcined with an equal weight of **Quicklime**, likewise the **Silver Calx**. Now also make a **Strong Water** <note>original: *Aqua Fortis*; nitric acid</note> from **Vitriol** and **Saltpeter** in equal parts.

->*Further.*<-

Then take the **Silver Calx** and mix it with the **Common Salt** that has been calcined with the **Quicklime**; put it in a vial glass, pour the **Strong Water** over it, distill it off and cohobate it up to three times, increasing the fire for the last time so that the substance in the glass melts. Thus you obtain a transparent **Silver**, from which one extracts a tincture with **Strong Distilled Vinegar** <note>original: *Acet. Dest. Fort.*</note> according to the rules of the art, as blue as **ultramarine** <note>a deep blue pigment historically made from lapis lazuli</note>.

### VIII. Salt and Tincture of Silver by Blancard.
<note>Steven Blankaart (1650–1702) was a Dutch physician and chemist known for his work in anatomy and his dictionary of medicine.</note>

Armon.*; an aqueous solution of ammonia</note>, one ounce; **Silver** made into thin plates, one ounce. And, if one desires the **Salt** or **Crystals**, evaporate it until a film appears, and place it in the cellar to crystallize.

### IX. Potable Silver by S. Cloß.
<note>Samuel Closset (S. Cloß) was a chemical author whose recipes for "potable" or drinkable metals were highly regarded in early modern medicine.</note>

First calcine the silver plates several times with **Sulfur**, and extract the **vitriol** <note>here referring to a soluble metallic salt</note> from them by washing; this is then to be dissolved in the **Compound Spirit** of **Common Saltpeter** <note>original: *Sal Comm. Separate the **dregs** <note>original: *feces*; the solid waste or residue</note> through digestion, bringing the blue tincture to a powder. From this, one can extract the true tincture using **Spirit of Wine**, which is useful against **epilepsy**.

### XI. Basilian Salt of Silver.
<note>original title: *Sal Lunæ Basilianum*. Refers to Basilius Valentinus, a legendary alchemist.</note>

### XIII. Lunar Spirit of S. Closset.
<note>original: *Spir. Lunaris S. Cloſſæi*. Samuel Closset was a 17th-century physician and chemist known for his pharmaceutical recipes.</note>

First one must make the **Silver Vitriol** <note>original: *Vitriolum Lunæ*; a salt formed by the action of sulfuric acid on silver</note>, which is done through **Sulfur** in the same way as **Copper Vitriol** <note>original: *Vitriolum veneris*</note>, but it requires at least 20 repeated **calcinations** <note>original: *calcinatien*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</note>. One can best make it from very fine silver filings, with three ounces of **water of lilies of the valley** <note>original: *Aqua liliorum convall.*</note>, strengthened with an ounce of **spirit of copper vitriol** <note>original: *ſpir. vitrioli ven.*</note> or with **distilled vinegar** <note>original: *acetum deſtill.*</note>. By leaving that to **digest** <note>original: *digereren*; heating gently over a long period</note> for a month in the ashes <note>referring to a sand or ash bath used to provide steady, indirect heat</note>, the **Spirit of Venus** [Copper] will be impregnated with the **Silver Tincture** <note>original: *Tinctura Lunæ*</note>, which is blue-green. When this has been drawn off, one adds other spirit of copper vitriol to it, which one extracts as often as necessary until nearly all the silver is dissolved. Then evaporate all the solutions until a film appears on top, and collect the crystals.

Once these are dried, they are placed in a **retort** <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, and one distills in the common manner, first the **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, tasteless distillate</note> from it, and the **spirit of Venus** [copper], which one shall separate alone; but after that, giving a greater fire, the **spirit of the moon** [silver] comes, and finally the **Oil**.
It is believed that this cures **Epilepsy** to the very root.

## XVIII. **Essence of Silver**
<note>original: *Essentia Lunæ*; in alchemy, the Moon (Luna) symbolizes silver</note>

Take the lime of silver <note>original: *kalk van zilver*; a "calx" or metal powder produced by calcination or precipitation</note>, which is dissolved in **strong water** <note>original: *Aqua fortis*; nitric acid</note>, and in the common manner of goldsmiths, precipitated to the bottom in a copper vessel, which is very white.

## XIX. **Magistery of Silver**
<note>original: *Magisterium Lunæ*; a "magistery" refers to a master-preparation where the "virtue" of a substance is concentrated into a solid form</note>

Take silver spread into very thin plates, and then rolled into little rolls, as much as you please: **strong water** <note>original: *Aqua fortis*; nitric acid</note> as much as is enough.
Then pour the **oil of tartar** <note>original: *Liquor tartari*; a saturated solution of potassium carbonate</note> into the solution. The sunken powder is washed and sweetened <note>original: *afgesoet*; the process of washing away corrosive salts with water until the substance is no longer acrid</note>.
One must pour much oil of tartar upon it before the proper precipitation is obtained, for in this way the corrosive salts are fended off, and then the precipitate can be sweetened with fresh water: for otherwise the taste is unpleasant, and it is black on top. It then also causes nausea and loathing.
It is useful in ailments of the head, five or six grains given with some suitable liquid.

## XX. Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar of the Moon (Silver).
<note>original: *Magisterium tartari Vitriolati Lunare*; in alchemy, the Moon (Luna) refers to silver. Vitriolated tartar is potassium sulfate.</note>

This is made in exactly the same way as the **Magistery of vitriolated tartar of the Sun** (Gold) described previously; for one takes **fixed silver** <note>original: *Luna fixa*; silver that has been chemically treated to remain stable in fire</note> dissolved in **strong water** <note>original: *Aqua fortis*; nitric acid</note>, and precipitated with **oil of tartar** <note>original: *Liquor tartari*; a saturated solution of potassium carbonate</note>, and washed until sweet <note>original: *afgesoet*; the process of rinsing away residual acids with water</note>, one part. **Vitriolated tartar**, three parts; once crushed, these are mixed in the same manner, and having been calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to create a powder</note>, it is kept until use.

The powers [of this medicine] are for the head, epilepsy, dizziness <note>original: *hooftswymel*</note>, dropsy <note>original: *water-sugt*; an old term for swelling or edema</note>, etc. Administered in doses of five to eight grains with some meat broth or wine in the morning.

## XXI. Lunar Sublimated Mercury.
<note>original: *Mercurius Sublimatus Lunaris*; a compound combining mercury and silver through sublimation.</note>

Take **sweet mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius dulcis*; mercurous chloride, also known as calomel</note>, which has been sublimated <note>a process where a solid is heated to a gas and then collected as it solidifies again to purify it</note> three times, six ounces; **leaf silver**, two ounces; let it all be rubbed together, mixed, and sublimated in a sand-bath; once everything has cooled, separate the volatile part, and crush the solid and crystallized part, and mix it with the dregs <note>original: *Faeces*</note> that were left behind; sublimate up to three times, as before, and finally wash it. It purges gently, the **dosage** <note>original: *Doris*; likely a printer's error for *Dosis*</note> being from six to eight or ten grains.

### XXIII. Hell-stone, or Silver Caustic.
<note>original: *Lapis Infernalis, ofte Silvere Causticum*; silver nitrate. This is a highly corrosive substance used in medicine to burn away tissue. Note: the text jumps from item XXI to XXIII.</note>

Take one part silver and three parts **spirit of nitre** <note>original: *Spir. Nitri*; nitric acid</note>. Place it in a **sand bath** <note>original: *in 't sand*; a container of sand heated from below to provide even, controlled temperature</note> and allow two-thirds of it to evaporate. While the remainder is still warm, pour it into a large **German crucible** <note>original: *duitse kroes*; Hessian crucibles were famous for their ability to withstand extreme heat and chemical reactions</note> that is quite wide, because the mixture will boil up. Place it then over a small fire and let it evaporate there until the substance, which will be very airy, sinks to the bottom. Gradually increase the fire, and the substance will become like an oil. Then pour it out into little molds that have been greased, and it will begin to **solidify** <note>original: *stremmen*</note>. This must then be kept in a narrow and tightly sealed glass, for if the air reaches it, it melts immediately <note>it is deliquescent, meaning it absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves</note>.

This serves to open fistulas and to eat away **proud flesh** <note>original: *quaad vleis*; unhealthy or granulated tissue in a wound</note>.

### XXIV. *The Tree of Diana, or the Silver Tree.*
<note>original: *Den Arbor Dianæ, ofte Silvere Boom*. In alchemy, Diana is the goddess associated with the Moon, which in turn represents the metal silver. The "Tree of Diana" is a famous chemical demonstration where silver crystals precipitate out of a solution in a branching, tree-like structure.</note>

Take one part silver and three parts **spirit of nitre** <note>original: *Spiritus Nitri*; nitric acid</note>. Once they are dissolved together, put the solution into a flask containing a pint of rainwater and two parts mercury—proportional to the silver—inside it. The flask must be full up to the neck; then let it stand still on a straw ring for fourteen days. Little by little, a tree will come forth with fine branches and small spheres, just as if they were fruits.

### XXV. *Green Silver Crystals of Tachenius.*
<note>original: *Crÿstalli Lunæ Virides Tackii*. "Luna" (the Moon) refers to silver. "Tackii" likely refers to Otto Tachenius, a famous 17th-century chemist and apothecary known for his work on salts.</note>

Take **saltpeter** <note>potassium nitrate</note> that has been prepared by art from **lime** <note>original: *Calx*; calcium oxide</note> and **common salt** <note>original: *Sal Commune*; sodium chloride</note>. From this, make a strong **lye** <note>an alkaline solution</note> in which you allow the silver to dissolve. After it has been evaporated somewhat, place it in the cellar to crystallize.

### XXVI. *Blue Silver Crystals.*
<note>original: *Crÿstalli Lunæ Ceruleæ*. While silver nitrate crystals are typically clear, impurities like copper (often found in "fine silver" of the era) would turn the solution and the resulting crystals blue.</note>

Dissolve your fine silver in **spirit of nitre** <note>nitric acid</note>, filter the solution, evaporate it, and let it crystallize according to the art.

But before one begins to do this, one first lets the silver plates be smoked with **mercury** <note>original: *quiksilver*</note> for four or five hours, until a portion of the mercury remains clinging to them; then one hangs them over vinegar <note>original: *asijn*</note> for fourteen or fifteen days, and then one shall scrape the *ultramarine* <note>While usually referring to lapis lazuli, here the term refers to a blue pigment produced chemically from silver</note> off the plates, and smoke them again.

## XXIX. **Musician's Silver**
<note>original: *Argentum Musicum*; a metallic pigment used for silvering wood, bone, or paper</note>

Take one and a half ounces of good tin; put it into a strong crucible. When it is about to melt, add one and a half ounces of **silver marcasite** <note>original: *Marcasita Argentina*; likely bismuth or a similar silvery mineral ore used to provide a metallic luster</note> to it, and mix it together with a small iron rod.
Take the crucible out of the fire and let it cool a little; then add six drachms of mercury <note>original: *quiksilver*</note> that has been heated on the fire until it begins to crackle. Pour the substance out onto a cold stone and afterwards grind it to powder on a stone.

## XXX. **Riverius's Tincture of the Moon**
<note>original: *Tinctura Lunæ Riverii*; a medicinal preparation named after the 17th-century French physician Lazare Rivière. In alchemy, the "Moon" (Luna) corresponds to Silver.</note>

Dissolve cupelled silver <note>silver purified by heating in a shallow vessel to remove base metals</note> in **aqua fortis** <note>nitric acid</note>, and precipitate it with **oil of tartar** <note>original: *Oleum tartari*; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note>; wash it with common water and dry it. Then extract the tincture with the same liquids as described in the **tincture of gold of Riverius**, and dissolve it again in that manner.
It is useful for diseases of the head, chronic epilepsy, dizziness, paralysis, consumption, pulmonary tuberculosis, etc.

## III. C H A P T E R.

# Of IRON or STEEL.

### I. Of the Grading-Purification of Iron to make Steel.

Take iron plates or rods, the thickness of a middle finger, one part. Powder of willow or beech-tree charcoal; <term>shavings of horn</term> <note>original: *rasur. cornu*</note>, one part, make a <term>stratification</term> <note>a process of arranging materials in alternating layers</note>, and place them in a strong fire in a closed vessel in a <term>wind-furnace</term> <note>a furnace that uses a natural or forced draft to reach high temperatures</note> for four or six hours.

### II. <term>Obstructive Saffron of Mars</term> <note>original: *Crocus Martis Obstructivus*; a red iron oxide powder used in both alchemy and medicine. "Mars" is the alchemical name for iron.</note>.

**R**everberate <note>to heat in a furnace where the flames are turned back or deflected onto the material</note> the iron filings in a very strong fire for so long, until they change into a light and very red <term>saffron</term> <note>original: *crocus*; refers to the color and fine texture of the powder</note>.

Common salt has the power to hasten the reverberation. Therefore, there are those who first sprinkle the filings of iron with <term>children’s urine</term> <note>original: *kinder-pis*; a common source of ammonia and nitrogen in early chemistry</note>, salt water, or vinegar, dry them again, and thereafter reverberate them. In this way, <term>Mars</term> <note>Iron</note> shall rise in the time of a day or two in a very red <term>flower</term> <note>original: *flos*; a fine powder produced by sublimation or chemical reaction</note>, which must be gathered daily, so that the same does not become black from the fire or become lost.

If any part should not yet be well calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, and you wish to separate it further, pour water over it,

### III. *Opening Saffron of Mars.*

This opens and **attenuates** <note>original: *attenuëert*; to thin or refine thickened bodily humors</note>.

# IV. *A calcination by cementation, from which Vitriol of Mars is made.*
<note>calcination is the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder; cementation involves layering a metal with other substances—in this case, sulfur—and heating it so they react.</note>

Take plates or filings of **Mars** <note>iron</note>, cement them with sulfur powder, bringing the fire to it gradually for one hour; thus the **Mars** will be <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a crumbly oxide or sulfide</note> once the sulfur has ignited. Then remove the material, crush it fine, and calcine it again on its own (just as one calcines **Antimony** in the preparation of **Glass of Antimony**) <note>a translucent, reddish substance used as an emetic</note> so that the **Sulfur** burns away entirely, stirring constantly until the iron clumps together.

Then take one pound of this calcined and ground iron and half an ounce of **Sulfur**, mix them well together, and calcine again for a quarter of an hour; then add as much **Sulfur** again, which is repeated up to five times or more. From this <term>calx</term> <note>the powdery remains of a metal after heating</note> one then makes the **Vitriol of Mars** <note>iron sulfate, often used as a tonic</note>.

# V. *Another way.*

Take iron plates, cement them with **Sulfur** and **Tartar** <note>original: *tartari*; potassium bitartrate</note> in equal parts of each, and remove the **Saffron** <note>original: *Crocus*; a fine iron oxide powder</note> that remains clinging to the plates.

## IX. *Calcination by Vapor.*

Take iron plates and hang them above a flask containing **strong water** <note>original: *sterk water*; nitric acid</note>; place this in warm sand. Through the power of the vapors, the **Saffron** <note>original: *Crocus*; a fine metallic oxide powder</note> will cling to the plates, which one can wipe off with a hare's foot <note>a traditional soft brush used by early chemists and artists</note>. This can be repeated several times.

## X. *Calcination by Coating.*

Take iron plates and coat them with **Oil of Sulfur** <note>original: *Oleum sulphuris*</note> or **Oil of Vitriol** <note>original: *Oleum vitrioli*; concentrated sulfuric acid</note>; or sprinkle iron filings with the same, and place them in a cellar <note>the damp environment of a cellar encouraged the metal to oxidize or react with the acid</note>. Then wash it with water, and the **Saffron** will sink to the bottom; calcine this a little until it turns red. 
It is useful for **cachexia** <note>a state of physical wasting and weakness</note> and is very "opening" <note>an "opening" medicine was believed to clear obstructions in the organs, particularly the liver and spleen</note>. The dose is three to four grains. In the same manner, one also makes **Saffron of Mars** <note>original: *Crocus Martis*; medicinal iron oxide</note> with **Spirit of Alum**, **Sal Ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>, **Niter** <note>saltpeter</note>, etc.; however, these Saffrons may only be used externally.

## XI. *Another Way of Making Saffron.*

Take **Strong Water** <note>original: *Aquafortis*</note> made from equal parts of calcined vitriol and common salt distilled with potter's clay; pour this into an iron spoon so that it evaporates. Immediately, the **Saffron** will remain, which one should scrape off and preserve in a glass, as it melts <term>by deliquescence</term> <note>meaning it absorbs moisture from the air and turns into a liquid</note> easily.

## XII. Another by Doctor S. Blankaart.
<note>Steven Blankaart (1650–1702) was a prominent Dutch physician and chemist who advocated for the use of chemical medicines in his practice.</note>

Take iron filings, spread them out on a large dish, sprinkle them with water, let them stand thus for several days and nights in the open air, occasionally sprinkling them; once it has become hard, crush it fine, pour water upon it, let the coarse parts sink, and then pour off the cloudy water in which the finest <term>Crocus</term> <note>original: *Crocus*; a fine powder, usually a metallic oxide, named for its saffron-like color</note> is found, and do this several times; your fine powder having settled, dry that, and <term>reverberate</term> <note>original: *reverbereert*; to heat a substance in a furnace where the flames are directed or "reverberated" back onto the material</note> it for an hour or two in the fire; in this way, you will have good <term>Crocus</term>. ## XXVI. Tincture of Mars by Basilius.
<note>Likely referring to Basilius Valentinus, a semi-mythical 15th-century alchemist famous for his work with metals and salts</note>

Dissolve iron filings in one part **Red Spirit of Vitriol** <note>original: *Spir. Vitriol, Rubr.*; a concentrated acid produced by distilling iron sulfates</note> and two parts **Spring Water** <note>original: *Aqua font.*</note>. Filter it while warm and crystallize it according to the art <note>the 'art' refers to standard chemical procedures of the time</note>. Dry the crystals under a crucible, stirring constantly, and you will have a purple <term>saffron</term> <note>original: *crocus*; in alchemy, a fine powder produced by heating a metal, usually an oxide</note>. Pour **distilled vinegar** over this and extract [the essence] according to the art. Then <term>abstract</term> <note>remove the liquid by evaporation or distillation</note> the moisture in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: *b. m.* or *balneum mariae*; a vessel of hot water used for gentle heating</note>. Then wash it with spring water, drawing the liquid off from time to time.

In the same way, one can make this from **Vitriol of Mars** <note>iron sulfate</note> that has been <term>reverberated</term> <note>heated in a furnace where the flame is reflected down onto the substance</note> until it is a very deep red; from this, one draws the **Tincture** or **Sulfur** <note>the 'sulfur' of a metal was considered its internal combustible or oily principle</note> by adding **Distilled Vinegar** <note>original: *Acet. Dest.*</note>. When this vinegar is drawn off, it leaves behind a red powder.

From the remaining <term>Earth</term> <note>original: *Terra*; the solid residue left after the extraction of the "spirit" and "soul"</note>, one draws the **Common Salt** <note>original: *Sal Comm.*</note> by adding **Corrosive Honey Water** <note>original: *Aqua Mellis Corrosiva*; a distilled solvent made from honey and often acidic additives</note>.

## XXVII. Another Tincture of Mars from the blue Slag or Dross of iron.
<note>original: *Scoriæ*; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note>

Crush the blue glassy slag or dross of the iron (otherwise <term>calcine</term> <note>heat to high temperature without melting to cause oxidation</note> it for 24 hours); then extract a red tincture from it with **distilled vinegar**. Filter and then abstract it; <term>edulcorate</term> <note>to wash a substance to remove salts or impurities</note> the remaining tincture several times with rainwater. This tincture melts <note>deliquesces, or turns to liquid by absorbing moisture from the air</note> of its own accord when placed in a cellar. It is more powerful if one draws the solution of the tincture out with **Spirit of Wine** <note>alcohol</note> and repeats the extraction again. It is much more powerful than the common Saffron of Mars made through reverberation.

It stops all fluxes <note>excessive or abnormal flows of bodily fluids</note>, such as excessive **menstruation** <note>original: *maandvloed*</note>, **nocturnal emissions** <note>original: *Saadvloed*; spermatorrhea</note>, **dysentery**, **diarrhea**, and **hemorrhages**, etc.

## XXVIII. Another Tincture of Mars from the Flowers of Mars.

**T**ake the **Saffron of Mars** <note>original: *Crocus Martis*; a fine red powder of iron oxide</note> produced by <term>reverberation</term> <note>heating a substance in a furnace where the flame is reflected downward onto it</note>; <term>sublime</term> <note>to heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again as a purified crust</note> it with **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sal armoniak*; ammonium chloride</note>. From these <term>edulcorated</term> <note>washed with water to remove salts or acids</note> **Flowers** <note>original: *Flores*; the crystalline sublimate produced during heating</note>, extract a tincture with **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Spir. Vini*; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note>. When this has been drawn off again, an **Essence** remains at the bottom—

## XXIX. Tincture of Mars from its own Calx.

**T**ake iron filings from which **sal ammoniac** has been distilled six or more times; extract these with **Spirit of Wine**, <term>decant</term> <note>to pour off the clear liquid while leaving the sediment behind</note>, and <term>abstract</term> <note>to remove a liquid by evaporation or distillation</note>, <term>cohobating</term> <note>the process of pouring the distilled liquid back onto the solid residue and re-distilling it to intensify the extraction</note> several times. Before the extraction, this powder can be <term>resolved</term> into a moisture <note>melted or dissolved into a liquid state</note>; once washed with water, this can also be administered internally.

## XXX. Another way.

**S**prinkle your well-<term>calcined</term> <note>burned to a powder or "calx" through high heat</note> **Saffron of Mars** with as much **Spirit of Vitriol** <note>original: *Spir. Vitroili*; sulfuric acid</note> as you please; <term>digest</term> <note>to soften or treat a substance with gentle, steady heat</note> it in warm sand until the Spirit is dried out. Then rub your material on a marble stone with **spring water**, <term>macerate</term> <note>to soak in liquid to soften or extract components</note> it in warm sand for three days, then filter it through paper. Thicken the result and extract the tincture with **Spirit of Wine**.
