### XXXI. Another Tincture, Manna of Mars.

**T**ake a good portion of steel filings, extract with the **Alkalized Spirit of Iron** <note>original: *Spiritus Martis Alcalisatus*</note>, filter, and <term>abstract</term> <note>to remove a liquid by evaporation or distillation, leaving the essence behind</note>.

### XXXII. The Kiss of Mars and Venus, or the Extemporaneous Tincture of S. Clowes.
<note>original: *Basium Martis en Veneris*; "Mars" refers to iron and "Venus" to copper. S. Closs likely refers to the physician Samuel Clossius.</note>

**M**ake a **vitriol** <note>a sulfate salt</note> out of **verdigris** <note>original: *spaans groen*; the green pigment or rust that forms on copper</note>: drive that through the <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> in the sand <note>a sand bath, used to provide even, indirect heat</note> until all the **Phlegm** <note>original: *Phlegma*; the watery, inactive part of a distillate</note> and **Volatile Spirit** are out of it. Pour that onto the steel filings in a narrow-necked flask; thus, in a quarter of an hour without fire, the **Venus** <note>copper</note> shall be impregnated with the **blood of Mars** <note>iron</note>. Abstract the phlegm, and pour **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Spir. Vini*; high-proof alcohol</note> onto the fusible **Saffron** <note>original: *Crocus*; a fine powder, usually an oxide, created through heat</note>, and extract it again.

### XXXIII. Sugared Salt and the Tincture of the Same Mars.

**P**our onto the **Saffron of Mars** <note>iron oxide powder</note>—which is made with sulfur—the water that remained after the precipitation of the **Butter of Antimony** <note>original: *Butyrum antimonii*; a chemical compound used in alchemy, often antimony trichloride</note> (which is called **Philosophical Spirit of Vitriol**) together with its **Phlegm**. (But for lack of that, use the **Diuretic Vitriolated Spirit of Common Salt** <note>original: *Spir. Sal. Comm. Vitriolat. Diuret.*</note> as shall be described hereafter.) Thus one extracts the yellow tincture in the sand bath; it has a sulfurous stench which immediately vanishes. Filter and <term>coagulate</term> <note>to thicken or solidify a liquid into a solid mass</note> it into a **Common Salt** that is as sweet as sugar, which is <term>circulated</term> <note>the process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel to "refine" the substance</note> so that it may have greater powers.

### XXXIV. *Red Tincture of Mars.*
<note>"Mars" is the alchemical name for Iron.</note>

**L**ayer thin iron plates with pumice stone, and **reverberate** <note>to heat in a furnace where the flames are turned back or deflected onto the material</note> them for 24 hours; thus the pumice stone shall become red, from which one draws the tincture with **Distilled Vinegar** <note>original: *Acetum Destill.*</note>: which can then be **coagulated** <note>solidified by evaporation</note> into a red Salt.

### XXXV. *The following pertains to Calcination by Reverberation.*

**C**alcine the iron filings without any preparation or admixture in a **reverberatory fire** <note>a high-heat furnace</note>, until it has changed from a deep red color into a white **calx** <note>a powder produced by roasting ore or metal</note>. This is administered in white wine in doses up to half a **drachm** <note>a unit of weight, approx. 3.9 grams</note>, which has been used successfully in cases of **ischuria** <note>original: *Ischuirie*; a medical condition where one is unable to pass urine</note>.

### XXXVI. *The Whitest Tincture or Magistery of Mars.*

### XXXVIII. *Flowers of Iron from Crystals*.

**Sublime** the crystals of **Iron** (made with **Nitrous Aqua Fortis** <note>original: *Aqua Fortis Nitrosa*; a strong nitric acid solution</note>) with sal ammoniac; in this way, you will obtain red **Flowers**, which one shall **sweeten** <note>wash</note>.

They **break up** <note>original: *incideren*; to cut into or thin thick humors</note> and **open** <note>original: *aperieren*; to clear blockages</note> all stubborn obstructions of the intestines and the womb.

### Another method.

Extract the tincture from the **calx** <note>a powder produced by heating a metal; an oxide</note> or **Saffron of Mars** <note>original: *Crocus Martis*; a reddish-brown iron oxide powder</note> (which is made with **Royal Water** <note>original: *Aqua Regia*; a highly corrosive mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>) using water; filter and **coagulate** <note>to thicken a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state</note>, and then set it aside to crystallize, or simply thicken it. ### XLI. Basil’s Salt of Iron.
<note>original: *Sal Martis Basilianum*; likely referring to the methods of the legendary alchemist Basilius Valentinus</note>

Pour the **Corrosive Honey Water** <note>original: *Aqua Mellis Corrosiva*</note> onto the material that remained from the preparation of the tincture (such as the **Tincture of Basil** <note>original: *Tinctura Basilii*</note>), and then extract the common salt according to the art. Then draw off the Honey Water and **sweeten** <note>original: *edulcoreert*; to wash a substance with water to remove acids or salts</note> with spring water. Draw off again through distillation, and finally clarify with **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Spir. Vini*; ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note>. The Dose is 6, 7, 8, etc. **grains** <note>a traditional unit of weight based on a grain of cereal, roughly 65 milligrams</note>.

## XLIII. *Salt of Iron from Dissolved Iron.*
<note>original: *Sal Martis Ex Soluto Marte*</note>

Dissolve the ***iron filings*** <note>original: *Limatura Martis*</note> with one part ***Red Oil of Vitriol*** <note>original: *Ol. Vitrioli Rubr.*; concentrated sulfuric acid</note> and two parts ***Aqua Fortis*** <note>original: *Aqua Fort.*; nitric acid</note>. Filter it while it is still warm and let it crystallize. The same can also be achieved using other sharp, acidic liquids.

## XLIV. *Purgative Salt of Iron.*
<note>original: *Sal Martis Purgans*</note>

Mix equal parts of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note> and iron filings together, grinding them on a marble stone. Then **sublime** <note>to heat a solid until it transforms into a vapor and then solidifies again upon cooling</note> them in a stone flask, first with a gentle fire and then with a stronger one, increasing the heat gradually by degrees. Once it has cooled, keep the topmost white substance to use in a new sublimation with filings. Also keep the middle substance, which is saffron-colored (this being the ***Diaphoretic Flowers of Iron*** <note>original: *Flores Martis Diaphoretici*; a preparation intended to induce sweating or perspiration</note>). But as for the ***Dead Head*** <note>original: *Caput Mortuum*; the residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</note>, dissolve it and extract a salt from it in the common manner; this is purified by repeatedly dissolving and **coagulating** <note>thickening or solidifying a liquid</note> it, and then store it tightly sealed. It is administered in doses of ten to twenty **grains** <note>a historical unit of measurement; one grain is approximately 65 milligrams</note>.

## XLV. *Liquor of Iron.*
<note>original: *Liquor Martis*</note>

The ***Liquor of Iron*** <note>original: *Liquor Martis*</note> is made from the ***Saffron of Mars*** <note>original: *Crocus*; a reddish-brown iron oxide</note> that has been produced through a moist **calcination** <note>heating a substance to high temperatures to change its chemical structure</note> and then set to melt. This serves as a liquor or balsam for treating wounds.

## XLVI. Tincture or Essence of Iron
<note>original: *Tinctura ofte Essentia Martis*</note>
### by Riverius.
<note>original: *Riverii*; referring to Lazare Rivière (1589–1655), a prominent French physician and professor.</note>

Take **iron filings**, place them in a crucible, and let them become glowing hot; then quench them in **distilled vinegar**. Repeat this thirty times or more. Then let the filings boil in that vinegar, and filter it while warm through a piece of blotting paper. Dry the filings, heat them to a glow again, and quench them once more in new distilled vinegar, as before; let it boil and filter again. After you have done this three times, you shall distill the filtered vinegars until they are dry. Pour over the residue as much **spirit of wine** <note>original: *Spiritus vini*; ethanol</note>—which has been well rectified and alkalized—as is enough to dissolve the tincture. Let it **digest** <note>to soften or extract using gentle heat over time</note> for eight days. When the spirit is then separated, the tincture will remain at the bottom.

This is a **cordial** <note>a medicine that stimulates the heart and improves spirits</note>, **astringent** <note>a substance that shrinks or constricts body tissues</note>, and **opening** <note>a "deobstruent" meant to clear blockages in the body’s "passages" or vessels</note> medicine. It is used primarily for the **red flux** <note>original: *roode loop*; dysentery</note>, common **diarrhea** <note>original: *buik-loop*</note>, **lientery** <note>original: *spys-loop*; a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note>, immoderate **menstruation** <note>original: *vrouwe-loop*</note>, **white flux** <note>original: *witte vloed*; leucorrhea</note>, **spermatorrhea** <note>original: *saad loop*</note>, spitting blood, nosebleeds, etc.

It heals wounds in a short time, cleanses them, and dries them. It is administered in doses of twenty to thirty **grains** <note>a traditional unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams</note> with a suitable cordial.

Add to this two parts of **chalk** <note>original: *Creta*</note>, and make with that—

### XLVIII. *Tincture of the Sweet Salt of Iron by Lancilot.*
<note>original: *Tinctura Sal Saccharinum Martis van Lancilot*; referring to Carlo Lancillotti, a 17th-century Italian chemist known for popularizing pharmaceutical recipes.</note>

Take <term>Crocus martis</term> <note>iron oxide</note> prepared with sulfur, as much as you please; pour onto it the water that remains after the precipitation of the <term>Algaroth powder</term> <note>original: *Pulvis algarot*; an emetic and purgative powder made from antimony</note>, or otherwise the water that remains after the precipitation of the <term>sweat-inducing tin</term> <note>original: *stagnum sudoriferum*</note>, described by him under the name of <term>butter of Jupiter</term> <note>original: *Butyrum jovis*; tin(IV) chloride</note>. Or, in its place, use the <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid</note> made with salt (as described in the previous chapter); let the liquid stand two fingers’ breadth above the solids, then digest in a warm place until the tincture has passed into the <term>menstruum</term> <note>the solvent used for extraction</note>; pour it off, filter, and **coagulate** <note>to thicken or solidify by evaporation</note>.

If one pours <term>spirit of wine</term> over this and **circulates** <note>a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</note> it for seven or eight days, a yellow tincture is obtained.

### XLIX. *Starry Regulus of Mars* by Lancilotti.
<note>original: *Regulus Martis Stellatus Lancilotti*. Carlo Lancillotti was a 17th-century chemist. In alchemy, a "Regulus" is the metallic heart of a mineral, and "Mars" refers to iron.</note>

## LVI. Fulminating Mars, or Thundering Iron.
<note>original: *Mars Fulminans*. "Fulminating" refers to the explosive or highly reactive nature of the compound.</note>

Dissolve iron filings in **royal water** <note>original: *Aqua Regia*; a highly corrosive mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, pour into the solution **oil of tartar made by deliquescence** <note>original: *Oleum tartari per deliquium*; a liquid form of potassium carbonate created by letting the salt absorb moisture from the air</note>; thus the iron shall precipitate, which one must sweeten <note>wash with water to remove residual salts</note> and dry.

## LVII. Martial Bezoar.
<note>original: *Bezoardicum Martiale*. In early medicine, a "bezoar" was a stone-like substance believed to be a universal antidote; alchemists created "chemical bezoars" from metals like iron (Mars) and antimony.</note>

The **Martial Bezoar** is made from the **martial regulus of antimony** <note>original: *Regulus Antimonii Martialis*; a metallic form of antimony produced by reducing the ore with iron</note>, which is distilled into a **butter** <note>original: *Butyrum*; specifically butter of antimony, a thick, oily liquid</note>, and precipitated with **spirit of nitre** <note>original: *Spiritus nitri*; nitric acid</note>.
**Rolfinkius** <note>Werner Rolfinck (1599–1673), a notable German physician and chemist</note> describes it thus: Take **martial regulus of antimony** and **sublimated mercury**, equal parts of each; distill the **butter** from them through the retort. Dissolve, precipitate, and fix <note>to make a substance non-volatile</note> with **spirit of nitre**, cohobate <note>redistill the liquid over the solid residue</note> three times through the **alembic** <note>a distillation apparatus</note>, and bring the remainder into a red chalk <note>a red powder</note> in a crucible by means of the **fire of the wheel** <note>original: *Ignis Rotæ*; a circular fire built around the vessel</note>.
It is useful in all **hypochondriacal passions** <note>original: *Hypochondriaque passien*; a 17th-century term for digestive distress, melancholy, or ailments of the organs in the upper abdomen</note>, given in doses of three to five grains with some suitable liquid or wine.

## LIX. Essence of Mars of Hartmann.
<note>original: *Eſſentia Martis Hartmanni*. Johann Hartmann (1568–1631) was a famous German chemist and physician known for his iatrochemical (chemical medicine) approach.</note>

# LXV. Astringent Tincture of Iron
<note>original: *Tinctura Martis Astringens*. In alchemy, "Mars" is the traditional symbol and name for the metal iron.</note>

Take a quarter pound of **iron filings** and half a pound of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride, a salt used as a catalyst in alchemical reactions</note>; sublimate these in a glass vial over a sand bath. First, set aside all the white **flowers** <note>original: *Flores*; the powdery substance that gathers at the top of a vessel during heating</note>, and then the yellow ones, which should also be kept separately and protected from moist air, otherwise they will melt. Furthermore, collect the black ones separately; these melt when exposed to the air and produce a very **astringent** <note>tissue-contracting</note> tincture, which one dilutes with other fluids.

It stops **hemorrhaging** <note>uncontrolled bleeding</note> when taken in doses of one to two grains in any suitable liquid.

# LXVI. Paracelsus's Lily from Iron
<note>original: *Lilium Paracelsi uyt Mars*. A "Lily" in alchemy refers to a perfected medicinal tincture or essence. Paracelsus (c. 1493–1541) was a pioneer of using chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>

Take **Regulus of Iron** <note>original: *Regulus Martis*; a metallic mass produced by smelting iron with antimony</note> prepared according to the art; dissolve it in a sufficient quantity of **Aqua Fortis** <note>nitric acid</note> and **Spirit of Salt** <note>hydrochloric acid</note>, taking an equal amount of each. Pour onto this solution the **Sulphur** <note>here referring to an oily extract or essence</note> extracted by boiling from the **slag of antimony**, until the precipitation is complete; this will be yellowish-red. **Sweeten** it <note>original: *edulcoreert*; the process of washing away acids or salts with water</note> and save it for fine use, administered in doses of four to six grains.

It causes strong vomiting, but to master or control this effect, do the following:

## LXVII. Potable Mars or Drinkable Iron
<note>In the alchemical tradition, "Mars" is the name and symbol for the metal iron.</note>

Take steel filings that have been ground very fine, and an equal amount of very white, raw Rhenish tartar <note>original: *rinfche tarter*; potassium bitartrate, a crystalline salt found in wine barrels, used here as a solvent</note>, and enough filtered rainwater to make marbles from them. Dry these little balls or marbles in the sun, and then place them in the oven until the bread is done baking. Grind them back into a powder and make marbles out of it again with the aforementioned water, and let them dry in the oven once more. Repeat this operation as many times as necessary until you find that the substance is soluble in all kinds of fluids.

In rainwater, it is administered by the spoonful; otherwise, in powder form, one gives from six to twenty grains.

## LXVIII. Another Method

Take one part of pure iron filings and two parts of **Flowers of Sulfur** <note>original: *Flores Sulphuris*; a fine, bright yellow powder obtained through the sublimation of natural sulfur</note>. Let them be ground together; pour rainwater onto them until the mixture has the consistency of a paste. Let everything stand in a warm **digestion** <note>a process of applying gentle, consistent heat to extract or mature a substance</note> for twelve hours; after this, pour on enough water so that it stands three or four fingers high above it. Let it all boil together until the yellow tincture is extracted from it. Pour that off and filter it, and boil it down until a fourth part remains; thus, after a few days' time, it will acquire a very red tincture.

## LXX. Astringent Extract of Mars.
<note>original: *Extractum Martis Astringens*. In alchemy, Mars is the symbol for iron. An "astringent" medicine is one that shrinks or constricts body tissues to stop secretions or bleeding.</note>

Take half a pound of iron rust, place it in an iron kettle, and pour four pounds of tincture of wine <note>original: *vin. tinct.*, likely *vinum tinctura*</note> over it. Once the pot is set upon the fire, let it boil while covered, stirring occasionally with an iron spatula until only one-third remains. Strain the clear liquid through a woolen cloth and evaporate it down to the thickness of an extract.
This stops all diarrhea <note>original: *buik-loop*</note>, dysentery <note>original: *roo-loop*; historically called "the bloody flux"</note>, and excessive menstruation; it is administered in doses of ten to forty grains <note>a grain was a traditional unit of weight based on the weight of a single seed of cereal</note>.

### LXXII. *Reddened Mars*, with a certain
### *Strong Water.*
<note>original: *Mars Rubificatus, met zeeker Aqua Fortis*. Mars is the alchemical name for iron. *Aqua Fortis* (Strong Water) is the historical name for nitric acid.</note>

Take four ounces of iron plates that have been heated to a glow four or five times, forged, and broken into pieces; place these in a flask <note>original: *kolf*; a long-necked glass vessel</note> and set it in the sand to distill. Continue this pouring until you have consumed sixteen ounces of the *Strong Water*.

### LXXIII. *Opening Essence of Mars by Zwelfer.*
<note>original: *Effentia Martis Aperitiva Zwelfieri*. Johannes Zwelfer (1618–1668) was a prominent German physician and apothecary famous for his influential pharmaceutical texts.</note>

Take four, five, or six ounces of very pure steel filings; place them in a large glass vessel. Add to this, drop by drop, three ounces of *spirit of nitre* <note>nitric acid</note> and two ounces of *rectified spirit of vitriol* <note>purified sulfuric acid</note>. Stir the substance occasionally so that it does not harden too much and break the glass. When all the spirits have been dripped in, dilute the mass—so that it does not clump together too much—with ten ounces of *phlegm of vitriol* <note>the watery, less acidic distillate obtained during the production of sulfuric acid</note>, or in its place, use the same quantity of *acidic spirit of sal ammoniac* <note>a solution related to ammonium chloride</note>. Thus, everything will turn very red, or at least very yellow; this serves to clear all obstructions <note>internal blockages of the organs</note>.

## LXXIV. Zwelfer’s Coralline Essence of Mars.
<note>Mars is the alchemical name for iron. Johannes Zwelfer (1618–1668) was a famous physician known for refining chemical medicines.</note>

Take six drachms <note>a drachm is roughly 3.9 grams</note> of Zwelfer’s <term>soluble magistery of true red corals</term> <note>original: *Magisterium ſolubile corallorum rubr. ver.*; a 'magistery' is a refined extract or precipitate believed to contain the full potency of a substance</note>; dissolve them in one and a half ounces of *cinnamon water*, to which one adds two ounces of the above-mentioned *Essence of Mars*. ## LXXV. Zwelfer’s Astringent Tincture of Mars.

Take pure steel filings, as many as you wish, and place them in a large and spacious glass; moisten them with Zwelfer’s *spirit of Venus* <note>original: *Spiritus veneris*; an acidic spirit distilled from verdigris (copper acetate)</note>, and let them dry again; repeat this process two or three times, until the filings have almost turned into a <term>Crocus</term> <note>original: *Crocus Martis*; a fine reddish powder of iron oxide used for its medicinal properties</note>; then pour the *spirit of Venus* over it again, until it stands about four fingers high. After a digestion <note>the process of soaking a substance in a liquid under gentle heat to extract its properties</note>, it will acquire a very beautiful red tincture; pour off the colored *spirit*, and add fresh spirit, repeating this until no more tincture appears. Combine all the tinctures and filter them; then draw off <note>distill away</note> all the *spirit* until the liquid reaches a proper thickness. This is then extracted with *spirit of wine* <note>original: *Spiritus vini*; ethanol</note>, filtered, and brought to an oily consistency through evaporation.

### LXXVI. Red Crystals of Mars.
<note>original: *Crystalli Rubri Martis*; Mars is the alchemical name for iron.</note>

First, make a good, strong water from <term>Vitriol</term> <note>original: *Vitri-ool*; various sulfate minerals used to produce strong mineral acids</note> and Saltpeter, an equal amount of each; take one pound of this, and melt into it four ounces of very pure and dry saltpeter. Then add six ounces of whole pieces of steel: place all of this in a large <term>flask</term> <note>original: *kolf*</note> that stands on the ashes <note>an ash bath was used to provide gentle, indirect heat</note>; one must stir it gently at times, and the ashes should be only lukewarm. When all the motion <note>referring to the bubbling or effervescence of the chemical reaction</note> has ceased, pour two and a half pounds of good, warm distilled vinegar onto it: this must be poured on gradually while stirring gently.

However, if any small pieces of steel should remain undissolved, they must be removed before pouring the vinegar over it. Then, combine all the crystals and dissolve them again in a good portion of distilled vinegar; filter the solution, and evaporate it again over a gentle fire in a water bath until half remains; then let it crystallize again as before. ### On COPPER, *Venus*, *Æs*
### or *Cuprum.*

### III. By Vapor, also called *Rust*, *Green of Copper*, and *Spanish Green*.
<note>original: *Ærugo*, *Viride æris*, and *Spaans Groen*. These terms all refer to verdigris, the green pigment or patina that forms on copper.</note>

Hang the copper plates above the steam of wine into which grape-stalks <note>original: *rofijn-takjens*; likely refers to the stems or vine-cuttings used in the fermentation process to create the acidic environment necessary for verdigris</note> have been thrown; thus the *Crocus* <note>original: *Crocus*; in alchemy, this refers to a fine metallic powder or oxide, named for its resemblance to the color of saffron</note> will cling to them, which one can wipe off with a hare's foot <note>a traditional tool used by early modern artists and chemists as a soft brush for collecting delicate powders</note>.

### IV. By Smearing.

Coat your copper plates with some acidic liquid, or something sharp; it is even done with common water in which a little salt or <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>original: *Sal Armoniak*; ammonium chloride, a salt used frequently in alchemy as a cleaning agent or flux</note> has been added.

### V. By Cementation.
<note>Cementation is a process where a metal is surrounded by a powdered chemical mixture and heated to alter its properties.</note>

Take copper plates and <term>stratify</term> <note>original: *stratificeert*; to arrange in alternating layers</note> them with common prepared salt; <term>calcine</term> <note>heat to high temperatures to oxidize the metal</note> them gently, gradually increasing the fire; when they are glowing hot, throw them into water and wash the blackness off thoroughly; stratify them again, and wash as before; finally, boil them and set them aside so that the *Crocus* may sink to the bottom, which one shall <term>edulcorate</term> <note>original: *edulcoreren*; a process of washing a solid to remove acids or salts until it is "sweet" or neutral</note> with water.

It is useful for all malignant ulcers, and is included in the <term>Opodeldoch Plaster</term> of <term>Felix Wurtz</term>.
<note>Opodeldoch was a famous medical plaster or liniment used for pain and wounds; Felix Wurtz (1518–1574) was a prominent Swiss surgeon who advocated for gentler wound treatments.</note>

### XIX. *Caustic Verdigris of the same* <note>original: *Viride Æris Causticum*</note>

Place one part **Verdigris** <note>original: *Viride Æris*</note> and two parts **Saltpeter** <note>original: *Nitrum*</note> in a bowl; light them with a coal until they burst into flame. Then melt the residue in the cellar **by deliquescence** <note>original: *per deliquium*; allowing a substance to absorb enough moisture from the air to become liquid</note>, or in a closed pig’s bladder placed in water.
   *It is good for driving away Venus pustules <note>referring to sores caused by the "Great Pox" or syphilis</note> and warts.*

## XXI. Making Coarse Green Copper according to Lancilot.

## XXIII. *Crocus Veneris*, or *Saffron* of Copper.

Take very thin copper plates, place them in a crucible with common <term>decrepitated salt</term> <note>original: *Sal decrepitatus*; salt that has been heated until it stops crackling, which removes its internal moisture</note>, making <term>layer upon layer</term> <note>original: *Stratum super stratum*; a method of alternating layers of materials in a vessel</note>. These are placed in the oven, and one gradually makes them glowing hot; then one throws them into fresh water, which one stirs thoroughly with a spatula or iron rod to wash away the salt and all sorts of impurities; then one calcines it again with new crackled salt as before, and throws it back into the water; then one lets the water boil to dissolve all the salt, which is then gently poured off; thus one finds at the bottom a beautiful red powder, which one shall edulcorate <note>edulcorate: to purify a substance by washing away soluble salts</note> and dry, which is the <term>Saffron of Venus</term> <note>original: *Crocus veneris*; a red oxide of copper</note>, serving in the <term>Opodeldoch Plaster</term> <note>original: *Emplastrum Opodeldoch*; a celebrated medical plaster for treating wounds and pains</note> of <term>Felix Wurtz</term> <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss surgeon known for his revolutionary wound care</note> and other ointments as well.

## XXV. Another Method.

Take burnt copper <note>burnt copper: copper oxide, usually prepared by heating copper with sulfur</note>, as described in Chapter XXII, finely pulverized, two parts, and one part pure sulfur; place it in a crucible to <term>calcine</term> <note>calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures to change its properties or reduce it to a powder</note>, stirring constantly with a copper spatula until all the sulfur is burned; then grind the said lime <note>lime: here referring to the powdery metallic ash or oxide</note> again, and mix an eighth part of its weight in sulfur into it; repeat this calcination five or six times; then pour all the substance into fresh water that is boiling hot, stirring with a stick for half an hour; then filter the liquid, let it evaporate to a third of its volume, then set it in a cool cellar to crystallize, and thus you will obtain beautiful crystals.

## XXVII. Another spirit of Venus with the admixture of Mars.
<note>In the symbolic language of alchemy, Venus represents copper and Mars represents iron.</note>

It serves for abscesses <note>original: *apostematien*; internal swellings or collections of pus</note> of the stomach or liver.

## XXVIII. *Flowers of the Vitriol of Venus.*
<note>original: *Flores Vitrioli Veneris*; in alchemy, "flowers" refer to a fine powder formed through sublimation, and "Venus" is the symbolic name for copper.</note>

## XXIX. *Tincture* and *Magistery of the Vitriol of Venus.*
<note>original: *Tinctura* and *Magisterium*; a tincture is a medicinal extract, usually in alcohol, while a magistery is a "master" preparation where the substance has been refined to its most potent form.</note>

After a month’s time the powder becomes yellow, and after that as red as blood.

Then put this substance into a tall flask, pouring over it very strong distilled wine vinegar; place a blind head <note>blind head: a still-cap without a spout, used to force vapors to condense and fall back into the flask (refluxing)</note> upon it, and let it stand in warm ashes for four or five days, occasionally stirring the material with a wooden spatula. ### XXXI. *To extract Venus from Mars.*
<note>In alchemy, Venus represents copper and Mars represents iron. This process describes what appeared to be the transmutation of iron into copper, though it is actually a chemical displacement reaction where iron replaces copper in a solution.</note>

## XXXVIII. Saffron of Venus. <note>original: *Crocus Veneris*; a reddish-brown copper oxide used both as a pigment and for medicinal applications, such as treating "proud flesh" in wounds.</note>

Take one pound of copper filings and one and a half pounds of common sulfur; calcine <note>original: *calcineertse*; heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or cause oxidation.</note> them together for an hour, stirring frequently with a copper spatula so that the filings are always properly mixed under the sulfur. Then burn the powder again with an equal amount of sulfur and calcine for two or three hours; grind the powder fine and store it.

## XXXIX. Tincture of Venus. <note>original: *Tinctura Veneris*; an alchemical extract or "essence" derived from copper.</note>

Take one pound of copper filings and half as much sal ammoniac <note>original: *zal armoniak*; ammonium chloride, often used as a flux or to create volatile metallic salts.</note>; place these in the open air until they have melted <note>referring to deliquescence, where the salts absorb moisture from the air to become liquid.</note> and taken on their green color. Then put it into a retort and distill it in a sand bath <note>a container of sand heated from below to provide an even, high temperature.</note>, first removing the moisture from it. After that, with a hotter fire, drive the *flowers* <note>original: *Flores*; a fine powder formed by sublimation, where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid on a cooler surface.</note> upward, which are saturated with the subtle parts of the copper. These are gathered together once the retort is broken, and then one precipitates them in water that is impregnated with *Salt of Tartar* <note>original: *Sal Tartari*; potassium carbonate, used here to cause the copper particles to fall out of the solution.</note>. The settled powder is gently washed off and dried. Pour over this a *menstruum* <note>original: *Menstruum*; a solvent used to extract the essential properties of a substance.</note> made of two parts *most highly rectified Spirit of Wine* <note>original: *Spiritus Vini Rectificatissimi*; concentrated ethanol.</note> and one part *Spirit of Sal Ammoniac* <note>original: *Spiritus salis Armoniaci*; a solution of ammonia.</note>. This is then digested <note>kept at a steady, gentle heat to encourage extraction.</note>, being well sealed, for two or three days in a *water bath* <note>original: *Balneo Maris*; literally a "Bath of Mary," a double boiler setup.</note>. Then store the tincture once it has been separated from the fine *dregs* <note>original: *Fæces*; the solid residue or sediment remaining after the liquid has been poured off.</note>.

### XXXVIII. *Saffron of Venus.* <note>original: *Crocus Veneris*; a reddish-brown oxide of copper often used in early modern medicine and chemistry.</note>

Take one pound of copper filings and one and a half pounds of common sulfur; calcine <note>original: *calcineert*; heating a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile matter or cause oxidation.</note> them together for one hour, stirring frequently with a copper spatula so that the filings are always properly mixed with the sulfur. Then burn the powder again with the same amount of sulfur and calcine for two or three hours. Grind the powder fine and store it.

### XXXIX. *Tincture of Venus.* <note>original: *Tinctura Veneris*; a medicinal or alchemical solution extracted from copper, usually characterized by a deep green or blue color.</note>

Take one pound of copper filings and half as much **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *zal armoniak*; ammonium chloride, used as a flux and cleaning agent in metallurgy.</note>. Place these in the air until they have melted <note>original: *gesmolten*; likely referring to deliquescence, where the salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to dissolve.</note> and lost their green color. Then put it into a **retort** <note>original: *retort*; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note> and first distill off the moisture in a sand bath. Afterward, using a hotter fire, drive the **Flowers** <note>original: *Flores*; solid crystals formed through sublimation, where a substance turns from a solid to a vapor and back to a solid.</note> upward, which are saturated with the subtle parts of the copper. These are gathered once the retort is broken, and then precipitated in water that is impregnated with **Salt of Tartar** <note>original: *Sal Tartari*; potassium carbonate, derived from the crusts left in wine barrels.</note>. Gently wash the settled powder and dry it. Pour over this a **solvent** <note>original: *Menstruum*; a liquid used to dissolve or extract a specific substance.</note> made of two parts **highly rectified spirit of wine** <note>original: *Spiritus Vini Rectificatissimi*; highly concentrated ethanol.</note> and one part **spirit of sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Spiritus salis Armoniaci*; an aqueous solution of ammonia.</note>. Let this digest, while well-sealed, for two or three days in a **water bath** <note>original: *Balneo Maris*; literally "Bath of Mary," a method of gentle heating using a vessel of hot water.</note>. Store the tincture once it has been separated from its **dregs** <note>original: *Faeces*; the solid sediment or waste left after a distillation or extraction process.</note>.

# XL. *Spirit of Venus by Zwelfer.* <note>Johannes Zwelfer (1618–1668) was a German physician and apothecary famous for his influential "Pharmacopoeia Regia."</note>

Take a good portion of high-quality verdigris <note>original: *Spaas-groen* or *Spaansgroen*; literally "Spanish Green," a green pigment or chemical formed on copper, chemically known as copper acetate.</note>, having been crushed, and place it in a glass flask, upon which one pours a good quantity of distilled vinegar until it stands some fingers’ breadth above it; having digested <note>original: *gedigereert*; the process of softening or dissolving a substance using gentle heat over a long period.</note> it for some time, pour off the colored liquid, and once again pour new distilled vinegar over it, which one digests and decants again; this is repeated so many times until the vinegar no longer extracts any tincture from it, and almost the entire verdigris is consumed, and only impurities remain lying on the bottom. Then filter all the solutions, evaporate everything in a copper pan until a film forms on top, and create crystals according to the art.

Now place these green crystals in a glass flask, and pour a good portion of **Rectified Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Spiritus Vini Rect.*; highly concentrated ethanol or grape brandy.</note> over them until it stands three or four fingers’ breadth above; draw this off three or four times by distilling. Then place these powdered crystals in a coated <term>luted</term> <note>original: *gewapende*; a "fortified" or luted retort was coated with a mixture of clay, sand, and hair to protect the glass from cracking in direct fire.</note> retort, and heat in an open—but not too hot—fire; from this the Spirit comes out, which shall be properly rectified in a sand bath.

This is useful for epilepsy, apoplexy, risings <note>original: *opstygingen*; a contemporary medical term for "hysterical vapors" or a sensation of rising in the body, often associated with the womb.</note>, spleen diseases, etc., and it dissolves all kinds of stones, and therefore it was held by Zwelfer to be an **Alcahest** <note>original: *Alcahest*; a legendary universal solvent sought by alchemists, capable of dissolving any substance into its primary elements.</note>.

### III. Calcination by Reverberation, or Minium.

The powder <note>original: *calk*; calx, the metallic oxide produced after heating</note> prepared above is stirred constantly in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace that reflects heat from the roof onto the material being processed</note> until it turns red <note>this produces minium, or "red lead"</note>. But ensure that the same does not melt and become fluid again, for then it would turn back into lead.

### VI. By Cementation, or Burnt Lead <note>original: *Plumbum Ustum*</note>.

Layer <note>original: *stratificeert*; an alchemical process of placing materials in alternating layers</note> the lead plates with powdered sulfur. Having been burned in this way, one washes the substance and dries it.

### *V. By Immersion.*

Although lead can be calcined by all kinds of acidic liquids, such as *aqua regia* <note>original: *aq. Regia*; "royal water," a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, spirit of common salt <note>original: *Spir. Salis Comm.*; hydrochloric acid</note>, nitre <note>nitric acid</note>, vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note>, and distilled vinegar <note>original: *Acet. Dest.*</note>, very few others are used.

### *VI. Sugar or Salt of Saturn.*

Pour distilled vinegar onto the powder <note>calx</note> of lead or minium; let it stand for a time, extract <note>dissolve the soluble parts</note>, pour off the liquid <note>original: *decanteert*</note>, filter, and thicken <note>original: *coaguleert*</note> by drawing off the moisture; this can then be dissolved and thickened again several times—first in distilled vinegar and then in water—to purify it, which finally can be made to crystallize, throwing away the dregs <note>original: *feces*</note>.

### VII. *Another way.*

Hang some thin lead plates partially above and partially in distilled vinegar within a flask. Then distill and cohobate <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue and re-distilling it to concentrate its properties</note>; then filter the distilled liquid together with what has remained on the bottom, adding to it the ceruse <note>original: *ceruis*; white lead or lead carbonate that forms on the surface of the plates</note> which has remained hanging on the plates. Let this digest <note>steep in gentle heat</note> for a long time. Finally, draw off a large portion with a gentle heat and set the remainder aside to crystallize. These crystals are then dissolved, filtered, and thickened <note>original: *coaguleert*</note> once more in order to purify them.

### VIII. *Magistery of Lead <note>original: *Magisterium Saturni*; a "magistery" is a potent alchemical preparation where the substance is dissolved and then precipitated into a fine powder</note>.*

Drop Oil of Tartar <note>original: *Oleum Tartari p.d.* (per deliquium); a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note> into the solution of lead <note>Saturn</note>, and the magistery will precipitate <note>fall to the bottom as a solid</note>.

This Sugar <note>Lead Acetate</note> and the Magistery (being of the same potency) taken in doses of 4, 5, or 6 grains, stills the desire for sexual intercourse <note>original: *lust tot byslapen*</note>. And if one rubs the genitals and the navel with it, it has the same effect. It is also useful for ulcers that are malignant and spreading <note>original: *voortetende*; "eating forward"</note>, against cancer, malignant sores, burns, and inflammations. It dissolves hard and scirrhous <note>original: *schirreurse*; hard, cancerous-like</note> swellings. It is applied to bruises and, when melted in some suitable liquid, to red eyes. The same substance made into crystals with saltpeter <note>original: *Sal nitrum*</note> is good for those who are short of breath <note>original: *aamegtige*</note>.

### IX. *Another Magistery of Lead, called Milk of Lead <note>original: *Lac Saturni*</note>.*

### XXIX. *Calcination of Lead.*

Take filings of **lead**, sprinkle them with urine, or add **salt of tartar** <note>original: *Sal tartari*; potassium carbonate</note> to it, or even **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Sal Armoniak*; ammonium chloride</note>. Let it stand for some time, and in time it will turn into a **calx** <note>The crumbly powder remains of a metal after it has been roasted or oxidized</note>.

### XXX. *Litharge.*

**Litharge** <note>original: *Lithargyrium*; lead(II) oxide, a byproduct of refining silver</note> is nothing other than a burnt lead, or a **frothy dross** <note>original: *Excrementum spumeum*</note> that remains during the purification of **silver** with lead. These are called "Golden" and "Silver" litharge based on their deep or pale color, although their properties are the same, the color appearing only from the greater or lesser degree of boiling.

For example, one takes a crucible made of bones or burnt horns <note>This refers to a "cupel," a porous vessel used in the process of cupellation to separate precious metals from base metals</note>; in this, one melts four or five parts of lead and adds fine silver. Once this is melted, one **reverberates** <note>subjects the material to intense heat in a furnace where the flames are "reflected" back onto the substance</note> it, so that the impurity of the silver mixes into the lead. When the dross is then removed, the silver remains pure—and this byproduct is the **litharge**.

### XXXI. *Red Oil of Litharge.*

Take **litharge** and **calcined vitriol** <note>sulfate minerals that have been roasted until they become a dry powder</note> of equal weight each. Distill through a retort according to the art, and you will obtain a red oil.
This is used for **gout** <note>original: *Podagra*; a painful form of inflammatory arthritis</note> when mixed with other remedies.

### XXXII. *Another method.*

### XXXIII. *To make Hematite from Lead.*

Take **Sugar of Saturn** <note>original: *Saccharum saturni*; lead acetate, so named for its sweet taste, though it is highly toxic</note> and **Vitriol of Mars** <note>original: *vitriolum martis*; iron(II) sulfate</note>; distill these through the retort, and thus the **Hematite** <note>original: *Hæmatites*; a reddish-black mineral of iron oxide</note> produced by art will not need to yield to the natural variety.

### XXXIV. *Butter of Lead and Cinnabar.*

Take **Hungarian Lead Ore** <note>original: *Ongerse Minera saturni*; likely galena or lead sulfide sourced from the Hungarian mining regions</note> which is volatile, grind it fine, and mix it with an equal part of **Sublimated Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius sublimatus*; mercury(II) chloride, also known as corrosive sublimate</note>; then distill it through the retort, and one will obtain a thick moisture, which is the **Butter** <note>original: *Butyrum*; in alchemy, a "butter" refers to a dense, oily substance, typically a metal chloride</note>, which one then rectifies. In the neck of the retort, one will find **Cinnabar** <note>mercury(II) sulfide, a bright red mineral used as a pigment and in medicine</note>.

### XL. **Magistery from the Marcasite of Lead** <note>a "magistery" is a concentrated medicinal precipitate; "marcasite" here refers to bismuth, which was historically confused with lead ores</note>

This is also done in the very same way as was previously spoken of concerning **Saturn**, but most often using distilled vinegar.

### IV. *Salt of Jupiter*. <note>original: *Sal Jovis*; a chemical salt derived from Tin.</note>

Just as one makes the **Salt of Lead** <note>original: *Sal saturni*</note>, so one also makes it from **Jupiter** <note>original: *Jupiter*; the alchemical name for Tin</note>, which can be further **exalted** <note>refined or made more potent</note> with **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Spir. vini*; concentrated ethanol</note>; take note that the **Tin** must be well-reverberated, otherwise one would labor in vain. One can also extract the **Salt** from the **flowers** <note>original: *flores*; the powdery sublimate or residue formed after heating</note> in this same way.

It is effective when used both internally and externally for **suffocations of the womb** <note>original: *moer-stikkingen*; a historical term for hysterical fits or respiratory distress believed to be caused by the movement of the uterus</note>. It is also used for foul-smelling ulcers, **fistulas** <note>abnormal passages in the body</note>, cancer, and spreading sores.

The **Dose** is 2, 3, 4, etc. **grains** <note>a small unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams</note>, administered several times.

### V. *Magistery of Jupiter*. <note>original: *Magisterium Jovis*; a "magistery" is a preparation where the substance is dissolved and then precipitated into a fine, potent powder without losing its essential qualities.</note>

This is done in the same way through **precipitation**. One can **solve** <note>dissolve</note> the reverberated **Tin** in distilled vinegar and **precipitate** it with **Spirit of Vitriol** <note>original: *Spir. vitrioli*; sulfuric acid</note>, though it does not always seem to succeed.

the powers are the same as those mentioned above.

Pour onto this powder the same water frequently—namely, that which is distilled from **calcined** <term>calcined</term> <note>burned to a powder or friable state</note> eggshells—and **cohobate** <term>cohobate</term> <note>to repeatedly distill a liquid by pouring it back over the solid matter remaining in the vessel</note> in the ash-bath, until the mercury is changed into a red and sweet powder.

It heals the sores in the neck of the bladder, even those which are considered incurable; it also heals external wounds and **ulcerations** <note>original: *ulceratien*; open sores or abscesses</note>.

### IX. Precipitate by the Tincture of 
### Emery, or Miraculous Precipitate. <note>original: *Præcipitatus door de Tinctura Smiridis, ofte Præcipitatus Miraculosus*</note>

It purges gently from both above and below <note>inducing both vomiting and bowel movements</note> when 3 or 4 grains are administered; however, it will only purge from below if it is kept on the fire for two hours. But if held so for five or six hours, it becomes fixed and **diaphoretic** <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>original: *diaphoretik*; a substance that induces sweating, often used to break a fever</note>. The emery is more suitable for extracting the tincture if it is first quenched in water several times.

### XIV. *Flesh-Colored Precipitated Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurius Præcipitatus Incarnatus*</note>

Take an ounce of **mercury** <note>original: *Quiksilver*</note>, dissolve it in two ounces of **nitric acid** <term>nitric acid</term> <note>original: *sterk-waters*; literally "strong waters"</note>, then add three ounces of warm water to the solution, then pour **fresh human urine** upon it; in this way a red powder will precipitate, which one shall wash with warm water and dry.
It causes only a purging of the bowels <note>original: *afgang*; an evacuation or laxative effect</note>, given in doses of six to ten grains.

### XV. *Yellow Precipitated Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurius Præcipitatus Luteus*</note>

This is done as above, but in place of urine, one pours **Solution of Salt of Tartar** <term>Solution of Salt of Tartar</term> <note>original: *Liquor Salis Tartari*; a liquid made from potassium carbonate, often used to neutralize acids</note> into it, which then precipitates yellow, and it is likewise sweetened <note>washed to remove harsh acidic salts</note> with clean water and then dried.
It is of the same strength and dose as the previous one.

### XVI. *Fixed, Sweetened Vitriolated Precipitated Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurius Præcipitatus Vitriolatus Fixus, Dulcificatus*</note>

Take pure **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note>, dissolve it in **nitric acid** <term>nitric acid</term> <note>original: *Aqua Forti*; here specified as being made from two pounds of vitriol and one pound of saltpeter</note>, draw it off <note>distill or evaporate the liquid</note>, and **cohobate** <term>cohobate</term> <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid matter left in the still to concentrate its "virtues"</note> up to three times; then pour **spirit of vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>original: *Sp. Vitrioli*; sulfuric acid</note> onto it, rectify, and distill, cohobating six times; then pour **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: *Spir. Vini*; high-proof ethanol</note> onto it, then cohobate again several times, or up to ten times; then **sweeten** <term>sweeten</term> <note>original: *edulcoreert*; to wash away the corrosive acidity</note> the precipitate with cordial waters, and store it.

## XXII Another *Gold of Life* <note>original: *Aurum Vitæ*</note>.

Take purified mercury <note>original: *Mercurius purificatus*</note>, five ounces, and half an ounce <note>Latin: *unc. sem.* (uncia semis)</note> of the purest gold leaf <note>original: *auri purissimi laminati*</note>; amalgamate these together, and wash the mixture with vinegar until all the blackness is gone from it.

It purges gently without causing vomiting, unless there is much foulness in the stomach. Administered in doses of three to eight grains with a little turpentine.

### XXXVII. Artificial Cinnabar of the Pharmacies
<note>original: *Cinnabaris Officinarum Artificialis*; cinnabar is mercuric sulfide, used as a red pigment and in medicine</note>

One then takes this out, discarding the impurities.

### XLI. Mercury of Life
<note>original: *Mercurius Vitæ*; despite the name, this was not liquid mercury but a white powder made from antimony (antimony oxychloride)</note>

**T**ake the aforementioned *oil* or *butter of antimony* <note>from the previous recipe</note>, pour water over it, and a white powder will precipitate <term>precipitate</term> <note>a solid that separates from a liquid solution during a chemical reaction</note> to the bottom; this is washed with water until it has no more sharpness <note>acidity or corrosiveness</note>, and then it is dried.

It is useful for the plague, head ailments, pox <note>likely syphilis</note>, bad ulcers, fevers, gout <note>original: *podagra*</note>, dropsy <note>original: *water-sugt*; swelling from fluid retention</note>, etc. Some always have the infusion ready, and it is as follows:

-> ℞ <note>Take</note>. Mercury of Life, half a dram <note>original: *dr. sem.* (drachma semis); approx. 1.9 grams</note>. <-
-> Noble wine, 18 ounces <note>original: *Vini gener. unc. xviii.*</note>. <-
-> Let an infusion be made <note>original: *F. Infusio*</note>. <-

One administers an ounce of this.

### XLII. Corrected Mercury of Life
<note>original: *Mercurius Vitæ Correctus*</note>

**B**ecause the Mercury of Life acts so violently, people have sought to improve it in this way.
Take then the Mercury of Life, put it in a glass, and place it on hot sand until it begins to turn red; then draw off spirit of wine <note>original: *Spiritus vini*; concentrated alcohol</note> from it several times <term>drawing off</term> <note>a process of pouring the spirit over the powder, let it sit, and then distilling or pouring it off repeatedly</note>.
Administered in doses of four to six grains, it purges quite easily from below <note>meaning it acts as a laxative rather than an emetic</note>.

# XLIII. *Purgative Mercury of Life.*
<note>original: *Mercurius Vitæ Catharricus*; "catharricus" refers to its function as a purgative or laxative</note>

1. First, let the *Mercury of Life* <note>antimony oxychloride</note> be rubbed for a long time and frequently with *common salt* <note>original: *Sal commune*; table salt</note>; afterwards, wash away the acidity with fresh water, and it shall then only purge from below <note>act as a laxative rather than causing vomiting</note>.
2. Add your *Mercury of Life* to saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> that is melting over the fire, throwing it in gradually and stirring it; after it has cooled, one shall find the *Mercury* at the bottom like a *metal clump* <term>regulus</term> <note>the metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible</note>, which one shall then <term>edulcorate</term> <note>purify by washing away salts or acids until the substance is tasteless</note>.

# XLIV. *Mineral Laxative.*
<note>original: *Laxativum Minerale*</note>

Let two ounces of saltpeter melt over the fire, then gradually add a half or nearly a whole ounce of the *Mercury of Life*: afterwards, wash away all the saltiness with water. Then add an equal amount of salt to the dried powder and rub it diligently for a whole day upon a marble stone: and wash it again with water.
One administers from six to twelve grains of this.

# XLV. *Mineral Bezoar, called Croll's Diaphoretic Antimony.*
<note>original: *Bezoardicum Minerale, Antimonium Diaphoreticum Crollii*; named after Oswald Croll, a 17th-century alchemist. A "diaphoretic" is a substance that induces sweating to break a fever.</note>

Take four ounces of purified *Butter of Antimony* <note>antimony trichloride</note>, for example, and drop onto it gradually as much *spirit of nitre* <note>nitric acid</note> or *aqua fortis* <note>literally "strong water," also nitric acid</note> as needed: then draw off the *spirit of nitre* <note>evaporate it</note>, and pour another ounce of the same *spirit* over it again, and do this further for a third time. Afterwards, rub this precipitate, wash it, and heat it until it glows <note>original: *gloeidſe*; calcination</note>.
It is a great antidote that induces sweating.

## XLVIII. *Croll’s Solar Bezoar.*

Take half a pound of *Butter of Antimony* <term>Butter of Antimony: *Butyrum antimonii*, a thick, caustic liquid (antimony trichloride) used as a base for many medicines</term> and dissolve it by gradually pouring *Spirit of Nitre* <note>original: *Spiritus Salis nitri*; nitric acid</note> over it.
Then take half an ounce of fine gold and dissolve it in *royal water* <term>Royal Water: *Aqua regia*, a powerful mixture of acids capable of dissolving "noble" metals like gold</term>. Pour both of these clear solutions together, gently draw off the *solvent* <note>original: *Menstruum*</note> through distillation, and pour the distilled liquid back onto the residue; to this, add another ounce of *Spirit of Nitre*. Draw it off again, and repeat this process several times. The *calx* <term>Calx: the powdery metallic residue remaining after heating or chemical treatment</term> must now be washed until sweet <note>original: *afgesoet*; a process of rinsing to remove caustic salts</note> and calcined <note>heated to a high temperature without melting</note>.
This is recommended for the pox, plague, gout <note>original: *podagra*</note>, dropsy <note>original: *water-sugt*; fluid retention</note>, fevers, and obstructions of the spleen, administered in doses of three to eight grains.

## XLIX. *The True Solar Bezoar.*

Take half an ounce of the *spiritualized gold* <note>original: *Aurum spiritualisatum*; gold that has been refined and "opened" through chemical processes to be more reactive</note> described previously and dissolve it in *royal water*. Then dissolve into this same solution four ounces (or six ounces, as others prefer) of rectified *Butter of Antimony*. Pour both solutions together and draw off the *solvent* using a retort <term>Retort: a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling liquids</term> through frequently repeated distillations. After this, place the substance in a covered crucible and heat it until it becomes a violet-colored powder through calcination; however, if one calcines it very strongly, it will turn purple.
It possesses the same virtues as the former, though it is more powerful.

## LIX. White Diaphoretic Spirit or Oil of Mercury.

Take one part of finely crushed *sublimated mercury* <note>mercuric chloride</note> and three parts of *Red Clay* <note>original: *Argilla Rubra*</note>; mix them together and, using common water, form them into small balls which are then dried in the shade. ## LX. Red Spirit or Oil of Mercury.

Take finely ground sublimate and steel filings, an equal amount of each, mix them together, and let them resolve <term>resolve: to dissolve a solid into a liquid state</term> through *deliquescence* <term>deliquium: the process of a substance absorbing moisture from the air until it liquefies</term> into a yellow oil, which should be carefully collected. Once it is coagulated and purified, add the oil to it; in this way, it will take on a golden or saffron color.

## LXII. The *Fragrant Oil*, called *Star of Mercury*.

<note>original: *Oleum Fragrans*, *Astrum Mercurii*</note>

## LXXVII. Riverius’s Mineral Bezoar.

## LXXVIII. Compound Red Precipitate or Zehner’s Golden Root.

Take eight parts of common mercury that has been well purified; one part of gold filings, and make an **Amalgam** <note>a mixture of mercury with another metal</note> of them. Let this stand in warm ashes for two months after putting it into a vial glass. Then the mass will gradually climb up like a kind of small golden tree, and it appears as if to glow; but it gradually sinks down again. When taken out from there, grind it, and it is a shining red powder.

It purges from below and above if the dose is increased, and if it is decreased, it works through sweating. One gives a grain or a grain and a half up to seven or eight, depending on whether they are children or adults.

### LXXX. Markgraaf's Mineral Bezoar.

Take as much of the icy *Butter of Antimony* <note>original: *Butyrum Antimonii*; a thick, caustic chemical used as a precursor for medicines</note> as is sufficient, and pour into a long-necked glass as much well-rectified *Spirit of Nitre* <note>original: *Spiritus Nitri*; nitric acid</note> as required, and do this drop by drop until the effervescence <note>bubbling or fizzing</note> ceases. Place it in a clean crucible and heat it until it glows slightly, so that the corrosive spirits fly away and the powder remains tasteless or slightly acidic.

It is a great sweat-inducing remedy in many major illnesses, given in doses of ten or twelve grains with some sudorific <note>sweat-inducing</note> vehicle.

## LXXXV. Mineral Turbith, and the purification of Mercury.

Take one part quicksilver (which has been stripped of all fine impurities through distillation) and three parts of the Oil of Sulfur made by the bell <note>original: *Oleum sulphuris per campanam*; sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur under a glass bell jar</note>. Distill this through the retort until it is dry; then pour new Oil of Sulfur made by the bell onto the remaining mass again, and proceed as before; and do this for a third time; then pour warm water on the remaining mass, and edulcorate <term>Edulcorate: to wash a substance with water to remove salts or acids until it becomes tasteless</term> according to the art.

To then purify the Mercury, do as follows. Mix your quicksilver with hammer scale <note>iron oxide flakes that fall from hot iron when struck by a hammer</note>, quicklime, iron slag, or copper slag: or in place of quicksilver, one makes the sublimate or precipitate "alive" <note>returning a chemical compound of mercury back to its metallic, liquid state</note> again with the aforementioned substances. But note, that the receiver <note>the glass vessel that collects the distilled substance</note> must be half full of water, so that the Mercury Precipitate may change into a running quicksilver. Wash this mercury with lye made from grapevine branches and quicklime, an equal amount of each, which is freed of all its blackness while stirring; wash it then three or four times with brandy, constantly shaking it and stirring as before, and thus your Mercury shall be purified of all fine impurities.

### LXXXVII. The Coagulation of Mercury.

Take equal parts of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and lead. Let the lead melt in a crucible. Then pour it into a cold crucible, onto which the quicksilver is immediately poured; thus they will instantly turn into a solid mass. Put this mass into another hot crucible (which is not yet red-hot), and once it is fluid, pour it again into a cold crucible: in this way, everything will be better mixed and form a harder mass, which, after having lain in smith’s water <note>water used by blacksmiths to quench hot iron, often containing iron particles and minerals</note> for several days and nights, becomes very hard.

It can be made as malleable as silver. It is worn as an *amulet* <note>original: *Amuletum*</note> against the plague and poison. It is used in plasters; it is sprinkled into old ulcers, for it is an *alkali* <note>a basic substance</note> that absorbs all acid.

### XCVII. *Tilingius’s Diaphoretic Mercury.* <note>Matthias Tiling (1634–1685) was a German physician and chemist known for his works on anatomy and the medicinal use of minerals.</note>

## XCIX. Another *Oil of Mercury.* <note>original: "Oleum Mercurii"</note>

## C. *Beguinus’s Precipitated Mercury.* <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620) was a French apothecary and author of "Tyrocinium Chymicum," one of the most influential early chemistry textbooks. His "red precipitate" was a staple of 17th-century medicine.</note>

Dissolve the **mercury** in **strong water** <term>Aqua forti: nitric acid</term>, and precipitate it according to the art through the evaporation of moisture, so that it becomes a red precipitate in the common manner. When the substance has been finely ground, put it into a strong matrass; pour over it **vinegar** <term>Acetum</term> that has been distilled three times, until it stands five finger-breadths above it, applying a **sand-bath** <term>sand-vuur: a container of sand heated by a fire, used to provide a steady, even temperature to glass vessels</term> so that the vinegar boils slowly for six hours, and the precipitate is completely dissolved. Once the solution has been filtered while warm, pour **brine** <note>original: "pekel"; salt water</note> over it; the mercury will then separate from the solvent, which one can wash and dry. This purges from below <note>acts as a laxative</note> when four to five grains are administered.

## CI. The Miraculous Precipitate of Mercury. <note>original: "Præcipitatus Miraculofus Mercurii"</note>

Take red **emery** <term>Smiris: a granular rock, typically used as an abrasive, but here used for its mineral properties</term>, finely crushed; place it in a crucible and set it in a very hot fire for four hours, until it begins to **vitrify** <note>turn into a glass-like substance</note> somewhat and sticks to the walls of the crucible. Having been removed from the fire, crush it into a subtle powder and place it in a **matrass** <term>matras: a long-necked glass flask used for heating and digesting substances</term>, over which you pour rectified **aqua regia** <term>Aqua regis: "king’s water," a highly corrosive mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</term>. Let it digest for twenty-four hours, then pour off the tinted fluid by tilting the flask, and pour fresh liquid onto the remainder as often as necessary until all the tincture has been extracted. Having combined all these tinctures, distill them until they reach the consistency of an oil.

Then take one ounce of that oil and pour it onto four ounces of **crude mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii crudi"; liquid quicksilver</note>; the mercury will immediately precipitate and will not cling to the oil. If one then distills this with a fairly strong fire, a small amount of the mercury will **sublime** <note>turn into vapor and then solidify again</note> after the oil has evaporated, but the largest portion will remain **fixed** <term>Fixum: a substance that remains stable and solid under high heat, resisting evaporation</term>.

Its use is for the **augmentation** <note>an alchemical process intended to increase the quantity or quality of a metal</note> of gold, and for red vitrification.

### CIII. A Specific Precipitate Against Gonorrhea <note>original: "Præcipitatus Specificus Contra Gonorrhæam"</note>

Dissolve three ounces of purified **mercury** <note>original: "mercurius"</note> in **nitric acid** <term>aqua Forti: "strong water," a highly corrosive acid used to dissolve metals</term>; also dissolve one ounce of **copper** <term>Venus: the alchemical symbol and name for copper</term> in the nitric acid: mix both solutions together and let them evaporate on a sand bath, stoking the fire more strongly at the end so that all the **vapors** <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> of the nitric acid evaporate from it. This should then be filtered while warm and **evaporated** <note>original: "exhalere"</note> by the steam of the bath. You will then find a green precipitate on the bottom. One gives four to six grains of this.

### CIV. Mercury Precipitate Against Ulcerations <note>original: "Præcipitatus Mercurius tegens d’ Ulceratien"</note>

Slake four pounds of **quicklime** <term>Calcis Vivæ: calcium oxide, which reacts strongly with water to create heat and a caustic solution</term> in twenty-five parts of **common water** <note>original: "Aquæ Communis"</note> and make it clear through filtration. ### CVII. Mercury Manna by Beguin.
<note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620) was a famous French apothecary and author of an early chemistry textbook.</note>

Dissolve your *Mercury* <term>Mercurius</term> in *Strong Water* <note>original: "Aqua Forti," known today as nitric acid</note>. Precipitate the same with seawater, then distill it through a flask from a sand bath, increasing the fire at the end so that the quicksilver <note>mercury</note> comes to sublimate <note>to turn from a solid directly into a vapor and back to a solid</note> on the walls of the flask. Once everything has cooled, one throws away the impurities that remained on the bottom and collects only the sublimate; then dissolve it again in the same water, redistilling it as before. Thus you have a snow-white *Celestial Eagle* <note>original: "Aquila Cælestis," an alchemical name for calomel or mercurous chloride</note>.

It purges only from below <note>acts as a laxative</note>, administered in doses of ten to fifteen grains against venereal diseases <note>original: "venus ziektens"</note>.

### CVIII. Mineral Turbith by Minsicht.
<note>Adrian von Mynsicht (1603–1638) was a German alchemist and physician famous for his chemical remedies.</note>

Dissolve as much *Sublimated Mercury* <term>Mercurius Sublimatus: mercuric chloride</term> in warm rainwater as you desire, filter the solution several times, and pour it into a glass; then gradually drip into it the *Oil of Salt of Tartar* <term>Oleum Salis Tartari: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term> as much as is needed, until no more red powder sinks to the bottom. Then pour off the liquid and keep the red powder, which must be sweetened <note>original: "edulcorere," a process of washing a precipitate with water to remove salts and bitterness</note>. Cohobate <note>repeatedly distill a liquid from its own solid residue</note> it six or seven times with a well-rectified *Honey Water* <note>original: "Aqua mellis"</note>; then take the powder out from there; then burn *Spirit of Wine* <term>Alcohol Vini: highly concentrated ethanol</term> over it, stirring constantly with an iron spatula.

This is administered to induce vomiting, in doses of four to seven grains in any suitable liquid.

### CIX. Corrected Mercury of Life.
<note>original: "Mercurius Vitæ Correctus." Despite the name, "Mercury of Life" was often a preparation of antimony (antimony oxychloride), though it was frequently categorized with mercurials in early pharmacy.</note>

The *Mercury of Life* was turned into a glass by means of *Borax*, and ground very fine, upon which one then pours *Distilled Vinegar* <term>Acetum destillatum</term>, which has first been sharpened with *Spirit of Saltpeter* <term>Spiritus salis nitri: nitric acid</term>; then one dries it on the ash-heat <note>a method of indirect heating using a tray of warm ashes</note>, and preserves it.

### CX. Crystals of Mercury.
<note>original: "Crystalli Mercurii," likely referring to mercuric nitrate crystals.</note>

Let as much *Mercury* as you please dissolve in *Strong Water* <term>Aqua fortis: nitric acid</term>, filter the solution; evaporate the filtered liquid to more than half, and let the moisture be placed in the cellar <note>a cool, damp environment conducive to crystal growth</note>; there one finds clear crystals in it. The remaining moisture can also be evaporated and crystallized in the same manner.

### CXII. White Precipitated Mercury,

### CXIII. Fixed Precipitated Mercury.
<note>original: "Mercurius Præcipitatus Fixatus." A "fixed" substance in alchemy is one that has been made resistant to the heat of fire, preventing it from evaporating or sublimating easily.</note>

->Sal Ammoniac <term>ammonium chloride</term>, 3 drams<-

### CXIV. Laxative Precipitated Mercury.
<note>original: "Mercurius Præcipitatus Laxativus." Mercury compounds were frequently used as powerful (and often dangerous) purgatives in early modern medicine.</note>

Take as much *Mercury* as you please, pour *Oil of Vitriol* <term>concentrated sulfuric acid</term> or *Oil of Sulfur* over it, until it stands one finger's breadth above it; place it in a sand-bath <note>a tray of sand heated from below to provide a steady, even temperature</note>, so the *Mercury* shall crystallize; then take these crystals, and if there is still some living <note>liquid/metallic</note> quicksilver with it, remove it; then put them in a crucible and let them glow <note>heat to a red-hot state</note> for an hour, then throw them into warm water, and it will become a yellow powder. Decant the water, edulcorate <term>to wash a solid to remove acids or salts</term> and ignite the *Spirit of Wine* <term>distilled alcohol</term> upon the dried powder.

# Chapter VIII.

## Of *ANTIMONY*.

### I. *Calcination of Antimony.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial N featuring stylized foliage and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>Take finely powdered *Antimony;* calcine <term>roast at high heat to remove volatile components</term> it in a wide, flat, and unglazed pan, constantly stirring the substance with a small iron rod so that it does not clump together. If clumping occurs, it must be pounded again. This must be done until the substance acquires a gray color and no more smoke rises from it.

### II. *Hyacinthine Glass of Antimony.* <note>original: "Vitrum Antimonii Hyacinthinum"; a reddish-orange or yellow transparent glass made from antimony</note>

Take a good quantity of the previously calcined *Antimony*, place it in a crucible <term>a ceramic or graphite container used for melting materials at high temperatures</term>, cover it with a stone, and set it in a wind furnace <term>a furnace that uses a natural or forced draft of air to reach intense heat</term>, in which you shall kindle a very strong coal fire surrounding the crucible so that the substance melts. After about an hour, open the crucible, dip the end of a small iron rod into it, and upon pulling it out, see if the material sticking to the iron is transparent enough. If it is now transparent, pour the contents of the crucible out onto a marble stone that has been thoroughly warmed; the glass will then harden upon it. Thus you will have a good *glass of antimony* <note>original: "vitrum antimonii"</note>, which you shall allow to cool and then preserve.

## XVIII. Common Saffron of Metals.
<note>original: "Crocus Metallorum Vulgaris"; "Crocus" or Saffron refers to the reddish-orange color of the resulting powder.</note>

Take antimony and saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, sixteen ounces of each, crush them fine and mix them together as one. Put this mixture into an iron mortar <term>a heavy, bowl-shaped vessel used with a pestle for crushing and mixing ingredients</term> and cover it, leaving just enough of an opening so that one can throw in a glowing coal—which must be removed immediately. The substance will then ignite and detonate <term>a rapid chemical reaction accompanied by noise and heat, often seen in early chemistry</term> greatly. When this is finished, let the mortar cool, then remove the mass from the mortar and separate the dross <note>scoriae; the stony waste matter</note> from the pure part by a hammer-blow. This is then called *Liver of Antimony* <note>original: "Hepar Antimonii"</note> because it has a liver-like color.

It is administered to induce vomiting in doses of two to six grains.

## XXII. *Another Shorter Method.*

First take equal parts of raw antimony and pure saltpeter, put them in a crucible, upon which one sets another inverted crucible that is perforated through its bottom, being firmly luted <term>sealed with a heat-resistant clay or paste</term> to the lower one: give it a circular fire <note>original: "circuleer vuur"; a fire that surrounds the vessel to provide even heat</note> so that the material may gradually calcine <term>turn to ash or oxide through heating</term>, and the smoke may come out through the hole; continue with this fire for one hour, after which the material shall be crushed and sweetened <term>the process of washing a substance with water to remove soluble salts</term> in warm water.

Then, for a second time, take two parts of this sweetened substance and one part of pure saltpeter, or equal parts of each, put them together in a crucible and do exactly as was done the first time.

This *diaphoretic antimony* induces sweating without any trouble.

### XXVI. *Common regulus of Antimony.*

->Take: Antimony, sixteen ounces <note>original: "Antim. unc XVI."</note><-

**C**rush all of these separately as finely as possible and mix them together. ### XXXIV. Fixed Red Antimony <note>original: "Antimonium rubeum fixum." In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a substance that can withstand heat without evaporating.</note>

Take as much good antimony as you please, pour royal water <term>aqua regia; a highly corrosive mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</term> upon it, and let it stand for some time in digestion <term>gentle, steady heat</term> until the calx <term>the powdery residue left after a metal is treated with acid or fire</term> at the bottom appears white. Reverberate <term>heat in a furnace where the flame is reflected onto the material</term> the dried powder in a closed crucible for six hours, and it shall become red.

This is administered in doses of four to twelve grains.

### XXXVII. Precipitated Regulus of Mars <note>original: "Præcipitatus regulus Martis." In alchemy, a "regulus" is the metallic form of a mineral, and "Mars" refers to iron; this is an antimony-iron alloy.</note>

**T**ake flowers of the regulus of Mars <term>flores reguli martis; the fine, crystalline powder collected after heating the metal until it vaporizes and reforms</term> (sublimated with sal ammoniac and dulcorated <term>washed until all salty or acrid tastes are removed</term>). Dissolve these in *aqua regia* <term>royal water; a powerful acid mixture capable of dissolving gold</term> (distilled from nitre and sal ammoniac). Digest this and then precipitate it after performing several cohobations <term>the process of redistilling a liquid back onto its own solid residue to concentrate its properties</term>. Wash the precipitate and reverberate <term>heat at high temperature in a furnace where the flame is reflected back onto the material</term> it so that the spirit of the royal water evaporates, stirring constantly with an iron spatula until it acquires a yellow color.

### XXXVIII. Flowers of Raw Antimony <note>original: "Flores antimonii crudi"</note> or of Antimonial Ore.

**T**ake finely ground raw antimony, as much as you wish, and place it in an earthen flask, which is set quite deep in the sand bath. Upon this, place a blind or curved helm <term>the "head" or cap of a distilling apparatus</term> with a receiver attached to it. Or, if you wish, stack five or six pots on top of one another, which fit together so that the mouth of one is received by the next. Increase the fire gradually, ensuring it is neither too strong nor too weak. For if it is too strong, the antimony will melt, and if too weak, the flowers will not [rise]...

### The Common Salt of Tartar is Impregnated with Distilled Vinegar in this way.

## The Honeyed Spirit of Wine.
