### LXVII. *Butter of Antimony and Cinnabar of Antimony. Likewise how to make Mercury from Cinnabar, and Sulfur of Antimony.*

Pulverize and properly mix together **antimony** <term>antimonie</term> and **corrosive sublimate** <term>corrosive sublimaat</term> <note>mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and corrosive white powder</note>, taking an equal amount of each. Fill half of the retort with this mixture; then place the retort in a **sand-oven** <note>a sand-bath used to provide even, indirect heat</note>, attach a **receiver** <note>a vessel used to collect the distilled liquid</note> and **seal it tightly with lute** <note>luteertse; to seal joints with a clay or paste to prevent vapors from escaping</note>, and distill as before, observing the circumstances carefully.

When the red vapors first appear, remove your **recipient** <note>receiving vessel</note> and attach another one without sealing it; increase the fire until the retort begins to glow, for three or four hours. Then let the retort cool, break it, and you shall find the **cinnabar** <term>cinnaber</term> <note>mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</note> **sublimated** <note>deposited as a solid from a vapor</note> at the neck of the retort; take it off and keep it.

It is an excellent remedy against the **smallpox** <note>pokken; in this period, the term could also refer to syphilis</note> and the **falling sickness** <note>epilepsy</note>, and it induces sweating; give from six to fifteen **grains** <note>a very small unit of weight, roughly 0.06 grams</note> in the form of pills or a small piece; it is not bad when taken in preserves.

This **Butter of Antimony** <term>Butyrum Antimonii</term> is also a **caustic** <term>caustycum</term> like the previous one we spoke of.

## LXXVII. Spirit from the Regulus of Antimony <note>original: *Regulus Antimonii*; the "regulus" is the metallic portion of the ore that settles at the bottom during smelting</note>.

First, fix <note>to "fix" a substance in alchemy is to make it stable and non-volatile so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat</note> the Regulus (which can be done by frequently fixing the same, whether it be done in a philosopher's egg <term>Philosoophs ei</term> <note>an oval-shaped glass vessel used for long-term heating or "digestion"</note>, or in a flask, daily, namely by pushing that which has been sublimated <note>vaporized and condensed in the upper part of the vessel</note> back down to the bottom).

Second, place the Fixed Regulus in a cellar for six months so that it may dissolve <note>original: *solvere*; here referring to deliquescence, where a substance turns into liquid by absorbing moisture from the air</note>; then filter that oil and coagulate it until it reaches a certain thickness. Set it to melt, filter it again, coagulate and dissolve it once more, and having been mixed with three times as much Tripoli <term>Tripol</term> <note>a fine-grained, earthy silica used as a medium for distillation</note>, distill it through the retort; thus first a white oil will come, and then a red one; then rectify <note>purify by redistilling</note> it.

It is useful for intermittent fevers <note>original: *gaande en komende koortsen*</note>, and is of wonderful power, especially in a quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every third day, historically associated with malaria</note>. It purifies the blood through sweating; it shatters the stone of the kidneys and bladder; drives out the matter of the gouty <note>original: *podagreuse*</note>, and even soothes pains externally when applied. The dose is from three to five grains.

## LXXVIII. Anti-epileptic Water <note>original: *Aqua Antepileptica*</note> of Saffron of Metals <note>original: *Crocus Metallorum*</note> by Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), an influential French physician and alchemist known by his Latinized name Quercetanus</note>.

Take Saffron of Metals <term>Crocus Metallorum</term> <note>an orange-red medicinal preparation made from antimony</note>, mix it with pulverized breadcrumbs, and extract a water from it through the flask with a fairly strong fire.

Great powers are attributed to this in treating epilepsy.

### LXXIX. Sulphurous Water of Antimony, Clyssus, otherwise called <note>original: *Aqua Stimni Sulphurea, Clyssus*; a "clyssus" is an alchemical term for a vaporous essence or spirit captured during the distillation of a substance, often through combustion</note>

->Take Choice Antimony <note>original: *Antim. Electi*</note>,<-
->Pure Niter <note>original: *Nitri Puri*; also known as saltpeter</note>,<-
->Pure Sulfur, of each 1 Pound.<-
->Mix <note>original: *M.* for *Misce*</note>.<-

Distill this through the retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note> into a large receiver in which there is a portion of water. The retort must have an opening at the top <term>tubulated retort</term> through which the material is thrown in by turns and then closed again. Shortly thereafter, the material will ignite, and the receiver will be filled with vapors; as these mix with the water, the receiver will become clear again. Then, one adds new material into the receiver, and so on. Finally, filter this water that is now filled with spirits, or if it pleases you, one can draw it off <note>redistill it</note> in a water bath <term>balneum mariae</term>.

It thins all tartarous mucus <note>original: *tarteragtige slymigheid*; referring to thickened bodily fluids that were thought to cause illness</note> and purges from below, as well as through sweating and salivation. It is effective against all kinds of obstructions <note>blockages within the organs or "vessels" of the body</note>.

### LXXX. Tartarous Water of Antimony <note>original: *Aqua Stimni Tartarea*</note>.

This is made in the same manner from Antimony, Tartar, and Common Salt <note>original: *Sal Commune*</note>, in equal parts. If one adds a little Sulfur to this, the distillation will proceed much better.

It is useful for obstructions and promotes sweating.

## LXXXI. *Compound Spirit of Antimony.* <note>original: *Spiritus Antimonii compositus*</note>

Take the Sulfur of Antimony, one part; Colcothar of Vitriol <note>original: *Collothar Vitrioli*; the red oxide of iron remaining after the distillation of sulfuric acid</note>, two parts; mix them thoroughly together, and sprinkle it three or four times with vinegar <note>original: *Acetum*</note>; then distill and cohobate <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its solid residue to further extract its essence</note>. Then put the powders into a large earthenware tubulated retort <note>a vessel with a side-neck and a top opening (tubulature) for adding materials</note> (for glass ones break easily) with a large receiver; stoke the fire in a closed reverberatory furnace for three full days, just as one does when distilling Oil of Vitriol <note>highly concentrated sulfuric acid</note>. Then separate the oil from the spirit and rectify <note>purify by redistilling</note>.
It is useful for fixing <term>fixing</term> (the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire) Mercury and Cinnabar.

## LXXXII. *Liquor* or *Balsam* from the Dross of the Regulus. <note>original: *Scorien van Regulus*; "regulus" refers to the metallic heart or purest part of a mineral, and "scoria" is the waste or slag left behind after smelting</note>

Take the dross of the Regulus (whether simple or compound); place it in damp air, and it will melt <note>through deliquescence, absorbing moisture from the air</note> because of the Salt of Tartar <note>original: *Sal Tartari*; potassium carbonate</note> and the Niter <note>original: *Nitrum*; saltpeter</note>.

## LXXXVI. *Another way.*

Take powdered *Antimony*, boil it in a strong lye, and precipitate with *Rainwater* <note>original: *Aqua Pluvialis*</note> (which is impregnated with *distilled Vinegar* <note>original: *Acetum distillatum*</note>), and then edulcorate <term>edulcorate</term> (to wash a substance with water until it is free of salts or acids).
It is safer for inducing vomiting than the *Saffron of Metals* <note>original: *Crocus Metallorum*; a common but often violent antimonial medicine</note>: administered from three to five grains <term>grains</term> (a small unit of weight, roughly 65mg).

## LXXXVII. *Diaphoretic Snow of Antimony.* <note>original: *Nix Diaphoretica Antimonii*</note>

Take the *Sulfur of Antimony* from this description, or the *Golden Diaphoretic Sulfur* <note>original: *Sulphur auratum Diaphoreticum*</note>, one ounce; *Oil of Vitriol* <note>original: *Olei Vitrioli*; concentrated sulfuric acid</note>, two ounces; mix it in a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</note>, so it becomes a mass as black as pitch; let it ferment for one night, after which an acidic Water will come out through reverberation <term>reverberation</term> (a heating process where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof of a furnace onto the material), and a very white powder remains on the bottom, which is very sweat-inducing; it is also useful against worms.

## LXXXVIII. *Sulfur from calcined Antimony.*

->*Take Antimony,*<-
->*Tartar, of each equal parts,* <note>original: *āā p. æq.* (ana partes aequales)</note><-
->*Mix.* <note>original: *M.* (Misce)</note><-

Let them melt together in the fire; then pour them into a pot full of warm Water, let it stand for a day; then pour off and precipitate the *Sulfur* by adding *Vinegar* <note>original: *Acetum*</note> to it, or simply by boiling.

## XCIII. *Sulfur of Antimony from the Scoria.*

Crush the Scoria <note>original: *Scorien*; the dross or slag left over from smelting</note> or remains of the *Regulus of Antimony* <term>Regulus</term> (the metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting, named "little king" by alchemists) (which we described above) somewhat coarsely, and let them boil in common Water for half an hour in an earthen pot; pour off the liquid, and pour Vinegar onto the filtrate, then a red powder will precipitate; filter and separate the precipitate, and keep it; which is called *Golden Sulfur of Antimony* <note>original: *Sulphur Auratum Antimonii*</note>.

## XCIV. *Another, or Golden Sulfur of Antimony.*

It causes vomiting, and sometimes purging <note>acts as a laxative</note>: administered up to six grains.

### XCV. Sulfur from the *Jovial Regulus of Antimony*.

Make the *Liver of Antimony* <note>original: *Hepar*; a sulfurated chemical compound named for its reddish-brown, liver-like color</note> from the *Regulus of Tin-Antimony* <term>Jovialis</term> (referring to the planet Jupiter, the alchemical symbol for the metal Tin) using *Niter* <note>saltpeter</note>; boil this "Liver" without washing <note>original: *ablutie*; the process of rinsing away salts</note> in a strong lye, so that the *Sulfur* may be drawn out from it; pour off the liquid and then precipitate it with *Distilled Vinegar*.

---

### XCVI. Another way.

->Take as much as you wish of *Crude Antimony* <note>original: *Rec. Antim. Crudi, Q.V.*</note><-

Precipitate it using *Aqua Regia* <term>Aqua Regia</term> (literally "Royal Water," a highly corrosive mixture of acids), and wash it until neutralized <note>original: *edulcoreert*</note>; boil the same in a lye made from *Tartar* <note>potassium bitartrate, often derived from wine barrels</note>; pour off the liquid and evaporate the colored lye, and the *Sulfur of Antimony* will remain at the bottom.

---

### XCVII. Sulfur from the *Cinnabar* of *Antimony*, or *True Sulfur of Antimony*.

Boil finely crushed *Cinnabar of Antimony* <term>Cinnabar</term> (a bright red mineral or compound; here, a specific byproduct of the distillation of antimony and mercury) in a very strong lye (made from *Potash* <note>original: *Cineres Clavellati*; literally "clubbed ashes"</note> and *Quicklime* <note>original: *Calx Viva*</note>, equal parts of each, or from *Salt of Tartar*, *Niter*, and *Quicklime*) for three or four hours; pour off the lye from the *Liquid Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurius Vivus*; quicksilver</note>, which will be at the bottom; filter the liquid; then let the red *Sulfur* settle. Once separated, it is washed with common warm *Water*; then dry it with a gentle heat.

## CI. *Another way.*

## CII. *Another, called Manna of Antimony.* <note>original: *Manna Antimonii*</note>

## CXII. *Tincture from the Regulus of Mars or Antimony, called the All-Expelling Antidote.* <note>original: *Antidotos Pantagogos*</note>

Take the <term>Calx</term> <note>original: *Kalk*; the powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or "burnt"</note> of the Regulus of Mars <note>antimony that has been reduced using iron, associated with the planet Mars</note> or of antimony; dissolve it, digesting for a whole day with Spirit of Rock Salt <note>original: *spiritus salis Gemmæ*; hydrochloric acid</note>; then distill with a very strong fire, so that finally a thick Oil comes over; which, having been <term>rectified</term> <note>purified by re-distillation</note>, has good Spirit of Wine poured upon it; one then <term>circulates</term> <note>heats a liquid in a closed vessel so the vapors condense and flow back down</note> and distills, <term>cohobating</term> <note>pouring the distilled liquid back onto the solid remains to re-distill it</note> twice; always throwing away the dregs <note>original: *feces*</note>, and carefully preserving that liquid.

It purifies the blood and creates an appetite; it strengthens the intestines and opens all blockages; two or three drops of it are to be administered.

Take one part <term>Regulus of antimony</term> <note>the purified metallic heart of the mineral antimony</note> (made from the <term>Mercury of Life</term> <note>original: *Mercurius vitæ*; a white powder of antimony and chloride</note> with equal parts <term>Tartar</term> and <term>Nitre</term> <note>potassium bitartrate and saltpeter</note> through <term>detonation</term> <note>a rapid chemical reaction involving flashes of light</note>), add to it an equal weight of Gold, let them melt together, and pulverize them; then add four times as much <term>Sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and <term>sublime</term> <note>to heat a solid until it turns to vapor and settles as a powder</note> as many times as necessary until the <term>star of antimony</term> <note>original: *astrum antimonii*; the refined crystalline essence</note> is raised; thus the useless <term>earth</term> <note>original: *terra*; the spent solid residue</note> shall remain at the bottom; then wash away the saltiness of the Sal ammoniac, and put the <term>flowers of gold and antimony</term> <note>original: *flores solis en antimonii*; the powdery sublimate of these metals</note> into a <term>Hermetic egg</term> <note>an oval-shaped glass vessel sealed airtight</note>, in the <term>fixing cupel</term> <note>original: *fixerende copelle*; a specialized vessel or furnace used to make a substance heat-stable</note>, and provide such a fire that they cannot be brought to melting, but that the substance becomes yellow, lemon-colored, and from lemon-colored to chestnut-brown. These <term>flowers</term> being then <term>fixed</term> <note>made resistant to heat</note>, one pours <term>alkalized distilled vinegar</term> <note>original: *acetum destillatum alcalisatum*</note> upon them, and after that <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>concentrated alcohol</note> to extract the <term>Tincture</term>.

This is held to be a great medicine for <term>gout</term> <note>original: *podagra*</note>, <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: *geelsugt*</note>, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: *waterfugt*; swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, etc. One administers a grain or two of it.

## CXIX. *Another from Basil*. <note>Refers to Basil Valentine, a legendary alchemist</note>

This purges gently and takes away fevers, administered in doses of one or two drops.

## CXXV. *Tincture from the Sulfur of Antimony.* <note>original: *Sulphur Antimonii*</note>

Take the sulfur of antimony made in the first manner, as much as is enough; extract according to the art with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: *spiritus vini*; high-proof alcohol</note> that is not too strong, for <term>pure alcohol</term> <note>original: *alcohol*; here referring to highly rectified, anhydrous spirit</note> does not extract [it]; <term>decant</term> <note>pour off the liquid leaving the sediment</note> and distill, <term>cohobating</term> <note>the process of repeatedly pouring the distilled liquid back over the solid remains and re-distilling to concentrate the essence</note> seven times through the <term>alembic</term> <note>a chemical apparatus used for distillation</note>: then drive it through a glass <term>retort</term> <note>original: *kolf*</note> out of the sand <note>a sand bath, used to provide even, high heat</note>, adding a <term>fire of suppression</term> <note>original: *suppressie vuur*; a method where the heat is applied from above or the vessel is buried in hot coals to force the vapors over</note>, so that a very red, sweet Oil comes over: <term>abstract</term> <note>distill off</note> the spirit of wine using a <term>water-bath</term> <note>original: *water-bad*; also known as a bain-marie</note>; and a Tincture shall remain at the bottom.

## CXXX. *Tincture from the Vitriol or Crystals of Antimony.*

Take the greenish <term>vitriol</term> <note>a sulfate salt</note> or <term>crystals of antimony</term>; pour upon it a great quantity of cold water, and through this a white powder shall precipitate, which through <term>reverberation</term> <note>heating in a furnace where the flames are reflected onto the substance</note> first becomes yellow and then red; then, according to the art, extract a red <term>Tincture</term> from it with <term>distilled vinegar</term> <note>original: *acetum destillatum*</note>: this having been drawn off again, one repeats the solution with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: *spiritus vini*; high-proof alcohol</note>, which one then finally draws off again.

## CXXXI. *Magisterial Tincture, or Basil’s Stone of Fire.*

Take <term>tincture of antimony</term> (made from the <term>glass of the ore</term> <note>original: *vitrum mineræ*; a glassy substance created by melting roasted antimony ore</note>) two pounds; <term>Salt of antimony</term>, two ounces; having been mixed together, let them be joined into one by <term>circulating</term> <note>a continuous distillation process in a closed vessel</note> for a month with spirit of wine: in the [water] bath, draw off the spirit of wine until it is dry, and thereafter, using a strong fire, [draw off] the red Oil with the <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</note>; then rectify this Oil again in the <term>water-bath</term> <note>a bain-marie</note>, so that a fourth part passes over.

Take then of this rectified Oil, and <term>precipitated antimonial mercury</term> (namely [the kind made] by the <term>spirit of vitriol of Mars</term> <note>original: *spiritus vitrioli martis*; an acidic spirit derived from iron sulfate</note>) of each an equal amount; then <term>digest</term> <note>heat gently over a long period</note> in a glass that is closed in the <term>Hermetic manner</term> <note>completely airtight, usually by melting the glass neck shut</note>; first the precipitate shall dissolve, and then everything shall be united, and display a red, solid, and meltable powder.

It is of the same potency as the <term>tincture of the sun</term> <note>original: *tinctura solis*; a medicinal gold preparation</note> of <term>Basil</term> <note>referring to Basil Valentine, a famous, likely semi-mythical, 15th-century alchemical author</note>.

### CXLIV. *Tincture from the Glass of Antimony of Boyle.*
<note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was a founding figure of modern chemistry. "Glass of Antimony" (original: *Vitrum Antimonii*) is a translucent, brownish-red substance made by roasting antimony ore.</note>

## CXLVI. *Tincture and Balsam of Antimony by Boyle.*
<note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was an influential Irish natural philosopher and chemist. Antimony was a favorite subject of his experiments due to its perceived "soul" or "virtue" that could be extracted for medicine.</note>

Take one, two, or three ounces of finely crushed Antimony: pour over it a good quantity of the **Oil of Turpentine** <note>original: *Oleum Terebinthinæ*; a spirit distilled from pine resin</note>, place it together in a glass in the sand-bath; stoke a gentle fire until it reaches a boil, and thus you will have a very beautiful red Tincture.

It dissolves all hard swellings and other external ailments.

From this Balsam one can obtain a red Tincture with **spirit of wine** <note>original: *alcohol vini*; highly distilled ethanol</note>, which can be made into a Balsam by evaporating it; and when driven through the retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, it solidifies in the neck of the same.

It is a good Medicine, used both externally and internally.

## CXLVII. *Anwaldine Panacea.*
<note>original: *Panacea Anwaldina*. A "panacea" is a universal remedy or "all-healer." This recipe likely refers to a preparation by the 16th-century physician Georg am Wald.</note>

Take the **Salt of mineral antimony** <note>original: *Sal antimonii mineralis*</note>, or in its place the **Salt of antimony**, rectified through sublimation, as much as you please; having been crushed into powder, pour over it **rectified spirit of vitriol** <note>original: *spiritus vitrioli rectificati*; a concentrated form of sulfuric acid</note> until it stands a finger's breadth above it: stir it well with a wooden spatula and evaporate it until it is dry: then pour just as much **spirit** over it again, and evaporate as before. Do this up to three times. This being done, pour the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *alcohol vini*</note> over it until it stands three fingers' breadth above it: let it stand in digestion <note>a process of gentle, continuous heating to extract active ingredients</note> for twelve hours, and then draw off the **spirit of wine** through distillation until it is dry.

# CHAPTER X.

->Regarding<-

# LITHARGE.
<note>original: *Lithargyrium*; lead monoxide, a secondary mineral form of lead</note>

## I. Salt of Litharge.

Take a good portion of finely ground **litharge** <note>original: *Lithargie*</note>, pour **distilled vinegar** <note>original: *acetum*</note> upon it; digest <note>heat gently over a long period</note>, decant <note>pour off the clear liquid</note>, filter, evaporate, and crystallize just as one does with **Salt of Saturn** <note>original: *Sal Saturni*; lead acetate, so named because Saturn was the alchemical symbol for lead</note>, having also the same powers.

## II. Liquor of Litharge.

Take the **Salt of Litharge**, let it dissolve in the cellar, and preserve it.

# CHAPTER XI.

->Regarding<-

# SALTS in General.

### I. Purification of Salts.

When **salts** <note>original: *Souten*; in 17th-century chemistry, this referred to any substance that could be dissolved in water and recrystallized, including mineral, plant, and metallic salts</note> are impure, one **dissolves** <note>original: *solveert*</note> them in warm water, which is then **filtered** <note>original: *filtreert*</note> so that the impurities remain in the paper; this filtered liquid is then evaporated until dry, or one **evaporates** <note>original: *evaporeert*</note> it until a **film** <note>original: *vlies*; a thin layer of crystals forming on the surface, indicating the solution is saturated</note> appears on top, and it is then set aside to **crystallize** <note>original: *crystalliseren*</note>.

### II. Calcination of Salts.

These are **calcined** <note>original: *gecalcineert*; a process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state</note> by **incandescence** <note>original: *gloeyinge*; heating until the material glows red or white</note>, either with or without **fusion** <note>original: *fusie*; melting</note>: for which purpose some substance that serves for purification is sometimes added, of which we shall speak specifically hereafter.

### III. Distillation of Salts.

The **distillation** <note>original: *distillatie*</note> of salts—because they are commonly pregnant with a fixed **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*; the volatile, often acidic or reactive essence of a substance</note>—is carried out using a **retort** <note>a teardrop-shaped glass or clay vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</note>, which is either simple or fitted with a tube; made of glass or of **clay** <note>original: *aarde*</note>; which is placed in a **sand bath** <note>original: *fand*; a container of sand heated by fire to provide even, controlled heat</note> or in the **open fire** <note>original: *blote vuur*; direct flame</note>, depending on whether the **liquid** <note>original: *vogt*; literally "moisture"</note> which one must distill has a greater or lesser degree of **fixity** <note>original: *vastigheid*; the resistance of a substance to being changed or evaporated by heat</note>.

## IV. *The distillation of a retort with a tube is then performed as follows.*

One must have an earthen **retort** <note>a teardrop-shaped vessel with a downward-pointing neck</note> at hand that is strong, which has an open tube or pipe at the top of its back, through which one can throw in the material in stages, and after the material has been cast in, can be covered again. One can coat this vessel with **lute** <note>original: *leem*; a mixture of clay and other materials used to protect glass from fire or to seal joints</note> if desired, and fix it into the distillation furnace with lute in such a way that the pipe stands upright, leaving one or two vent-holes open. At the snout of the retort, one then places a large **receiver** <note>original: *ontvanger* or *recipient*; a large vessel to catch the distilled vapors</note> (because the escaping spirits require a great deal of space). All the joints are then sealed tightly; once the lute has dried gently, one first ignites a soft fire, and then a stronger one, until the retort glows. Then pour bit by bit through the tube, immediately stopping this tube with wet material, lute, or a plug, until all these violent **spirits** <note>original: *spiritus*; the volatile, reactive vapors released during heating</note> have **coagulated** <note>thickened or turned from gas to liquid</note>, being mixed into the water that is in the receiver, and the receiver becomes clear. Then add more through the tube, and stop it again as previously described; and in this manner one makes <term>Clyssus</term> <note>original: *Clyffus*; a 17th-century term for the condensed vapors or the "essence" of several substances distilled together, a term popularized by Paracelsus</note>; see the third figure of the first plate regarding this.

## V. *Regarding the sublimation of Salts.*

**SUBLIMATION** <note>the process where a solid substance is heated until it turns directly into vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface</note> is primarily applied to Salt, as well as to **arsenic** <note>original: *arcenicum*</note>, for the <term>flowers of common salt</term> <note>original: *flores salis communis*; the fine, pure crystals that collect at the top of a vessel during sublimation</note> are obtained in one and the same manner of distillation.

## VI. *On the Fixation of Salts.*

**THE** <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable enough to withstand heat without evaporating</note> of salts is performed in various ways, which will be discussed specifically in their proper place.

## VII. *On the Liquation of Salts.*

**SALTS** can melt <note>original: *smelten*; in this context, it refers to deliquescence, where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid</note>, either if they are placed in moist air or sprinkled with some moisture.

# COMMON SALT. <note>original: *Sal Commune*</note>

## 1. *On the Purification of Salt.*

**THE** purification of common sea salt <note>original: *Zee-sout*</note> occurs in the usual manner, namely: by dissolving it in water, filtering it, and evaporating it until a film <note>original: *vlies*; a thin crust on the surface of the liquid signaling it is ready to crystallize</note> appears, and then setting it aside to crystallize.

## II. *Calcination of Common Salt, or Decrepitated Salt.* <note>original: *Sal decrepitatus*</note>

**PLACE** an unglazed pot in the middle of the coals, put an ounce or two of sea salt into it, and cover the pot: it will then crackle and turn to powder. This crackling they call <term>decrepitation</term> <note>the sharp, snapping sound caused by water molecules trapped inside salt crystals expanding and bursting when heated</note>. From this, one then distills a spirit through the retort according to the art.

## XII. *Sweet Spirit of Salt.*

It is considered very good for fevers and the plague, and is also an effective <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent used to dissolve other substances</note>. Ten or twelve drops of it are administered in some liquid.

## XVI. Sweet Spirit of Common Salt
## which dissolves Gold.
<note>original: *Spiritus Salis Communis Dulcis*</note>

Quench glowing pieces of stone five or six times in the **oil of common salt** <note>original: *Oleum salis communis*; a concentrated form of hydrochloric acid</note>; then distill them, and an acidic **spirit** will come over, by which one can dissolve **gold leaf** in the palm of the hand, as well as **pearls**.

*Secondly*, the **flower of salt** <note>original: *flos salis*; the fine, frost-like sublimation that forms on the vessel walls during heating</note> or sweet crystals will hang at the neck of the <term>retort</term> <note>a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> after the distillation, and will produce the same effect when <term>digested</term> <note>steeped in gentle heat</note> for a considerable time with **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note>.

*Thirdly*, the **spirit of common salt**, after a long distillation, will lose its fine acidity and become sweet.

*Fourthly*, the same, when mixed with the **ardent spirit of Saturn** <note>original: *spiritus ardens saturni*; likely acetone or a similar spirit derived from the distillation of lead acetate</note>, gives another sweet <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent used to extract or dissolve substances</note>, which causes gold to dissolve.

*Fifthly*, from the **spirit of May-dew** <note>original: *spiritus roris majalis*; dew collected in May was highly prized by alchemists as it was believed to contain a "celestial nitre" or life-force from the atmosphere</note> and the <term>calcined</term> <note>heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile parts</note> **Salt**, another solutive water is produced, being <term>dulcified</term> <note>neutralized or "sweetened" of its harsh acidity</note> through a long digestion and <term>irroration</term> <note>a rhythmic moistening or sprinkling process</note>, by which the gold is turned into a volatile and **potable gold** <note>original: *drinkbaar Goud*; "Aurum Potabile," a legendary medicinal elixir made of dissolved gold, believed to be a universal cure</note>.

## XVII. Crystals of Sweet Common Salt, or
## Coagulated Spirit of Common Salt.
<note>original: *Crystalli Salis Comm. Dulc. ofte Spiritus Salis Communis coagulatus*</note>

## XXVII. *The Resurrection of Common Salt.*
<note>original: *De weder opstandinge van het Sal Commune.*</note>

Distill it then; in this way you make everything **volatile** <note>original: *vlug*; capable of being evaporated or turned into vapor</note>; then rectify it three or four times and preserve it.

## II. *Purification of Saltpeter.*

This is then the *sal prunellæ* <note>original: *sal prunellæ*; also known as "plum salt," a medicinal salt prepared from saltpeter and sulfur</note>; to have this thoroughly pure, dissolve <note>original: *smelt*; literally "melt," but in this context refers to dissolving in liquid</note> it in sufficient water, then filter it and crystallize it as was said before regarding the purification of saltpeter.

It is administered to cool [the body] and to provoke urine in burning fevers, throat inflammations, gonorrhea <note>original: *saad-loop*; literally "seed-flow," a historical term for seminal discharge or gonorrhea</note>, and other diseases arising from heat and blockages.

The dose is from ten grains to one dram <note>a dram is approximately 3.9 grams</note>; it is given in some soup or suitable liquid.

## IV. *Another method.*

->Take: *Pure saltpeter, 3 or 4 pounds.* <note>original: *Rec. Nitri puri, libr III of IV.*</note><-
->*Quicklime, 4 pounds.* <note>original: *Calcis vivæ*; unslaked lime</note><-
->Mix. <note>original: *M.*; abbreviation for the Latin *Misce*</note><-

Cement <note>a process of heating a solid in contact with a powder without melting it</note> for five or six days, then extract the *Sal nitrum* <note>saltpeter</note> from it by pouring warm water over it, filtering, and inspissating <note>original: *inpisseren*; thickening a liquid by evaporation, usually over heat</note>. The first crystallization is the best.

It is said that it dispels jaundice <note>original: *geelsugt*</note>, breaks fevers and stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, when ten to sixty grains are administered.

## V. *Another method.*

Take a good portion of saltpeter, pour *spirit of urine* <note>original: *spiritus urinæ*; a solution of ammonia derived from fermented urine</note> over it; distill gradually, then apply a stronger fire until it flows: repeat this five or six times, constantly pouring new *spirit* over it.

It makes metals malleable.

This is done so that the urine-like taste <note>saltpeter has a distinctively sharp, salty, and somewhat bitter metallic taste</note> should not be offensive.

### VII. Pearled Nitre.

One dissolves the nitre in three or four parts of distilled vinegar, and also dissolves two parts of Salt of Pearl <note>a preparation made by dissolving pearls (calcium carbonate) in an acid</note> in the distilled vinegar; add them together, coagulate by evaporating; then place it in a warm location to crystallize.
It is a good cordial <note>a medicine intended to invigorate the heart</note> for burning fevers.

### VIII. Coralline Nitre.

This is prepared in the same manner as the pearled nitre, taking Salt of Coral and nitre, equal parts of each.
The powers are the same as the previous one.

### IX. Saturnine Nitre.

This is made in the same way as before, taking the sugar of Saturn <term>sugar of Saturn: lead acetate, a sweet-tasting but highly toxic lead compound used historically in small doses for its astringent properties</term> and purified nitre, or mineral crystal <note>original: *lapis prunellæ*</note>.
It is useful for shortness of breath <note>original: *engborſtigheid*</note>, heart pain, and heartburn <note>original: *zode*</note>, administered in doses of six or seven grains with some liquid.

## XII. Crystals of Salt of Nitre, or the Fortified Dragon. <note>original: *Crystalli salis nitri, ofte Draco Fortificatus*</note>

Digest the very purified nitre <note>original: *nitrum*; saltpeter</note> in the spirit of salt of nitre <note>original: *spiritus salis nitri*; nitric acid</note>, so much that the same dissolves conveniently; abstract it <note>remove the liquid by distillation</note>, and a phlegm <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, tasteless part of a distillate</note> comes over; pour other spirit upon it again, digest and distill, until it comes over as sharp as it was when poured upon it; then the Dragon has been sufficiently impregnated <note>original: *verswangert*, literally "made pregnant"</note>; then place the moisture that remained in the retort in the cellar to congeal into stone: then dissolve these stones in water, and bring them again to crystals.

It is thought that they drive out all tartareous humors <note>original: *tarteragtige humeuren*; refers to stony deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty "chalkstones," which alchemists compared to the tartar crust in wine barrels</note>, promote urine, and cause looseness of the bowels; taken up to one scruple with some liquid.

### XIII. *Foliated Earth of Salt of Nitre.* <note>original: *Terra Foliata salis Nitri*</note>

Heat **Salt of nitre** <note>original: *Sal nitrum*; saltpeter</note> in a crucible until it glows, and throw a glowing coal into it from time to time, so that the **Salt of nitre** burns up; continue this until it stops burning. Dissolve the remainder in **spirit of vinegar** <note>original: *spiritus aceti*</note>; filter it, coagulate it <note>thicken it into a solid</note>, and let that be repeated three times with new **vinegar** <note>original: *acetum*</note>. Finally, dissolve it in **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; high-proof alcohol</note>, which is then distilled; thus there remains on the bottom a talc-like earth of saltpeter, as meltable as wax.

It serves, it is said, in the obstructions of the **chyle** <note>the milky fluid taken up by the lacteals from the food in the intestine during digestion</note>, spleen, etc., administered in doses of up to half a drachme <note>approx. 1.9 grams</note> with some aperitif <note>a medicine that opens the natural passages of the body</note>.

### XIV. *Antimonial Nitre.* <note>original: *Nitrum Antimoniatum*</note>

This is the saltpeter which (once the **diaphoretic antimony** <note>original: *antimonium diaphoreticum*; a medicinal preparation of antimony used to induce sweating</note> has been prepared) is leached out with water, filtered, and crystallized.

It is considered good for use in hot fevers.

## XXIII. Another method with Sulfur.

Take refined saltpeter <note>original: *salpeter*; potassium nitrate</note>, as much as you like, and put it into a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> that has a pipe on its back <note>This refers to a "tubulated retort," which has an opening at the top to add materials during the process</note>; attach a large receiver to it, in which there is some water. Kindle the fire so that the saltpeter melts; then, through the pipe, throw a little pure sulfur onto the flowing saltpeter. Repeat this until the saltpeter is consumed; then a liquid or the spirit of nitre <note>original: *spiritus nitri*; nitric acid</note> will come over like a *butter of antimony* <note>original: *butyrum antimonii*; here referring to a thick, oily consistency rather than the actual antimony compound</note>. Then <term>dephlegm</term> <note>Remove the watery part (phlegm) through gentle heating</note> and <term>rectify</term> <note>Purify a liquid by distilling it again</note> it; that which remains in the retort is a *fixed salt of nitre* <note>original: *Sal nitrum fixum*; the alkaline residue, usually potassium carbonate</note>.

## XXIV. Sweet Spirit of Nitre.

Take good spirit of nitre and *alcohol of wine* <note>original: *alcohol vini*; concentrated ethanol</note>, eight ounces of each; put them into a <term>matrass</term> <note>A long-necked glass flask</note> and set it on some straw under the chimney. Thus the moisture will become hot without any fire, and after half an hour or an hour, it will boil strongly. Guard yourself against the red vapors that fly abundantly out of the neck of the matrass. This boiling being over, you shall find a clear liquid; pour it into a vial and keep it; this is called *sweet spirit of nitre* <note>original: *spiritus nitri dulcis*; a mixture of ethyl nitrite and alcohol, often used as a diuretic or sedative</note>.

It is good against colic with wind <note>gas</note> and the pain of the <term>gravel</term> <note>Small stones or crystals in the kidneys or bladder</note>. Likewise, it is good against <term>mother-convulsions</term> <note>original: *moertrekkingen*; historical term for hysterical spasms or uterine cramps</note> and all obstructions.

It is administered in doses of four to eight drops in some broth or a suitable liquid.

### XXVI. *Common Strong Water.* <note>original: *Aqua fortis communis*; a historical term for nitric acid</note>

Crush and mix together thirty-two ounces of purified, dry saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> with an equal amount of vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfate</note> that has been <term>calcined</term> <note>heated to remove moisture and volatile components</note> until it becomes white, as we shall describe hereafter. Place this mixture with an equal amount of dried clay or earth into a stone or <term>luted</term> <note>coated with a protective layer of clay or paste to withstand high heat</note> glass <term>retort</term>, but ensure that a portion of it remains empty. Place the retort in a closed <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" the heat from the roof back onto the vessel</note> and attach a wide receiver to it; seal <note>original: *luteert*</note> all joints tightly. Begin heating first with a small fire and make the retort hot gradually; thereafter increase the fire. But when you see the drops of the spirit coming into the retort in the form of a red vapor <note>nitrogen dioxide gas</note>, then keep the fire burning for eight or nine hours. Finally, stoke the fire as strongly as you can until white vapors appear in place of the red ones. Let the vessels cool then, and disconnect everything; you will have thirty-four ounces of strong-water in the receiver. Store it in a well-stoppered earthenware jar; it is only suitable for dissolving <note>original: *solveren*</note> metals.

### XXVII. *Royal Water or Gold-Dissolver.* <note>original: *Aqua regia ofte Stygia Chryſulca*; a mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</note>

->Take Saltpeter.<-
->Sal ammoniac, of each 2 parts.<- <note>original: *Sal nitri. Sal armon. ää p. II.*</note>
->Crushed flint, 3 parts.<- <note>original: *Silic. contuſ. p. III.*</note>
->Mix.<- <note>original: *M.*</note>

Distill this through a retort with a pipe on its back <note>a tubulated retort, which has an opening at the top for adding materials or regulating pressure</note>.

## XXVIII. Another Method.

Take saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, as much as you please, and mix it with three parts of crushed clay; distill in an open fire through a <term>retort</term>, and you will have the spirit of nitre <note>original: *aqua nitri*; nitric acid</note>. Afterward, extract a salt from the ashes <note>original: *cineres*</note> with warm water, continuing until the ashes are stripped of all sharpness. Mix these ashes with as much sal ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniac*; ammonium chloride</note> as the weight of the nitre was previously. Distill this through an open fire with a retort, and thus you have your royal water <note>original: *aqua regia*; a powerful acid mixture capable of dissolving gold</note>.

## XXIX. *Tincture of Nitre.* <note>original: *Tinctura nitri*</note>

This is prepared in the same manner as one makes the *Tincture of common salt*. It is a good restorative and a <term>sudorific</term> <note>a substance that induces sweating, often used to break a fever</note>.

## XXX. *Riverius’s Tartarized Spirit of Fixed Nitre.* <note>original: *Spiritus nitri fixi Tartarisati Riverii*; named after Lazare Rivière (1589–1655), a famous French physician</note>

Pour one pound of rectified spirit of nitre into a wide glass <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass bulb</note>; gradually pour an equal amount of liquor of tartar <note>original: *liquor tartari*; a solution of potassium carbonate</note> onto it. Continue pouring as long as you see it foaming. Then the nitrated tartar <note>original: *tartarum nitratum*</note> will sink to the bottom. Decant the liquid and <term>dulcify</term> <note>to neutralize or sweeten a substance, often by washing it or adding a milder liquid</note> it with rosewater. It is given in cases of long-lasting illness along with suitable liquids, in doses of six to eight <term>grains</term> <note>a historical unit of weight, roughly 0.06 grams</note>, in crayfish water <note>original: *Kreeftewater*; a medicinal broth or distillate made from crayfish</note> or kidney-water <note>original: *Niere-water*; a medicinal infusion intended for kidney health</note>, and it is a good remedy against fever.

### XXXI. Purification of Saltpeter.

The best purification is achieved through fixed alkalis <note>original: *alcalia fixa*; stable alkaline substances like potassium carbonate that do not vaporize easily</note>; therefore, make a strong lye from salt of tartar <note>original: *Sal tartari*; potassium carbonate derived from burnt wine lees</note> or from potash; infuse the nitre <note>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note> in this, and thus the fixed salt will take all the bad acid <note>original: *acidum*</note> unto itself. Then one evaporates the excess moisture and allows it to form into crystals.

### XXXII. Sweet Spirit of Nitre. <note>original: *Spiritus nitri dulcis*; a mixture of ethyl nitrite and alcohol, often used as a diuretic</note>

Take one part of spirit of nitre <note>nitric acid</note> that has been well rectified <note>purified by re-distillation</note>; add to it three parts of spirit of wine <note>original: *spiritus vini*; ethanol/alcohol</note>: digest <note>warm gently to allow a reaction</note> and distill through a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distilling liquids</note> in a sand bath.

### XXXIII. Spirit of Nitre and Vitriolated Nitre.

->Take 2 pounds of Nitre.<-
->Take 1 pound of rectified Oil of Vitriol.<-
->Mix.<-

Put these in a retort and distill by degrees <note>slowly increasing the temperature</note> until it is dry; thus you have a very strong spirit of nitre: on the bottom there remains the vitriolated nitre <note>original: *nitrum vitriolatum*; potassium sulfate</note>. This is used for all heat of the blood <note>a historical term for fevers, inflammations, or high blood pressure</note>.

### XXXIV. Regeneration of Nitre.

Take half an ounce of spirit of nitre; drop into it the liquor of tartar <note>original: *liquor tartari*; a saturated solution of potassium carbonate</note> until the effervescence <note>bubbling or fizzing caused by a chemical reaction</note> ceases; then evaporate it until it is dry, and thus you have a regenerated nitre.

## XXXV. Fulminating Nitre. <note>original: *Nitrum Fulminans*; a mixture of saltpeter, potassium carbonate, and sulfur that explodes when heated</note>

->Take 3 drams of purified Nitre.<-

->Take 1 dram of Sulphur.<-
->Mix.<-

## XXXVI. Nitrated Nitre. <note>original: *Nitrum Nitratum*</note>

->Mix.<-

## XXXVII. Ammoniacal Nitre. <note>original: *Nitrum Armoniacale*</note>

It is highly praised for use in fevers.

## XXXVIII. Red Essentified Nitre. <note>original: *Nitrum Rubrum Effentificatum*; a medicinal saltpeter preparation flavored and colored with fruit juice</note>

Take <term>lapis prunellæ</term> <note>a purified form of saltpeter (potassium nitrate) fused with a small amount of sulfur, used to treat fevers and sore throats</note>, ten ounces, and <term>barberry juice</term> <note>original: *succus berberorum*; the acidic juice of the Berberis berry</note>, two and a half pounds, and mix them together. Macerate until all the nitre is dissolved; then filter through a cloth. Next, evaporate the excess moisture; then place it in a cool spot to crystallize. The remainder that has not crystallized is evaporated again, and set once more to crystallize, and this is done for as long as crystals appear. These crystals are then dissolved again in fresh barberry juice and crystallized in the manner described above; this can be repeated several times.

It is considered useful for hot fevers, administered elsewhere in doses of forty to sixty grains.

## XXXIX. Vitriolated Nitre of Mynsicht. <note>original: *Nitrum Vitriolatum van Minsicht*; a chemical preparation attributed to Adrian von Mynsicht (1603–1638), a famous German alchemist and physician</note>

->Take 1 part prepared Nitre. <note>original: *Nitri præp. p I.*</note><-
->Take 2 parts rectified Spirit of Vitriol. <note>original: *Sp. vitrioli rect. p. II.*; a concentrated form of sulfuric acid</note><-
->Mix. <note>original: *M.* for *Misce*</note><-

Distill this through a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note> with increasing degrees of fire, first gentle and then stronger, until finally the retort glows. When no more spirits rise up, allow it to cool gradually, and thus a white powder remains at the bottom of the retort, which is then almost no longer corrosive. Upon this, one then pours as much <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid</note> as is needed for a complete solution; then filter it and evaporate it by half.

### XL. Flowers of Nitre <note>original: *Flores Nitri*; in alchemy, "flowers" refer to a substance that has been sublimated into a fine, powdery crust, often resembling blossoms</note>

Dissolve purified saltpeter in rose water; afterward, place it in a new glazed pot and set it for a time in a cold location until the *flowers* penetrate through the pot and hang on the outside of the vessel. These are wiped off with a rabbit’s foot <note>a traditional tool used by early chemists and artists to gently collect delicate powders or gold leaf without damaging them</note> and preserved for later use.

It is useful for fevers and cools all "heats" of the internal organs.

### XLI. Quintessence of Nitre <note>original: *Quinta Essentia Nitri*; the "fifth essence," representing the most purified and potent form of a substance</note>

Take purified saltpeter and an equal amount of decrepitated common salt <note>original: *gedecrepiteert gemeen sout*; table salt (sodium chloride) that has been heated until it stops crackling, indicating all moisture has been driven out</note> that is very white. Put these together into a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-sloping neck used for distilling liquids</note> placed in the ash; heat it by degrees until it finally reaches a very strong fire. Then, one distills its red <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; a volatile, concentrated liquid produced by distillation</note>, which does not quickly turn into moisture. Once distilled, let everything stand for another full day so that the spirit finally turns to liquid. This spirit must then be rectified <note>purified through repeated distillation</note> seven times upon its <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>literally "dead head"; the useless solid remains left in the retort after all volatile components have been driven off</note>, and purified of its <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, tasteless part of a distillate</note> through distillation. Then, add this to the <term>salt</term> that has been extracted from the *caput mortuum*, which must first be made very pure, artificially "sweetened" <note>likely meaning neutralized or stripped of corrosive properties</note>, and turned red.

This spirit is held to be equal to <term>potable gold</term> <note>original: *aurum potabile*; a legendary alchemical panacea consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid, believed to cure all diseases and grant longevity</note>.

# ROCK SALT <note>original: *Sal Gemmæ*; a transparent, gem-like mineral salt found in mines, distinct from sea salt</note>.

## I. Spirit of Rock Salt, Spirit of Fusible Mercurial Rock Salt <note>original: *Spiritus Salis Gemmæ, Spiritus Salis Gemmæ Fusibilis Mercurialis*</note>.

This is made in the same manner as the *spirit of common salt* <note>the 17th-century name for hydrochloric acid</note>; namely, one mixes the rock salt with three times as much pot-earth <note>original: *potaarde*; a type of clay used as a medium to prevent the salt from melting into a solid mass during heating</note>, and one distills it through a <term>retort</term> over an open fire.

## II. Balsam of Rock Salt or Liquor <note>original: *Balsamus Salis Gemmæ ofte Liquor*</note>.

Take two pounds of rock salt; let it melt over the fire, then dissolve, filter, and <term>coagulate</term> <note>the process of thickening a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state, usually through evaporation</note> it: one repeats this dissolution, filtration, and coagulation so many times until the rock salt is brought to the utmost subtlety <note>fineness or purity</note>, which one knows has been achieved when a small portion of it is held to a candle and it melts immediately.

It is considered a great *arcanum* <note>a secret, powerful remedy</note> for ruptures <note>hernias</note>, used both externally and internally.

## II. Flowers of Sal Ammoniac. <note>original: *Flores Salis Armoniaci*; "flowers" refers to a fine powder produced by sublimation</note>

Take finely crushed <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note> and filings of steel, an equal amount of each; once they are mixed together, put them in a <term>flask</term> <note>original: *kolf*; a glass or ceramic vessel used for heating</note>, and <term>sublimate</term> <note>to heat a solid until it becomes a vapor and then settles again as a solid, leaving impurities behind</note> them from a sand bath; in this way, the impurities will remain lying on the bottom, and the ammonia will rise up pure, along with a little of the steel.
Then take some of this <term>sublimate</term>, and fused <term>common salt</term> <note>original: *Sal Commune fusum*; ordinary table salt that has been melted to remove moisture</note>, an equal amount of each; sublimate again, and repeat this up to seven times, always throwing away the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>literally "dead head"; the useless residue remaining after the process</note>: always adding a little fused common salt to the mixture.
These rouse the spirits, purify the blood of all sharp acidity, and open all obstructions <note>referring to blockages in the body's internal systems or "vessels"</note>.

## III. Another method.

Let everything be finely crushed and properly mixed together: put this mixture into a stone flask; set it in the sand bath, and place a <term>blind helm</term> <note>original: *blinden helm*; a lid or cap for a flask that has no outlet pipe, used to collect vapors</note> upon it; then heat it first with a gentle fire; increase it gradually, until you see the white <term>flowers</term> <note>original: *flores*</note> rising up in the form of flour, which will hang in the helm and the upper part of the flask: keep this fire going until nothing more rises; then let everything become cold, and gently take off the helm; collect the flowers with a feather, then seal them tightly in a glass: they possess the same powers as the Sal Ammoniac: but one administers it in fewer <term>grains</term> <note>a traditional unit of weight; approximately 0.06 grams</note> than the other, namely from four to fifteen grains.

## IV. Fixation of Sal Ammoniac and Calcination.

It was <term>fixed</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate when heated</note> with <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: *levende kalk*; calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance</note>, taking an equal amount of each: once mixed together, it is heated rapidly with a strong fire, blowing with a bellows: this is then <term>leached</term> <note>original: *loogt*; washing the mixture with water to extract the soluble salts</note> with water: it is evaporated until it is dry.

## V. Volatile Spirit of Sal Ammoniac. <note>original: *Spiritus volatilis Salis Armoniaci*; a strong alkaline solution, essentially ammonia dissolved in water</note>

Take one pound of **Sal Ammoniac**, and three pounds of quicklime; crush both separately, and having mixed them in a mortar, pour six ounces of common water upon them. Stir the material properly, then put it immediately into a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note>, half of which should remain empty: set the retort in a <term>reverberatory oven</term> <note>original: *reverbereer-oven*; a furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat back onto the vessel</note>, attach a wide <term>receiver</term> <note>original: *ontvanger*; a glass vessel used to collect the condensed vapors</note> to it; seal everything tightly with <term>lute</term> <note>original: *luteert*; an airtight paste or clay used to seal the joints of alchemical apparatus</note>, then the <term>distillation</term> begins with a slow fire for two or three hours; gradually increasing, until no more comes out: remove the receiver, and immediately pour the *spirit* into a vial, but guard your nose against the strong and sharp vapors; stop the glass tightly with wax to preserve the spirit; thus you have five ounces and six <term>drachms</term> <note>original: *dragmen*; a historical unit of weight</note>.

This spirit is excellent for all diseases that come from any obstructions or rotting of the <term>humors</term> <note>original: *vogten*; the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which early medicine believed must stay balanced to maintain health</note>, such as malignant fevers, <term>falling sickness</term> <note>epilepsy</note>, paralysis, plague, and smallpox, driving out the bad fluids, either through sweating or through the urinary tracts.

Crush and mix thoroughly together eight ounces of **Sal Ammoniac** and as much **Salt of Tartar** <note>original: *Sal tartari*; potassium carbonate, often used as a reagent in alchemical processes</note>: put this mixture immediately into a glass flask; mix into it three ounces of rain-water: place a <term>helm</term> <note>original: *helm*; the top part of a still, also called an alembic, that directs vapors into the cooling neck</note> upon it, and attach a receiver, and everything being sealed <note>original: *toe geluteert*; made airtight using a sealant</note> with a wet bladder, place your flask in the sand <note>a "sand bath" used to provide even, indirect heat</note>; heat at first with a gentle fire: and increase it thereafter gradually, so that the <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long neck</note> remains nicely hot, and that the spirits run out drop by drop: but when no more will run out, then remove the receiver; then seal everything tightly with the <term>common lute</term> <note>original: *gemeene lutum*; a paste made of clay or lime used to seal joints</note>, and increase the fire to the third degree, and let it continue so for two hours, and then white **white flowers of sal ammoniac** <note>original: *flores salis armoniaci albi*; the solid crystalline substance that forms directly from the vapor</note> shall sublimate, which shall remain hanging on the underside of the helm in the form of flour.

One gathers the **flowers** with a feather: which can be used as those described previously, of which you shall have half an ounce.

## VII. Sweet Spirit of Sal Ammoniac.
<note>original: *Spiritus Salis Armoniaci dulcis*; a solution of ammonium carbonate in alcohol, considered "sweet" because the addition of spirits of wine masked the harshness of the salt</note>

Take four ounces each of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note> and **salt of tartar** <note>potassium carbonate</note>, crush them separately, and mix them well together in a marble mortar; put the mixture into an earthen flask; pour over it ten ounces of well-rectified **brandy** <note>high-proof distilled wine used here as a solvent</note>; stir everything well with a wooden spatula; place a <term>helm</term> <note>the cap or "head" of a still that collects vapors</note> upon it, and <term>lute</term> <note>to seal a joint using a paste (lute) to make it airtight</note> a receiver to it; then place it in a furnace on the sand <note>a sand bath, used to provide steady, indirect heat</note>, and light a small fire beneath it to warm the flask; in this way, the **volatile salt** <note>the transcription reads "fout," a common OCR error for *zout* (salt)</note> shall rise and stick to the helm; continue this until no more comes over. The operation is finished within four or five hours: then let everything cool and detach the vessels; then you will find the volatile salt in the helm, and the spirit in the receiver: immediately put both into a flask and place it on the sand; attach a receiver and seal everything well; then distill with a gentle fire; <term>cohobate</term> <note>the process of pouring the distilled liquid back onto the remaining solids and re-distilling to increase potency</note> up to three times, and keep the distilled liquid in a tightly closed glass: nearly all the **volatile salt** <note>original: *Sal volatile*</note> is dissolved in the brandy, and what remains will dissolve in the bottle.

It is a good remedy for **sleeping sickness** <note>historically referring to states of lethargy, stupor, or coma</note>, **paralysis**, **scurvy**, **malignant fevers**, and for **hysterical disorders** <note>original: *moerqualen*; literally "mother-ailments," a term for conditions believed to originate in the womb (the "mother")</note>. It can be used in place of the *spirit of sal ammoniac* described before; it does not have such an unpleasant taste. It drives out the humors through sweating, or through **insensible perspiration** <note>the release of moisture through the skin that evaporates before it can be seen as sweat</note>.

It is administered in doses of twelve to thirty drops with any suitable liquid.

# CHAPTER XVI.

->Concerning<-

## A L U M.

### *I. Purification or Crystallization of Alum.*

The purification of **alum** <note>a mineral salt used historically in medicine, dyeing, and tanning</note> occurs in the common manner, namely: that one dissolves the same in warm water; filters it, and evaporates it until a thin film appears upon it, which one then sets aside to crystallize.

### *II. Calcination of Alum.*

One places the coarsely crushed alum in an earthen pan, sets it upon the fire, and evaporates all the **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, inactive part of a substance</note> out of it, so that it becomes spongy.

### III. *Salt of Alum.*
<note>original: *Sal Aluminis*</note>

Take the **burnt alum** <note>original: *alumen ustum*</note>, or its **dead head** <note>original: *caput mortuum*; the residue remaining after distillation or intense heating</note>; boil it in water and filter it, which is then evaporated until it becomes a salt.

## IV. Phlegm and Spirit of Alum.
<note>original: *Phlegma en Spiritus Aluminis*</note>

Distill a good portion of alum through a retort in a sand bath <note>a container of sand used to distribute heat evenly around the glass vessel</note>; thus you shall draw off the **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, non-medicinal part of the substance</note> with a gentle fire. But by stoking the fire more strongly, a very white **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*; the acidic, volatile vapor of the alum</note> comes over.

## V. Sweet Spirit of Alum.
<note>original: *Spiritus Aluminis dulcis*</note>

Take the **spirit of alum**, rectify <note>purify by repeated distillation</note> it several times with **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; concentrated ethanol</note>, and it shall become pleasantly sweet. 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It is a diuretic <note>original: *pisdryvent*; promoting the passage of urine</note> when four or five drops are administered with wine. The **phlegm** is used upon wounds, and it cleanses the gums.

## VI. Magistery, or Magisterial Spirit of Alum.
<note>original: *Magisterium, ofte Spiritus Aluminis Magisteriatus*; a 'magistery' is a preparation where the chemist seeks to capture the full essence or 'mastery' of the starting material</note>

Take purified alum, put it in a glass, sprinkle water upon it, and let it dissolve; then filter and distill it in the ashes <note>another form of heat bath using warm embers or ash</note> from a low flask until it is dry. Then dissolve it again in the same manner as before, and distill. Repeat this solution and coagulation until the entire substance of the alum has passed over. 
*This is a good styptic.* <note>original: *stypticum*; a substance that contracts body tissues to stop bleeding</note>

After it has stood for 24 hours, draw off the liquid again, and do this up to five or six times. Having then saved the **phlegm**,

## II. *Emetic White Vitriol, or Gilla Vitrioli.*
<note>original: *Vitriolum Album vomitivum*; *Gilla Vitrioli* was a term popularized by the alchemist Paracelsus for purified white vitriol (zinc sulfate) used as a gentle emetic to induce vomiting.</note>

Dissolve a good portion of white vitriol in Water, or **phlegm of vitriol** <note>original: *phlegma vitrioli*; the watery, acidic liquid obtained during the distillation of vitriol</note>, and once filtered, evaporate it in a glass flask until two-thirds have vanished: then set the remainder for five days in the cellar in a cold place, and then separate the crystals: then evaporate once more a third of the remaining moisture, and set it in a cool cellar to obtain new crystals; continue in this way with crystallizing and evaporating until you have all the crystals: then lay these crystals in the Sun to dry, and preserve them. They cause very gentle vomiting; one gives them from twelve grains to one **drachm** <note>original: *drachma*; a unit of weight approximately equal to 3.9 grams</note> in some soup or other liquid.

## III. *Calcination of Vitriol.*
<note>Calcination involves heating a substance to high temperatures, often in the open air, to change its physical or chemical state—in this case, dehydrating and oxidizing iron sulfate.</note>

Take as much green vitriol as you desire, put it into an unglazed earthen pot, and set it in the fire, and let the vitriol melt in the water: boil it until the moisture has vanished, or until the material has become grey; resembling a white color: then take the pot from the fire; and the pot having been broken, one calls that material vitriol that is calcined to whiteness.
If you now calcine this white vitriol for a long time through the fire, it shall become as red as blood; which one calls ***colcothar*** <note>original: *colcothar*; the chemical remains (mostly iron oxide) after the distillation of sulfuric acid from vitriol, used as a pigment or a styptic to stop bleeding</note>: which, when placed upon a wound, stills the bleeding.

### IV. *Emetic-Purging Vitriol.*

It causes more purging than vomiting, given from thirty to sixty grains against fevers, administered with some liquid.

It induces vomiting when a dose of twenty to sixty <term>grains</term> <note>A tiny unit of weight, approximately 65 milligrams.</note> is administered.

## VIII. Calcination of Vitriol, performed in a closed vessel.

Take <term>vitriol</term> which has been repeatedly dissolved, coagulated, and well-purified, and which has been dried with a gentle heat: put it into a <term>matrass</term> <note>A long-necked glass flask with a round or flat bottom, used in distilling and heating.</note>, and seal it in the <term>manner of Hermes</term> <note>original: *wyse van Hermes*; a "hermetic" seal made by melting the glass neck of the flask shut to make it completely airtight.</note>: then place this matrass in warm ashes, which are no hotter than the heat of the Sun in Summer: leave this standing until the vitriol turns from yellow to a blood-red color; which is usually accomplished in about twenty <term>full days</term> <note>original: *etmalen*; a period of 24 hours comprising both day and night.</note>.

## IX. Dew of Vitriol.
<note>original: *Ros Vitrioli*; a subtle spirit or moisture drawn from the raw mineral.</note>

Draw the vapor from the <term>crude vitriol</term> <note>Raw, unrefined sulfate minerals.</note> in a hot water bath, using a flask that is not too high.
It is useful for hot headaches, and it strengthens the internal organs; it is also good for <term>scorbutic ulcers</term> <note>original: *scheurbuikige ulceratien*; sores in the mouth caused by scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).</note> of the mouth: one administers two <term>drams</term> <note>A unit of weight; one dram is roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of it daily.

<note>original: *Aqua Vitrioli fecunda.*</note>

After the previously described red dew has been distilled off, place your <term>flask</term> <note>original: *kolf*; a glass vessel used for heating and distilling.</note> in the sand bath, and distill off as much as you are able.

It cleanses, it is said, the kidneys, and soothes all internal corrosives; it removes inflammations and eases pains.

## XI. *Acid Phlegm of Vitriol.*
<note>original: *Phlegma Vitrioli acidum*; "phlegm" refers to the watery, less potent distillate that comes over before the stronger spirits.</note>

Distill a good portion of blue vitriol from the ashes <note>A heat-diffusing "ash bath" used for gentle, even heating.</note> through the <term>alembic</term> <note>A classic distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cap with a downward tube.</note>; then <term>cohobate</term> <note>The process of pouring the distilled liquid back onto the residue to re-distill it, concentrating its properties.</note> up to seven times, driving it off strongly from the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>Latin: "dead head"; the solid, useless residue left in the vessel after all volatile substances have been distilled away.</note> on the final round.

It is said that this is useful against headaches and epilepsy.

## XII. *Volatile Spirit of Vitriol.*
<note>original: *Spiritus vitrioli Volatilis.*</note>

Heat the well-purified and dried vitriol through the <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances that require higher heat.</note> in an open fire using graduated heat <note>Increasing the temperature in stages.</note>, so that after the phlegm, the spirits that may be within follow; add two parts distilled Rainwater to the resulting moisture, and distill once again in a water bath; then the subtle spirit of vitriol flies upward with the Water, leaving the sour oil at the bottom. It is very penetrating in all hot fevers.

# XVI. *Sweet Oil and Spirit of Vitriol.*

Pour distilled vinegar over three pounds of well-calcined <note>Calcination involves heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile parts, leaving a dry powder.</note> vitriol, until it stands three or four fingers' breadth above it; digest <note>Digestion is the application of gentle, consistent heat to a substance over a long period to encourage dissolution or chemical change.</note>, decant, and pour new distilled vinegar on it again: do this five or six times; always digesting for several days. # XVII. *Another Method.*

## XVIII. Philosophical Spirit of Vitriol, called *Cojob* <note>original: *Cojob*; likely a variation of 'cohob,' referring to a substance that has been redistilled or concentrated.</note> of Antimony.

Evaporate the water with which the **Mercury of Life** <note>original: *Mercurius Vitæ*; a white powder (antimony oxychloride) used as a potent purgative and emetic.</note> is dulcorated <note>original: *gedulcoreert*; to wash a substance with water to remove salts or acidic residues.</note> in a water bath, until it begins to turn yellowish and sour: this moisture can then be rectified <note>Rectification is the process of refining a liquid through repeated distillation to increase its purity and strength.</note> through an earthen retort.

It possesses greater power than common spirits against fevers; it eases the pain of the pox <note>original: *pokken*; likely referring to syphilis, which was commonly treated with chemical preparations in this period.</note>, restores obstructions in the spleen and mesentery <note>original: *darmscheil*; the fold of membrane that attaches the intestine to the abdominal wall.</note>, and strengthens the stomach. It is used against melancholy, hypochondria <note>Historically, hypochondria was viewed as a physical disease of the "hypochondrium" (the area below the ribs), often linked to the spleen and digestive vapors.</note>, epilepsy, and all other ailments of the head. It is administered in doses of 3, 4, and up to 8 drops.

It serves to induce sweating <note>original: *sweeten*; used in the sense of a diaphoretic to "sweat out" a disease.</note>, and is used for all obstructions, thick blood, scurvy of the skin <note>original: *schurft des huids*; a general term for itchy or scaly skin conditions like scabies or eczema.</note>, etc. It is administered in doses of 20 to 30 drops.

# XX. Alkalized Spirit, or the Opening Water of Penotus, and Muffet’s Anti-Dropsy Remedy.

<note>original: *Spiritus Alcalifatus, ofte Aqua Aperiens Penoti, en Antihydropicum Muffetti*. Bernard Penotus (c. 1519–1617) and Thomas Muffet (1553–1604) were famous physicians and alchemists who promoted chemical medicines.</note>

It is considered effective for all obstructions <note>Historically, "obstructions" referred to blockages in the liver, spleen, or other organs thought to cause illness.</note>; it is administered in doses from one scruple to three drachms in wine.

## XXII. Diaphoretic Spirit of Vitriol.
<note>original: *Spiritus Vitrioli diaphoreticus*. A 'diaphoretic' is a medicine used to induce sweating, believed to help the body expel "morbid humors" or toxins.</note>

->Take: 6 ounces of Common Spirit of Vitriol.<-
->Common Salt.<-
->Tartar.<-

<note>original: *Sp. Vitr. vulg.* (Spiritus Vitrioli vulgaris), *Sal. Comm.* (Sal Commune), *Tartari*, *C.C. uſti* (Cornu Cervi ustum). Burnt hartshorn was a source of ammonia and was frequently used in early chemistry.</note>
->Mix.<-

## XXIII. Antiepileptic Spirit of Vitriol for children’s convulsions.
<note>original: *Spiritus Vitrioli antepilepticus voor de kinder ſtuipen*.</note>

Take four pounds of Hungarian Vitriol <note>original: *Ongerſe Vitriool*. The powdered residue <note>original: *caput mortuum*; literally "dead head," the solid waste left in the vessel after the volatile parts have been driven off.</note> is driven in an open fire, which is first stoked gently, into a large receiver; this can be rectified <note>To 'rectify' is to purify a liquid through repeated distillation.</note> once again and preserved.

This liquid is mixed with some other antiepileptic remedies against the convulsions of children.

## XXIV. Another by Basilius.
<note>Basilius Valentinus was a legendary 15th-century alchemist, though the name was likely a pseudonym for the salt-maker Johann Thölde. His works bridge the gap between medieval alchemy and early modern chemistry.</note>

Pour warm distilled vinegar <note>original: *acetum distillatum*</note> over a good portion of verdigris <note>original: *Spaans-groen*; a green pigment or crust formed by the action of acetic acid on copper, often used in medical preparations.</note>; extract and decant; draw off the moisture through the helm <note>The 'helm' is the cap of a still or alembic where vapors gather to be condensed.</note>; dissolve the remainder in rainwater <note>original: *aqua pluviali*</note>, filter it, evaporate it until a skin forms on top, and allow it to crystallize.

This is administered for the falling sickness <note>An archaic term for epilepsy.</note> and convulsions with some suitable liquid, in a dose of up to one scruple <note>original: *scruipel*; a unit of apothecary weight, approximately 1.3 grams.</note>.

## XXVI. Paracelsus's Antiepileptic Spirit of Vitriol.
<note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals and chemicals in medicine, moving away from purely herbal ancient remedies.</note>

### XXXI. Another which is red.

### XXXII. Another method.

## XXXIV. *Another Oil from the Sulfur of Vitriol.* <note>original: *Oleum uit de Sulphur Vitrioli*.</note>

It is useful for those diseases in which one normally uses the sulfur of vitriol.

## XXXV. *Flowers of the Earth of Vitriol.* <note>original: *Flores van de Terra Vitrioli*; "Flowers" refers to a powder produced through sublimation.</note>

Sublime the black earth of vitriol, or the ochre <note>The mineral residue, mostly iron oxide, left after processing vitriol</note> from which the salt has been extracted, with equal parts of sal ammoniac <term>Sal armoniacum; ammonium chloride used as a flux or to aid sublimation</term>; stoke first a gentle fire, and thereafter a stronger one, until no more smoke is seen to rise: then pour rainwater upon the sublimate, and let it stand for a day and a night in the water-bath <note>A *balneum mariae*, providing steady, moderate heat</note>, so the subtle powder will sink to the bottom, which one can then further dulcorate <term>wash with water to remove any remaining salts or impurities</term>. This powder, when placed in the fire, partly burns and partly melts into copper.

## XXXVI. *Flowers of the Sulfur of Vitriol.* <note>original: *Flores Sulphuris Vitrioli*.</note>

Take the sweet sulfur of vitriol, sublime it without any addition, using a low sublimation vessel, adding the material bit by bit, and each time lifting the helm <note>The "head" or cap of the distilling apparatus</note> and then replacing it.

## XXXVII. Flowers from Raw Vitriol. <note>original: *Flores ex vitriolo Crudo*; "Flowers" in alchemy refers to a fine, powdery substance produced by sublimation—heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collects again as a solid.</note>
