## XXXVIII. Ochre Earth of Vitriol. <note>original: *Terra Vitrioli Ochrea*</note>

Dissolve pure vitriol in spring water; let it stand for a long time, and the earth or *terra vitrioli* will subside <note>settle to the bottom</note> of its own accord, like an ochre.

## XXXIX. Sweet Sulfur of Vitriol. <note>original: *Sulphur Vitrioli dulce*</note>

Dissolve pure vitriol in warm water, drop the **oil of tartar per deliquium** <term>oleum tartari p. d.; a liquid form of potassium carbonate created by allowing the salt to absorb enough moisture from the air to liquefy</term> into it gradually, and the *sulphur vitrioli* <note>In this context, "sulfur" refers to the flammable or oily principle of the mineral, not just the yellow element sulfur</note> will precipitate, which one must edulcorate <term>edulcoreren; to wash away salts or acids with water until the substance is tasteless and pure</term> and dry.
It is said that the same is good for lung diseases.

## XL. Purging Sulfur of Vitriol. <note>original: *Sulphur Vitrioli purgans*</note>

Pour as much **phlegm of vitriol** <term>phlegma vitrioli; the watery, non-acidic liquid first produced during the distillation of vitriol</term>, or otherwise distilled water, over a good portion of vitriol until it stands four fingers' breadth above it; let it digest <note>heat gently over a period of time</note>, and the earth will settle; filter the moisture, and drop in the **oil of tartar per deliquium**, and the *sulphur vitrioli* will precipitate; decant <note>pour off the top liquid</note>, edulcorate with warm water, and dry.
The dose is from five to ten grains.

->Further.<-

In the same way, one makes **purging sulfur of vitriol of Mars** <note>original: *sulphur vitrioli Martis purgans*; "Mars" is the alchemical name for Iron</note>, dissolving it in the phlegm of vitriol, purifying it, and precipitating it with the **oil of tartar per deliquium**.

## XLI. Fixed or Martial Sulfur of Vitriol. <note>original: *Sulphur Vitrioli Fixum, ofte Martiale*; "Martial" refers to Mars, the alchemical symbol for iron, indicating this preparation involves iron or steel.</note>

Take one part filings of steel, purified of all uncleanness, and two parts blue **Hungarian** *vitriol* <note>original: *Ongerse vitriool*; Hungarian vitriol was a high-quality mineral sulfate often imported for chemical work</note>; once they are crushed, mix them together, place them in a glass, and saturate them with *distilled vinegar* <term>acetum destillatum</term>, so that it stands two fingers' breadth above the mixture: boil this in a sand bath <note>a container of sand heated to provide even, controlled temperature</note> until it is dry, and at the end, let it reach a glow <note>heated until the material glows red-hot</note>: then add as much distilled vinegar to this powder again, so that it stands four fingers' breadth above it, and extract the tincture according to the art: then drop into this the **oil of tartar per deliquium** <term>oleum tartari p. d.; a liquid form of potassium carbonate used as a precipitant</term>, so the *sulfur of vitriol* sinks to the bottom; edulcorate <term>edulcoreert; to wash a precipitate with water until all traces of salt or acid are removed</term> with fresh water.

From this, one makes an *anodyne* <note>a medicine used to relieve pain</note>, which is called *laudanum* <note>In the 17th century, "laudanum" referred to several "most praised" medicines, often compounded with minerals or opium</note>.

## XLII. Salt of Vitriol. <note>original: *Sal Vitrioli*</note>

Calcine <term>calcineren; to heat a substance to high temperatures in a crucible to drive off volatile matter or change its state</term> blue Hungarian *vitriol* in a crucible until it changes into a dark purple powder; then pour common water upon it, stirring it gradually so that it does not clump at the bottom; the water will then become warm, and it should be stirred until it is cold: let it stand thus for 24 hours; filter it, and evaporate it gently, and the remaining salt will be somewhat incarnate <note>a pale pink or flesh-colored hue</note> in color, which is brought to a white powder by pulverizing.

This is administered to induce vomiting, in doses of ten to forty grains <note>a grain was a small unit of weight, approximately 65 milligrams</note>.

### XLIII. *Narcotic Anodyne Extract of Vitriol.* <note>original: *Extractum Vitrioli narcoticum anodynum*; "Anodyne" means a painkiller, and "narcotic" refers to its sleep-inducing properties.</note>

Take half a pound of pulverized vitriol <note>likely iron sulfate or "green vitriol"</note> that has been turned white with a gentle heat <note>a process called calcination, which removes the water of crystallization from the mineral</note>, and pour thirty ounces of **rectified spirit of wine** <term>spiritus vini rectificati; high-proof distilled alcohol</term> upon it: let this stand for a month in **horse manure** <note>manure was used as a natural "incubation" source to provide a constant, low heat for slow extraction</note>; decant it from the fine impurities without making it cloudy: then distill it off in a **water bath** <term>balneum mariae; a vessel of water used to heat the mixture gently and evenly</term> until a yellow liquid remains that is not unlike an oil: that which has passed over [the distillate] is to be saved: and that which remains behind should be put away well-sealed, as it is a precious extract.

It is said to be a pain-reliever, just like **opium**, and does not yield to it (yet is without danger) <note>the author suggests this mineral extract provides the benefits of opium without its addictive or toxic risks</note>; it is administered in doses of six to twelve drops in any suitable liquid.

### XLIV. *Essence of Sulfur of Vitriol.* <note>original: *Essentia Sulphuris Vitrioli*</note>

Take the **oil from the sulfur of vitriol** (described previously); drop **distilled vinegar** <term>acetum destillatum</term> into it, so that a brown powder sinks to the bottom, which one sweetens <note>original: *afsoet*; to wash a precipitate with water to remove salts or acids</note> and dries: digest this with **spirit of wine** in a warm place in a sealed glass for eight days and nights, and then the very sweet **essence of sulfur of vitriol** will float on top in the form of an oil, which one can separate from the spirit of wine using a funnel and preserve.

Its powers are like the **tincture of antimony**; it is useful for **dropsy** <note>original: *watersugt*; swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, diarrhea, **dysentery** <note>original: *roo-loop*; historically called "bloody flux"</note>, nosebleeds, **leukorrhea** <note>original: *witte vloed*; a white vaginal discharge</note>, etc., given in doses of one to four drops in any liquid.

### XLV. Another Tincture, called Manna of Vitriol. <note>original: *Manna Vitrioli*</note>

Extract the tincture from a good portion of purified vitriol by digesting it in the **most subtle essence of spirit of vitriol** <note>original: *spiritus vitrioli subtilissimus essentificatus*</note> (that is, with its own fine **alkalized salt** <term>sal gealcaliseert; a salt that has been burned until it becomes alkaline and can act as a solvent</term>): filter it then and coagulate <note>to thicken a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state</note>, and thus you have the **manna** or yellow tincture of vitriol. <note>In alchemy, "manna" refers to a prized, purified substance that "falls" or precipitates like the biblical food; here it denotes a yellow, concentrated extract.</note>
Its powers are the same as the previously mentioned **essence of sulfur**. <note>See recipe XLIV on the previous page.</note>

### XLVI. Tincture of Vitriol. <note>original: *Tinctura Vitrioli*</note>

Draw from a good portion of **green vitriol** <note>iron sulfate</note> the **phlegm** <term>phlegma; the watery, tasteless part of a substance that comes over first during distillation</term> in an **ash bath** <note>a container of warm ashes used to provide gentle, even heat to a glass vessel</note>; then, using that same phlegm, draw a green tincture from the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum; the solid remains left in the flask after distillation</term> (even in a cold place, though shaking it frequently) according to the art. This tincture should be gently poured off and distilled until it reaches the thickness of honey, which, when placed in the cold, shall shoot into crystals.

Take then four or five pounds of these crystals and **circulate** <note>a process where a liquid is boiled and the vapors are condensed and returned to the same flask in a continuous cycle</note> them with **rectified spirit of wine** <term>spiritus vini; high-proof alcohol</term>, the glass being **hermetically sealed**; then distill through the **alembic** <term>alembicum; a hood-like distillation apparatus</term> in a sand bath: **cohobate** <term>cohobation; the process of pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue and re-distilling to concentrate the essence</term> it then; then pour **spirit of vitriol** upon it: distill through the **retort** <term>a glass flask with a long, downward-pointing neck</term> for four days, so that the spirit and the **red oil** come over: draw off the spirit of wine in a **water bath** <note>original: *bad* (balneum mariae)</note> and the spirit of vitriol in the **ash bath**, and thus the oil or very red tincture remains.
It is of great power in all kinds of illnesses.

## XLVII. Masterful Tincture, or Magistery of Vitriol. <note>original: *Tinctura magisteriata, ofte Magisterium Vitrioli*</note>

Add the preceding tincture <note>referring to the Tincture of Vitriol described in recipe XLVI on the previous page</note> to its own **spirit of vitriol** <note>acidic vapor distilled from vitriol</note> that was drawn from it; digest it for a long time, and it shall become sweet.
It is useful for epilepsy, apoplexy, paralysis, vertigo, madness, fainting, general ailments, cachexia <note>a wasting syndrome of the body</note>, dropsy <note>swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, and the stone.
One gives one or more drops of it.

## XLVIII. The same Tincture, but in another manner.

Take the **common salt of vitriol** <note>original: *Sal commune vitrioli*</note> that has been drawn from the **reverberated** <term>reverberated; heated in a furnace where the flame is reflected back onto the material</term> **dead head** <term>caput mortuum; the solid remains left after distillation</term> and well purified, as much as you please; pour onto it the **spirit of vitriol** (which was saved during the preparation of the tincture) until it stands two fingers high; then digest and distill. Pour new spirit onto it; digest and distill; and continue this until the volatile part rises above the solid, carrying the solid with it, and **volatilizes** <note>turns into a vaporous state</note> the **fixed common salt**. Then permeate and incorporate this **sublimated common salt of vitriol** <note>sublimation is the process of a solid turning directly into vapor and then solidifying again, used here to purify the salt</note> with the oil or that tincture; digest in the **athanor** <term>athanor; a "slow-cooker" furnace of the alchemists designed to maintain a steady, constant heat for long periods</term> with varying degrees of heat to make them unite, and it shall finally become purple-colored. Several months are required for this transformation to occur.
It is a **universal medicine**, administered in doses of one or two drops.

### XLIX. Masterpiece of Vitriol. <note>original: *Magisterium Vitrioli*</note>

Distill a good portion of vitriol in the usual manner, and refine both the spirit and the oil together through the **retort** <term>retort; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term>: then, using the **phlegm** <term>phlegm; the watery, tasteless distillate that comes over first during distillation</term> or common water, extract the **common salt** <note>original: *Sal commune*</note> from the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum; the solid remains left in the vessel after distillation</term>; then distill off the phlegm, frequently **cohobating** <term>cohobating; the process of pouring the distilled liquid back onto the solid residue and re-distilling it to increase its potency</term> and digesting <note>gentle heating over time</note>.

->Furthermore.<-

->Take Common Salt, 2 parts.<-
->Spirit or Oil of Vitriol, 1 part.<-
->Mix.<-

## LIII. Magisterial Dead Head
### by Riverius. <note>Lazare Rivière (1589–1655) was a French physician to King Louis XIII, known for incorporating chemical and alchemical remedies into traditional medicine.</note>

Take the *dead head* <term>caput mortuum; the solid residue remaining in a flask after all liquids and spirits have been distilled off</term> of *strong water* <term>aqua fortis; nitric acid</term> (which is made from purified saltpeter <note>original: *nitrum rectificatum*</note> and vitriol that has been well calcined); from this, make a lye using warm distilled rainwater, and then extract the salt according to the art: dissolve it twice more in distilled water, and crystallize it.

Then take one part purified saltpeter and two parts of the aforementioned salt: once the saltpeter has been melted in a crucible using the second degree of heat <note>A moderate heat level in early chemistry</note>, gradually add the salt to it, and ensure that the fire keeps everything melted for three hours. Then place the mass into the *strong water* that was drawn from the top, and add to each pound:

->*Flowers of antimony from the regulus of Mars, 3 oz.* <note>original: *Flor. antim. ex regulo martis*; a white vaporous sublimate of antimony produced using iron</note><-
->*Gold leaf, 3 drams.*<-
->*Coral.*<-
->*Pearls.*<-
->*Eggshells, 2 drams of each.*<-
->*Mix.*<-

Place it in a warm location and digest <note>original: *digereert*; the process of extracting substances using gentle, steady heat</note> for four days.

Once this is done, distill until it is dry; then knead the remaining mass with *spirit of wine* <term>spiritus vini; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</term>; digest for eight days, and distill again until it is dry.

Store the *dead head* in well-sealed glasses.

Administering twelve to eighteen drops cures hypochondriac diseases <note>In this period, "hypochondria" referred to physical ailments of the upper abdomen, often linked to melancholy or digestion</note>. It removes all obstructions and great fevers: it is useful for dropsy <note>original: *water-sugt*; swelling caused by fluid retention</note> and scorbutic <note>original: *scheurbuikige*; relating to scurvy or vitamin C deficiency</note> bodies, etc.

## LIV. Anodyne or narcotic of vitriol by Riverius. <note>Lazare Rivière (1589–1655) was a renowned French physician. An "anodyne" is a pain-relieving medicine, while a "narcotic" refers here to a sleep-inducing or numbing agent.</note>

->**Take:** Roman Vitriol <note>original: *Vitrioli Rom.*; blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note><-
->Tartar, one pound of each. <note>original: *Tartari ana libr. I.*; "ana" indicates equal parts</note><-
->Iron filings, 5 lbs. <note>original: *Lim. chalyb.*; *limatura chalybis*, or steel filings</note><-
->**Mix.**<-

**O**nce everything is well-pounded and mixed together, place it in a glass flask, saturate it with distilled vinegar <term>acetum destillatum</term>, and let it stand two fingers deep above the mixture; let it digest for three days. After this, coagulate <term>coaguleert; to thicken or solidify a liquid through evaporation</term> it with a moderate fire, and pour vinegar over it once more, following the same procedure as before. After you have congealed it, pour enough distilled vinegar over it so that it stands six fingers deep; then, in a gentle heat, you will obtain a red color. Decant <note>to pour off the top liquid while leaving the sediment undisturbed</note> the liquid and pour fresh vinegar of the same kind over it again to extract more; then pour vinegar of tartar <term>acetum tartari</term> over it "by drop" <note>original: *p.d.*, likely *per deliquium*, a specific chemical preparation method</note>, and all the sulfur <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to the flammable, oily, or "soul" principle of a substance, not just the chemical element</note> will sink to the bottom. Dry this well, and pour three pounds of rectified water of life <term>aqua vitæ rectificatæ; high-proof distilled alcohol</term> over it. Seal the glass well with mastic <note>a resin used as an adhesive</note> and egg white, and let it stand in warm horse manure <note>Horse manure was a standard laboratory tool for providing a gentle, constant fermenting heat</note>, which you shall replace every four days. After forty days, distill it; the tincture will remain at the bottom of the glass.

This narcotic is useful for all sharp, burning, and malignant fevers, especially when accompanied by delirium <note>original: *yl-hoofdigheid*; literally "light-headedness" or frenzy</note>. It also serves against "uprisings" <note>original: *opstyginge*; often referring to "hysterical" vapors or "rising of the mother"</note>, colic, kidney pain, and in all diseases where laudanum <note>an opium-based tincture</note> is used; administered in doses of five to twelve drops.

# LV. Sulfur of vitriol, or the first essence of Venus. <note>In alchemy, "Venus" is the symbolic name for copper. Vitriol of Venus refers to copper sulfate. The "first essence" or *primum ens* refers to the fundamental, purified power of the substance.</note>

Take the red earth of vitriol <term>terra vitrioli</term> that has been dulcorated <note>washed with water until all the biting salts are removed</note>; and sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniak; ammonium chloride</term>, half a pound of each; pound everything separately into a red powder; then mix them together thoroughly, and sublime <note>heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then back to solid on a cooler surface</note> from a stone flask in an open fire with a glass helm <note>the lid or head of a still</note>, until something rises. In this way, yellow flowers <term>flores; the fine powder produced by sublimation</term> will come over; these must be separated from the helm with pure water. Now, the water containing the flowers should be evaporated <note>original: *uit-wasemen*</note> in a clean pot over a low flame <note>original: *jagt-vuurtjen*, literally a "chase-fire" or quick, gentle heat</note> until it is dry. Thus, the red flowers will remain lying on the bottom. One shall separate the sulfur <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to the flammable, oily principle or the "soul" of the material</note> from the sal ammoniac by digesting the flowers for one night with alcohol <term>alcohol vini; rectified spirits of wine</term>, which, after being decanted and evaporated, leaves behind the pure sulfur of vitriol, which is called the first essence of Venus <note>original: *primum ens Veneris*</note>.

It is suitable for preparing various secrets <term>arcana; hidden or highly effective remedies</term> of the chemists.

## LXII. *The Secret of Vitriol by Tilingius* <note>Matthias Tiling (1634–1685) was a prominent German physician and professor of medicine.</note>

Dissolve twelve pounds of Roman or Hungarian Vitriol <term>sulfate minerals; "Roman" and "Hungarian" denoted high-quality sources of iron or copper vitriol</term> in common distilled water; then place it in warm ashes so that the water evaporates until a crust forms on the surface. Dissolve it again in distilled water and let it stand for 24 hours in the ash; many impurities will then sink to the bottom. Decant <note>carefully pour off the liquid without disturbing the sediment</note> the clear liquid, coagulate it, and place it again in a glass in the warm ash; dissolve it again, and so on, until no more impurities settle on the bottom and the vitriol has become sweet. Note well: one must carefully preserve its greenness, otherwise the effort is in vain.

Then, put this vitriol into a phial-glass, which shall be closed in the manner of *Hermes* <term>hermetically sealed by melting the glass neck shut to create an airtight container</term> and placed in a philosophical oven <term>an alchemical furnace designed to provide steady, graded heat over long periods</term>; you shall increase the fire of this oven by degrees every ten days, so that the vitriol approaches redness. Then, put this red vitriol into a glass flask, then pour—

## LXIII. *The Secret of Vitriol* <note>original: *Arcanum vitrioli*</note> by *Mynsicht.*

Distill the red oil from the native vitriol <note>original: *vitriolum nativum*; naturally occurring iron or copper sulfate</note>. Then extract the final salt from the dead head <term>original: *caput mortuum*; the solid remains left in a flask after distillation</term>. Take three parts of this salt and two parts of the oil, and let them dry together over the fire; repeat this process until the salt has doubled in weight. Then place it in a glass flask and pour as much of the oil onto it as needed, sealing it in the manner of Hermes <note>original: *op de wijse van Hermes*; hermetically sealed or airtight</note>. Set it to putrefy <note>to sit and break down in a gentle heat</note>, and thereafter place it in hot sand. In a few days, it will have congealed and be prepared.

It is considered a good stomach remedy and a very powerful means for all kinds of illnesses, as well as for preserving health. It is administered elsewhere in doses of three to eight grains.

## LXV. *Red Earth of Vitriol* <note>original: *Terra Rubra vitrioli*</note> *by Felix Wurtz.* <note>Felix Wurtz (1518–1574) was an influential Swiss surgeon known for his practical approach to wound care and his rejection of traditional, often painful, treatments.</note>

Take two pounds of calcined <term>roasted or reduced to powder through heat</term> *vitriol*, let it glow in a pot for an hour, then break the pot into pieces and boil the vitriol for a long time with vinegar; finally pouring spring water into it. Evaporate this until half remains; after it has stood away from the fire for a while, pour it off. Pour new water again onto what remained in the pot: repeat this as long as the liquid turns red in color. Then evaporate all these tinctures until a red earth remains. This earth being glowed anew, throw it back into the water, boil it, and pour off the tinged liquid. Continue pouring new water on it as long as tincture comes out of it; then evaporate them all again until dry, and glow it again as before, also pouring water on it and boiling it. That which is poured off is dried again for fine use.

### LXIX. *Philosophical Lime of Vitriol*, or the *Sympathetic Powder* of Digby.

Take the crystals of vitriol <term>a sulfate mineral, usually iron or copper sulfate</term>; place them in a glazed pan, spread out from one another during the dog days <note>the hottest period of the summer, typically late July to August, believed to be the best time for solar preparations</note>, and set them in the hot sun to calcine <term>to heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off moisture or reduce it to powder</term> into a white powder, which one then sifts; that which remains in the sieve is not yet sufficiently calcined and should be placed in the sun again.
It is said and believed that when one places a little of this powder onto a bloodied handkerchief, it causes all bleeding to stop. <note>This refers to Sir Kenelm Digby’s famous "Powder of Sympathy," which was claimed to heal wounds by being applied to a blood-stained cloth rather than the wound itself, acting through "sympathetic" resonance.</note>

## XI. Regulus of Arsenic <note>original: *Regulus Arcenici*; the "regulus" refers to the metallic heart or purified button of a mineral found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note>.

Take one pound of finely ground arsenic, mix into it six ounces of potash <term>original: *cineres clavellati*; potassium carbonate derived from wood ashes</term>, and knead into this one pound of soft soap; then put the material into a crucible, cover it with a stone lid that has a hole in the middle: set the crucible in a wind-furnace <term>a furnace designed to use a natural or forced draft of air to reach high temperatures</term>; first giving it a gentle fire; afterwards stoke it harder to make it completely fluid; then pour the same into an iron mortar that has been greased, or into a crucible; strike all around it with your tongs, and let the material become cold, and take it out, and so you will find in the bottom of the crucible the *regulus of arsenic*, which must be cleaned of the fine slag <note>original: *scorien*; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note>; it is less caustic than the raw arsenic, and slower acting.

## XII. Sublimated Arsenic <note>original: *Arcenicum Sublimatum*</note>.

Take coarsely ground arsenic, put it in a crucible, set it on a gentle fire under the chimney to calcine <term>to heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile impurities</term>, until one third has evaporated; meanwhile, avoid the fumes <note>arsenic fumes are highly toxic</note>; then grind the remainder fine in a mortar; take one pound of this, with an equal weight of decrepitated salt <term>salt that has been heated until it stops crackling, indicating all moisture has been removed</term> mixed therein; put this mixture into a matrass <term>a long-necked glass flask used in distilling and heating</term>, but let two-thirds remain empty: set the matrass in sand in a small furnace, and first stoke a gentle fire, and increase it gradually to the third degree <note>in alchemy, the "third degree" of heat is a strong heat, often a hot sand bath or direct flame</note>, so that the arsenic may sublime <term>to turn directly from a solid into a vapor and then solidify again on a cooler surface</term>; persist as long as no more rises, and within five or six hours you shall have a complete operation: the vessel being cold, take it out, and collect that which has remained stuck to the top of the matrass,

## XIII. Caustic Arsenic <note>original: *Arcenicum Causticum*</note>.

->Take: Arsenic,<-
->Saltpeter, of each 1 pound.<-
->Sulfur, half a pound.<-
->Mix.<-
<note>original Latin: *Rec. Arcenici, Nitri, āā libr. I. Sulph. libr. sem. M.*</note>

Once accurately mixed together, put it in an iron mortar; then place a lid on it in which there is a small hole; then poke a glowing iron rod or a glowing coal through that hole, and the powder will catch fire with a great explosion, which is called detonation; this being done and the material cooled, grind it to a coarse powder, and calcine <term>heat to a high temperature without melting to remove impurities</term> in an open crucible with a strong fire; then let it become cold, and so you have a caustic medicament, which can be divided into small pieces while breaking, and kept in bottles closed tight, and it is used like the common caustics <note>substances capable of burning or eating away living tissue</note>.

## XIV. Oil of Arsenic <note>original: *Oleum Arcenici*</note>.

->Take: <term>Vitriol cooked almost to yellow</term>,<-

->1 pound.<-

<note>original Latin: *Boracis*</note>

Mix this very finely in a warm mortar, then calcine <term>heat to a high temperature without melting</term> it until it is red,
->Take: <term>Crystalline Arsenic</term>, 1 pound.<-
<note>original Latin: *Arcenici Cryst.*</note>

Mix this into the previously mentioned calcined material, and it will easily melt in the air; then add as much raw vitriol as the previous weight, mixing in a little <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original Latin: *nitrum*</note>; then create <term>layers</term> <note>original Latin: *S.S.S.* for *Stratum Super Stratum*, meaning "layer upon layer"</note> in a <term>crucible</term> <note>original: *kroes*; a heat-resistant pot</note> until it is full; upon this, one then sets four or five <term>sublimation pots</term> <note>vessels used to collect vapors that solidify upon cooling</note>.

First, cement it with a moderate fire that is gradually increased, leaving it in a state of melting for an hour, but without smoke; then let it glow, so the arsenic remains attached at the top like a crystal stone; this is then driven through a <term>retort</term> <note>a glassware vessel with a long neck used for distillation</note> again, so the fixed and medicinal part will remain on the bottom like a crystal; then crush it finely and let it rot in <term>horse manure</term> <note>alchemists used the steady, gentle heat of fermenting manure to facilitate chemical changes</note> for a month, and then distill it like <term>nitric acid</term> <note>original: *aqua fortis*</note> into a blood-red oil: rectify <term>purify through redistillation</term> this in a [water] bath until it is a golden-yellow oil.

It induces sweating; given up to four drops in any liquid, it makes the bowels reasonably soft <note>acting as a mild laxative</note>.

## XV. The Quintessence of Arsenic <note>original: *Quinta Effentia Arcenici*</note>.

->Take: <term>Arsenic</term>,<-
-><term>Saltpeter</term>, equal parts of each.<-
<note>original Latin: *Nitri, ää p. eq.* (ana partes aequales)</note>
->Mix.<-
<note>original Latin: *M.* (Misce)</note>

Once ground to a fine powder, distill it through a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> into a large receiver until all the vapors have passed over. Then break the retort into pieces, crush the substance finely, and place it in a new retort. Pour the distilled <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; the liquid that passed over during distillation</note> back onto it and distill again. Repeat this process three or four times, until the arsenic and saltpeter are very finely <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a dry powder by heat</note>. Next, place the substance in a <term>crucible</term> <note>a heat-resistant pot</note> and maintain a fire for an entire day. Dissolve this <term>calx</term> <note>the powdery residue left after heating</note> in distilled rainwater, filter it, and then evaporate until dry. Calcine again with a strong fire until no more impurities appear in the solution; then evaporate until dry once more. Add the distilled spirit back to it, but the spirit must first have been <term>rectified</term> <note>purified by repeated distillation</note> seven times. Place it in a <term>bain-marie</term> <note>original: *balneo mariæ*; a warm water bath</note> until the two are united, then remove all moisture in the bath through distillation. Thus, the buttery <term>calx</term> of the arsenic remains at the bottom, which should be kept in a tightly closed container.

It is used for cancer, the bites of <term>mad dogs</term> <note>historically referring to rabies</note>, malignant <term>ulcers</term> <note>open sores</note> and <term>fistulas</term> <note>abnormal tube-like passages in tissue</note>, spreading scabies, etc.

## VII. Milk of Sulfur.
<note>original Latin: *Lac Sulphuris*</note>

->Take Flowers of Sulfur, 1 part<-
->Salt of Tartar, 3 parts<-
->Mix.<-

Put them together in a glazed pot or a <term>flask</term> <note>original Dutch: *kolf*, a glass vessel with a long neck used for boiling</note>, add a <term>mingele</term> <note>an old Dutch liquid measurement, approximately 1.2 liters</note> or one and a half of water, and let it boil in the <term>sand</term> <note>a sand bath, providing indirect heat</note> for five or six hours, stirring constantly with a wooden spatula, until nearly all the sulfur is melted and the liquid is red. Then filter while it is warm, and pour tart wine or distilled vinegar onto the filtered liquid until the liquid turns white; the "milk" then sinks to the bottom, which one <term>edulcorates</term> <note>washes with water to remove salts or acids until it is tasteless</note> and dries.

## VIII. A Shorter Method.

->Take Sulfur<-
->Salt of Tartar, equal parts of each<-
<note>original Latin: *ana partes æquales*</note>
->Mix.<-

Melt them together in a crucible, then let them dissolve <term>by moisture</term> <note>original Latin: *per deliquium*, the process where a salt absorbs enough water from the air to turn into a liquid</note>; then pour warm water on it, filter, and gradually pour wine into it, so the liquid becomes white; then wash it and dry it.

It is used in all head and lung ailments, adding to any liquid as much as is needed to make it white, or up to a <term>drachm</term> <note>original: *drachma*, a unit of weight approximately 3.9 grams</note>.

### X. *Spirit of Sulfur of Clossaeus.*
<note>This likely refers to the preparations of Ewaldus Vogelius, also known as Clossaeus, a 16th-century alchemist.</note>

### XI. *Spirit or Oil of Sulfur by the Bell.*
<note>original Latin: *Spiritus of oleum Sulphuris per Campanam*. This is a classic alchemical method where sulfur is burned under a bell-shaped glass to collect the acidic condensation.</note>

Take a stoneware vessel that the French call *Grez* <note>original French: *grès*, a hard, non-porous ceramic</note>, in which you shall place a small pot made of the same earth; place another on top of this filled with melted sulfur. Enclose these two pots in a glass funnel that is specifically made for this purpose, having a neck as long as that of a <term>flask</term> <note>original Dutch: *kolf*, a round-bottomed glass vessel</note> and one inch <note>original Dutch: *duim*, literally "thumb"</note> thick. Ignite the sulfur; do not stop up the hole of the funnel at all, so that air may always enter, otherwise the sulfur would be extinguished. When the sulfur has burned away, add new sulfur again until you have enough spirit in the inverted pot; then store it in a glass.

It is added to cooling drinks to provide a pleasant taste and to temper the heat of continual fevers. It is also used in lung diseases.

## XIV. *Balsam of Sulfur with Turpentine, or Ruby of Sulfur.*

Put one and a half ounces of **flowers of sulfur** <note>original Latin: *flores sulphuris*; the fine powder formed when sulfur is heated to a vapor and then cooled quickly</note> into a small <term>matrass</term> <note>a glass flask with a long neck, used in distillation and digestion</note>; pour eight ounces of **oil of turpentine** over it; set the matrass in the sand; keep a fire under it for two hours to <term>digest</term> <note>the process of extracting substances or promoting chemical reactions using gentle, steady heat</note>: increase the fire for the following four hours, so the oil shall turn red: once the matrass has cooled, pour off the clear balsam from the residue that has not dissolved.

This balsam is an excellent remedy for **lung ailments**; it is administered in doses of one to six drops in any suitable liquid.

One can also mix this balsam into salves, and evaporate the excess moisture by the fire, which can then be used to cleanse wounds and sores.

To make **anise balsam of sulfur** <note>original Latin: *balſamum ſulphuris aniſatum*</note>, one uses oil of anise instead of turpentine oil, and proceeds as before. This is more pleasant than the previous kind, and less sharp.

## XVI. *Tincture of Sulfur.*
<note>original: "Tinctura Sulphuris"</note>

After the **spirit of turpentine** <note>original: "spiritus therebintinae"; a thin, volatile oil distilled from pine resin</note> has been poured off from the balsam (the method of separation is found in the section on the balsam), pour **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini"; high-proof alcohol or brandy</note> onto it, and draw out the spirit in a <term>water bath</term> <note>also known as a bain-marie; a container of water used to heat a vessel gently and evenly</note>; thus you have a tincture. Then <term>digest</term> it <note>heat gently to extract properties</note> and separate the impurities.

This is given for chest ailments in doses of three to four drops.

## XVII. *Clowes's Tincture of Sulfur.*
<note>original: "Tinctura Sulphuris Clossei"; likely referring to a recipe by the English surgeon William Clowes or the chemist Quercetanus/Duchesne, often cited in Dutch pharmaceutical texts.</note>

->Take: Saltpeter, 1 pound.<- <note>original: "Nitri, libr. I."</note>
->Sulfur, 4 ounces.<- <note>original: "Sulph. unc. IV."</note>
->Mix.<- <note>original: "M."</note>

Put the same by spoonfuls into a glowing red-hot pot, and burn it with a strong fire until all the crackling stops and it has become a red mass; then pour the **tartarized spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini tartarisatus"; alcohol that has been distilled over potassium carbonate (salt of tartar) to remove water and increase its purity</note> onto the crushed powder of this mass, and draw out the tincture.

This is used for the plague, fevers, scurvy, obstructions of the liver, and lung ailments; administered in doses up to eight drops.

## XVIII. *Another One.*

Melt saltpeter in water—boiling one pound of sulfur in six pounds of this water—until the liquid is red. # CORALS.

### I. *Sweet Salt of Corals.*
<note>original: "Sal dulce Corallorum"</note>

Let the corals **calcine** <note>burn or roast at high temperatures</note> in a potter's oven for two days until they are very white; then **dissolve** <note>original: "solveert"</note> them in distilled vinegar; pour off the **solvent** <note>original: "menstruum"</note>, and gently evaporate it; this salt can then be dissolved, filtered, and **coagulated** <note>solidified or thickened</note> several times in **May-dew** <note>dew collected in May, which early chemists believed held special vital or celestial properties</note>: then place this salt in the **ashes** <note>a bed of warm ashes used to provide gentle, consistent heat</note> for three weeks, so that it loses most of its sharpness.

## II. Solution of Corals.
<note>original: "Solutio Corallorum"</note>

Take corals, ground to an impalpable fine powder on a porphyry stone, as much as you desire: put them in a wide **matras** <note>a long-necked glass flask used for digestion or distillation</note>; then pour distilled vinegar over them until it stands four fingers high above it, and thus a great **effervescence** <note>bubbling or fizzing caused by the chemical reaction between the acid vinegar and the calcium carbonate in the coral</note> occurs; this being done, let your matter **digest** <note>soften or dissolve through gentle heat</note> for two days in warm sand, stirring the matras from time to time: then let the coral settle to the bottom and pour the clear liquid into a bottle; pour again as much distilled vinegar on the remainder as before; digest again for two days, and separate the clear liquid, and pour new distilled vinegar over it yet again: and do this until almost all the coral is dissolved: then combine all the solutions together; put them in a glass or glazed earthen flask, and evaporate two-thirds of the liquid over a sand fire, or until a thin film remains on top: filter this **impregnation** <note>a saturated solution</note> and save it to make salt and **magistery** <note>a fine powder precipitated from a solution</note>, as will be described below.

One can administer it for the same conditions as its salt: the dose being ten to twenty drops in any suitable liquid.

### XV. Another [method] using *vinegar of corals*.

<note>original: "Aqua mellis"; a liquid distilled from honey</note>

Once this is sweetened <note>washed of its salts</note>, one extracts the tincture with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>distilled alcohol</note>.
This is administered in doses of four to twelve grains.

## XVIII. *Another [method] by a tempered water.*

Take the salt of corals made by the *spirit of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note>, then extract the tincture according to the art with a tempered water (made from *spirit of wine* and *spirit of vitriol*). Decant, filter, and abstract.

## XIX. *Another [method] by the phlegm of Saturn.*
<note>original: "phlegma Saturni"; in alchemy, Saturn represents lead; the "phlegm" is the watery, inactive distillate of lead acetate</note>

Pour the *phlegm of Saturn* onto calcined coral, along with the sharp *spirit of Saturn* <note>the volatile, acidic spirit distilled from lead acetate</note>; digest these while sealed shut until the <term>menstruum</term> <note>the solvent liquid</note> turns red. Then draw it off in a vapor bath. Pour *spirit of wine* onto it and digest again, then drive it through the retort: in this way, one obtains the *essence of corals*. Furthermore, draw off the *spirit of wine* until it reaches a consistency.
It is a good cordial <note>a medicine intended to stimulate the heart and spirits</note>, and is useful for children subject to frights and convulsions, administered in doses of three to five drops.

## P E A R L S.

### I. Salt of Pearls. <note>original: "Sal Margaritarum"</note>

This is done in the same manner as the salt of corals. <note>This refers to the process of dissolving the material in acid and then crystallizing or evaporating it to create a "salt" thought to contain the concentrated essence of the pearl.</note>

### II. Salt or Magistery of Pearls by Riverius. <note>original: "Sal of Magisterium Margaritarum Riverii"; Lazarus Riverius (1589–1655) was a prominent French physician whose recipes were widely influential in 17th-century pharmacy.</note>

Take very finely crushed pearls, as many as are required, make them into a paste with lemon juice <note>original: "succus citri"</note>, and let it remain so for a long time; afterward, dissolve the same with a good portion of distilled vinegar <note>original: "aceti dest."</note> until the pearls are nearly dissolved: then mix the solution with a third part of river water; distill in a sand bath <term>sand bath</term> <note>a container filled with sand and heated, providing a steady, even temperature for the glass vessels placed within it</note>, first with a gentle fire, and then with a strong one: pour the distilled liquid back onto the residue <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>literally "dead head"; the solid remains left in the flask after distillation</note>, dissolve, filter, and evaporate very slowly; thus you will have the magistery of pearls <term>magistery</term> <note>original: "magisterium perlarum"; a refined medicinal precipitate believed to hold the full power of the original substance.</note>.

### III. Magistery of Pearls. <note>original: "Magisterium Perlarum"</note>

I. The common method occurs through solution with distilled vinegar <note>original: "acetum destillatum"</note>, which one then precipitates with the liquid of tartar <term>liquid of tartar</term> <note>original: "liquor tartari"; a solution of potassium carbonate used to force dissolved substances out of a liquid.</note>.

II. The buttery version is made like that of the corals.

III. The feathery version is made like that of the corals.

## V. *Essence, Tincture, or Arcanum of Pearls.* <note>original: "Essentia, Tinctura, ofte Arcanum Perlarum"; an "arcanum" refers to a "secret" or a high-order medicinal mystery.</note>

Dissolve the **salt of pearls** <note>original: "sal perlarum"</note> in distilled vinegar; filter and evaporate; and repeat this several times, always discarding the impurities, until the pearls are entirely pure. Then dissolve them in **rainwater** <note>original: "aqua pluviali"</note> or **May dew** <note>original: "rore majali"; alchemists believed dew collected in May was a potent solvent infused with celestial energy</note>; distill all the moisture off, and repeat this as often as necessary until the pearls have become "sweet" <note>meaning the acidic taste of the vinegar has been completely removed or neutralized</note>. Digest this salt in a sealed glass vessel in a water bath for ten days and nights with **alcohol of wine** <note>original: "alcohol vini"</note>, which must stand two fingers' breadth above it; thus the essence will gradually come to float on top like an oil. This must be carefully separated; then pour new alcohol onto it again, and repeat this as many times as desired. These oils are then circulated for a while longer with alcohol, which is afterwards gently drawn off by distillation.

### X. Essence of Pearls according to Riverius. <note>original Latin: "Essentia Margaritarum Riverii." Lazare Rivière (1589–1655) was an influential French royal physician who advocated for the use of chemical remedies.</note>

Digest the pearls in the vinegar of antimony <note>original Latin: "acetum antimonii"; a specialized alchemical solvent</note>, and then treat them according to the art <note>following standard laboratory procedures</note> until the salt becomes white; namely until, through various washings, it has left its sharpness <note>acidity or corrosiveness</note> behind. # CHAPTER XXIV.
->Concerning<-
## PEBBLES or FLINT and CRYSTAL.

### I. Calcination or Calcining of Pebbles and Crystal. <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to a high temperature in order to change its physical or chemical structure, often making it brittle enough to grind into powder.</note>

Heat your pebbles <note>original: "keyen"</note> in the fire until they glow, and quench them in common water: repeat this three or four times, until they can be easily rubbed into pieces into an impalpable powder <note>a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers</note> after they have been dried. For this, one must choose river pebbles which have various colors and veins.

In the same manner, one also calcines crystal, but it can be rubbed into pieces more easily than the pebbles; from this, one can also extract a liquid and a tincture, in the same manner as the liquid and tincture of pebbles, which I shall now describe, as they possess the same powers.

# Succinum or Amber.

### I. *Whitening of Amber*, to make Amber white. <note>original Latin: *Succini dealbatio*</note>

Take one pound of yellow amber <note>original: *succinum*</note>, put it in an earthenware flask, add three pounds of common salt to it; then pour on as much rainwater as is needed to dissolve the salt; then pour a good quantity of water on it still, place a blind helm <note>a still-head without a spout, used to condense vapors and let them drip back into the vessel for continuous boiling</note> on the flask; boil it gently for fourteen days and nights <note>original Dutch: *etmalen*</note>, or until it has become white.

## IV. *Fixed Sweet Magistery of Amber.* <note>original Latin: *Magisterium Succini dulce fixum*</note>

Take a sufficient quantity of white powdered amber <note>original Dutch: *barn-steen*</note>; pour enough distilled vinegar over it so that it stands four fingers’ width above the powder; let that boil together for several days (and if the liquid has evaporated, pour new liquid over it again) until the liquid turns red; filter it and draw off the liquid <note>evaporate it</note>, so the magistery <note>a concentrated medicinal precipitate</note> remains lying on the bottom: then dissolve that in rose-water; filter and draw off the liquid, and do this up to three times; then precipitate it with the *oil of vitriol* <note>original: *oleum vitrioli*; concentrated sulfuric acid</note>, or with *lemon juice* <note>original: *succus citri*</note>.

## II. *Elixir of Lapis Lazuli.*
<note>original: *Elixir Lapidis Lazuli*. Lapis lazuli, the deep blue semi-precious stone, was used in Renaissance medicine to treat "melancholy" and "malignant fevers."</note>

One <term>calcines</term> <note>heats to a high temperature to reduce to a powder</note> the **lapis lazuli** in a stone oven, which is then dissolved in **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; high-proof distilled spirits or brandy</note>. ## III. *Essence or Extract of Lapis Lazuli.*
<note>original: *Eſſentia ofte Extractum Lap. Lazuli*</note>

Take as much **lapis lazuli** as you see fit; make it glowing hot and <term>quench</term> <note>rapidly cool a hot substance by dipping it in liquid</note> it seven times in **spirit of wine** <note>original: *ſpir. vini*; concentrated ethanol</note>. Make a very fine powder of it, and <term>digest</term> <note>to steep a substance in a solvent under gentle heat</note> it for three or four days with **spirit of wine**. Then draw off the **spirit of wine** and preserve what remains. 
One administers this in a dose of half to a whole **scruple** <note>original: *ſcruipel*; a traditional apothecary weight equal to about 1.3 grams</note>.

## IV. *Purging Crystals of Lapis Lazuli.*
<note>original: *Cryſtalli purgantes Lap. Lazuli*</note>

<term>Calcine</term> the same with a strong fire until it turns white, rub it on a marble stone, and boil it for five or six hours in a sufficient quantity of **distilled vinegar** <note>original: *acetum deſtill.*</note>. Then pour the vinegar into an unglazed earthenware pot with a narrow neck that holds five or six ounces. Close the mouth of the pot with wax and place it in the cellar. In a few days, a **crystalline woolliness** <note>this refers to "efflorescence," where minerals seep through the porous, unglazed clay and crystallize on the outside of the pot</note> will begin to grow on the outside, which one gathers; one then waits for more to form.

## II. Second method.

Take then good **talc** <note>original: *talk q. v.* (quantum vis); as much as you wish</note>, pound it in a glowing-hot mortar (it allows itself to be pounded better this way) until it no longer gives off any luster; sift the powder, and mix it with an equal weight of **linden-wood charcoal** <note>original: *carbones Tiliæ*</note>; then <term>calcine</term> <note>heat to high temperatures to reduce to powder</note> in a potter’s oven for two or three days long.

## III. Third method.

### VIII. **Distilled Oil of Talc** <note>original: *Oleum Talci destillatum*</note>, being a **Cosmetic White** <note>original: *Blanketsel*; a white cosmetic lotion or paste used to whiten the skin</note> by Hartmann <note>Johannes Hartmann (1568–1631) was a notable German chemist and the first professor of chemistry at a European university</note>.

### IX. **Talcated Oil of Camphor** <note>original: *Oleum Camphoræ Talcatum*</note>.

Take one part of raw <term>talc</term> (though calcined is better), having been well crushed; two parts of **oil of camphor**; then <term>digest</term> <note>to apply gentle, steady heat to a substance over a long period, often in a sealed container</note> it until the oil turns white.

### X. **Liquor of Talc** <note>original: *Liquor Talci*</note>, or **Oil by Deliquescence** <note>original: *Oleum per deliquium*; a method where a salt or powder absorbs enough moisture from the air to dissolve into a liquid</note>.

Take very well-calcined <term>talc</term>; obtain an extract from the first, second, and subsequent calcinations using distilled <term>vinegar</term>; filter and <term>coagulate</term> <note>thickening or solidifying a liquid into a semi-solid state</note> it; <term>edulcorate</term> <note>to wash a substance with water to remove salts or impurities</note> it, and place it in a cellar to melt. Others <term>circulate</term> <note>a process where a liquid is distilled and then allowed to flow back into the same vessel repeatedly</note> the oil further with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: *spir. vini*; concentrated alcohol</note>, removing it by <term>cohobating</term> <note>redistilling a liquid by pouring it back over the solid matter remaining in the vessel</note> it several times.

## XI. Liquor of Talc by S. Closs. <note>likely referring to Samuel Clossius, a 17th-century physician and chemist</note>

**O**ne rubs the *talcum* to a very fine powder, which occurs in four ways: either one mixes the loosened or flaked <term>talc</term> <note>a soft mineral with a pearly luster, notoriously difficult to reduce to a fine powder due to its slippery, plate-like structure</note> with whole river stones; these are placed in a long bag and are continuously and vigorously kicked back and forth by two people; or it is continuously rubbed upon a pumice stone, and the powder falling below is collected, which, however, is not very pure; or it is pounded in a hot mortar: but I do this better with a goldsmith's polishing file. Having gathered half a pound of that, I mix it with a pound of <term>Salt of Tartar</term> <note>original: *Sal tartari*; potassium carbonate, used here as a flux to help the mineral melt</note> (the Author says <term>Salt of Venus</term> <note>original: *veneris*; typically refers to copper salts or verdigris</note>, but I consider it to be the former); I set this for twelve hours in a <term>wind-furnace</term> <note>a furnace designed to draw in air to reach higher temperatures</note> to <term>calcine</term> <note>heating a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile matter or to oxidize it</note>, and then the calcined material is placed in a cellar; I separate the molten part from the unmolten. The remaining lime, being put in a pot, is calcined again with a very strong fire, adding four parts of <term>nitre</term> <note>original: *nitrum*; saltpeter</note> to it: in this way, the talc shall melt into a white, transparent mass, which, being placed in the cellar, melts into a glue-like moisture <note>the substance absorbs moisture from the humid cellar air and turns into a liquid, a process called deliquescence</note>.

It drives away all freckles and spots of the face; it makes the skin white, but the moisture must not be left on there for long; rather, one must immediately wash the face with some <term>bean-flower water</term> <note>original: *aqua fabarum*; distilled water of bean blossoms, used to soften skin</note>, <term>water-lily water</term> <note>original: *nenupharis*</note>, etc., so that the epidermis is not eaten through <note>meaning the caustic nature of the alkaline salts does not cause a chemical burn</note>.

### XIII. Cream of Talc.

Crush the talc in one of the above-mentioned four ways; pour **distilled vinegar** on it up to three times, boiling gently in a glass dish on the fire; gather from it the foam floating on top with a skimmer as long as there is any; then evaporate the **distilled vinegar** that is under the **cream**: then dissolve the cream again in the <term>phlegm</term> <note>the watery, less active portion of a distillate</note> of the **spirit of common salt** <note>hydrochloric acid</note> or mix it into some pomade <note>an ointment or scented cream for the skin</note>.
The same is useful for making the face white. <note>Talc was a prized ingredient in Early Modern cosmetics for its ability to provide a pale, shimmering complexion.</note>

### XIV. Tincture of Talc.

Take the best very finely crushed **talcum**, <term>as much as you wish</term> <note>original: *q. v.* or *quantum vis*</note>; <term>digest</term> <note>to expose to steady, gentle heat</note> it with the **philosophical spirit of vitriol**, and place it for three or four months in **horse manure** <note>a common alchemical practice for maintaining a steady, low heat through the natural process of decomposition</note>, so the talc shall melt, and something will float on top like fatness: then pour **spirit of wine** <note>alcohol</note> on it; digest and <term>abstract</term> <note>to distill or remove a liquid from a solid</note>, often <term>cohobating</term> <note>the process of pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue and re-distilling it to concentrate the "essence"</note>, and so it shall finally go over the **helm** <note>the "alembic" or cap of the distillation vessel</note>.

## XV. Another method.

Take <term>calcined</term> <note>heated to a high temperature to change its state or remove impurities</note> **talc**, extract it with common **green spirit of vitriol** <note>original: *spir. vitrioli vir.*; sulfuric acid produced from green vitriol or iron sulfate</note>, <term>decant</term> <note>pouring off the liquid while leaving the sediment</note>, <term>abstract</term> <note>distill off the liquid</note>, and <term>cohobate</term> <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue and re-distilling it to concentrate the essence</note> several times, so that finally the **tincture** will come over the **helm** <note>the "head" or top part of a distilling apparatus</note> with a red color.

It is a preservative against the **plague** <note>original: *peft*, a common spelling variant of *pest*</note>, used daily in doses of up to six grains. It is best to use **red talc**, if it can be obtained.

## XVI. Another.

Take as much **talc** as you please, pour **spirit of vitriol** <note>sulfuric acid</note> onto it, and draw it off several times; mix it with **sulfur**, and <term>reverberate</term> <note>to heat a substance in a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" onto the material</note>; then extract the **tincture** from it.

The **solar sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur solare*; in alchemy, this refers to the "soul" or essential flammable principle of a substance, often associated with the sun or gold for its curative powers</note> extracted from the **talc** is a good remedy in very severe illnesses.

## II. *On making fixed Salts from all kinds of Wood, Herbs, Seeds, etc.*

Take, for example, dried **blessed thistle**, <note>original: *carduus benedictus*; a plant long used in herbal medicine for digestive issues and as a general tonic.</note> or **wormwood**, <note>original: *absinthium*</note> or something similar; once dried, burn it to ashes. Then place these ashes in a pot and let them **calcine** <note>To calcine means to heat a substance to a high temperature in the air to remove volatile parts and reduce it to a mineral state.</note> until they are completely white. Then pour a good portion of hot rainwater over them so that the saltiness <note>original: *siltigheid*; refers to the mineral salts, primarily potassium carbonate, found in plant ash.</note> is drawn into it. Filter this **lye** <note>original: *loog*; the alkaline solution created by soaking ashes in water.</note> and gently evaporate it until it is dry; thus you will have a brownish salt. If you desire this to be whiter, calcine it again, after which you pour water over it once more, filter, and evaporate. This is done repeatedly until the salt is white enough.

In the same manner are made:

# III. *Essential Salt of Plants.*

Take, for example, a good quantity of **wormwood**, <note>original: *alsem*</note> or of **blessed thistle**, <note>original: *carduus benedictus*</note> or a similar herb: boil it for a considerable time, then press it through a cloth; let the decoction settle; **decant** <note>To pour off the top layer of liquid, leaving the sediment behind.</note> and filter: then evaporate this decoction by about two-thirds in an earthenware pot: then place it in a cool cellar, and after several days you will find the crystals hanging around the pot, which you shall separate and keep in a glass vessel, tightly closed.

They induce sweating when taken in doses of 6 or 8 **grains** <note>A grain is a historical unit of mass based on the weight of a single seed of cereal; approximately 65 milligrams.</note> with some suitable liquid.

# IV. *How to make an acidic Spirit, Oil, and Salt from all kinds of Wood.*

## VI. Oil and Spirit of Linen, Cotton, and Paper.

Fill a **retort** <note>A glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note> with old linen, cotton, or paper, all being cleanly washed and without writing; place it in a **reverberatory furnace**; <note>A furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat from the roof onto the material being heated.</note> attach a receiver, and everything being well **luted**, <note>Sealed with "lute," a paste or clay used to make joints airtight.</note> stoke a gentle fire for two hours to warm the retort gradually; increase it then by two or three coals and continue this for three hours; then stoke with the **third degree of fire**: <note>A measurement of heat in early chemistry; the third degree typically refers to a moderate red heat.</note> the receiver shall be filled with white clouds; stop stoking when no more come out.

The operation is completed within seven or eight hours: once everything has become cold, detach the receiver; then pour it through a gray paper <note>Filter paper.</note>, so that the **spirit** <note>In this context, the thin, acidic liquid product of the distillation.</note> runs through it, and the **black, stinking oil** remains upon it; then keep both in glass vessels.

It is a worthy remedy against **deafness**; by dropping some into the ear with a bit of cotton, the ringing will gradually subside.

It is also good against **scabies** <note>original: *schurft*; a contagious skin infestation.</note> and **ringworm** <note>original: *hairworm*; likely *tinea capitis*.</note>, toothache, **rising of the mother** <note>original: *opstygingen*; a historical term for "hysterical" vapors or fits believed to be caused by the womb.</note>, etc.

## VIII. Extracts from Herbs, Roots, Seeds, Woods, etc.

Pulverize, for example, several ounces or pounds of the best **rhubarb** <note>original: *rhabarber*</note>, or another substance, and soak it for twelve hours in a sufficient amount of warm rainwater; specifically, let the water stand four fingers high above the material. Theatrum Chemicum.

## XVII. *Spirit and Oil of Tartar.*

Fill two-thirds of a **retort** <term>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</term> with coarsely crushed **tartar** <note>crude potassium bitartrate from wine barrels</note>: place it in a **reverberatory furnace** <term>a furnace that reflects heat from the roof back onto the vessel</term>, and attach a receiver to it; begin the distillation first with a slow fire for the first three hours, so that first a *phlegma* <term>a watery, tasteless distillate</term> will come out; you should simply throw away this tasteless liquid. Then attach the receiver again and seal everything tightly with **lute** <note>a paste used to create airtight seals in chemical apparatus</note>: increase the fire gradually, and the spirit will fill the receiver with clouds: continue until the oil passes over: when you see that nothing more is distilling over, let the vessels cool and detach the receiver. Then let the liquid filter through **blotting paper** <note>original: *klad-papier*, used here as a crude filter</note>; the *spirit* will run through it, and the oil will remain upon it; then, having separated the two from each other, you can store them individually in a bottle.

It is useful for **hysterics** <note>original: *moertrekkingen*, literally "womb-twitchings," a condition once believed to be caused by the womb moving or spasming</note> when rubbed under the nose: it is also beneficial for paralysis and pains arising from **cold humors** <term>bodily fluids thought to be excessive or sluggish, leading to stiffness or illness</term> when the parts are rubbed with it; however, it is little used because of its great stench.

Pour the spirit into a glass flask and **rectify** <term>to purify a substance through repeated distillation</term> it. It is good against paralysis, tightness of the chest, and scurvy, and it drives out all harmful humors through the urinary tract and the sweat pores: it is used against womb ailments and for the **falling sickness** <note>epilepsy</note>: it is administered in doses from one **dram** <note>about 3.9 grams</note> to three drams, with some suitable liquid.

In the retort, one finds a black mass from which, as will be mentioned below, a salt is extracted.

Theatrum Chemicum.

### XVIII. Fixed Salt of Tartar and Liquid or Oil by Deliquescence.

**B**reak into pieces the retort that you used to distill the tartar; then take the black mass that was inside it and calcine it <term>to heat a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to oxidize it or remove volatile parts</term> in the coals until it has become white; then place it in a good amount of warm water and prepare a lye <note>an alkaline solution</note> from it, which you shall filter, and in a glazed pot over a sand fire, evaporate all the moisture; thus you shall find a white salt, which is called *alkali salt of tartar* <note>original Latin: *Sal alcali tartari*; this is potassium carbonate</note>.

This salt opens: it is used to extract the tincture of plants, and to open obstructions <note>referring to blockages in the body's internal organs according to the medical theories of the time</note>. It is administered in doses from ten to thirty grains, with broth or some laxative decoctions <note>original: *weiksels*, infusions or liquids in which herbs have been soaked</note>.

If one sets this salt away in a glazed pot in the cellar for several days, it melts into a moisture, which is improperly called *oil of tartar by deliquescence* <note>original Latin: *oleum tartari per deliquium*; deliquescence is the process where a salt absorbs enough water from the air to dissolve completely</note>.

It is used for ringworm <note>original: *hair-worm*, likely referring to tinea or similar fungal skin conditions</note>, as well as to disperse fluids: ladies mix it into lily-water to cleanse the skin of the face and the hands.

### XIX. Tincture of Tartar.

## XXV. Distilled Vinegar, Fixed Salt, and Radical Vinegar <note>original: *Acetum Radicatum*</note>.

Place six pints of very sharp vinegar in a stone pot: evaporate one pint from it in a *Bain-marie* <note>original: *Balneo Mariæ*; a water bath used for gentle heating</note>, which is merely a *phlegm* <term>the watery, tasteless part of a distillate that lacks the active medicinal properties</term>; pour the remainder into a glass or stone flask: then distille in the sand bath with a strong fire, until a substance remains in the flask as thick as honey; keep this vinegar well-stopped, which is called *spirit of vinegar* <note>original: *spiritus aceti*; concentrated acetic acid</note> by many.

Its primary use is for dissolving and precipitating, which is useful in certain preparations; it is also added to heart-strengthening drinks to resist putrefaction. The dose or administration is half a spoonful: one mixes it with water, and that *oxycrate* <note>original: *oxycratum*; a medicinal drink made of water and vinegar</note> is given to staunch bleeding that flows from the nose; externally, it is used to soothe inflammations.

## XXVI. *Burning Spirit of Roses* <note>original: *Spiritus Rosarum Ardens*</note>.

Take 1 pound of pale roses, plucked from their green buds; place them in a small oak barrel: over these, one then pours three pounds of fresh yeast <note>original: *biergift*; the "gift of the beer," or the foam/yeast produced during fermentation</note>, and ten pounds of hot water: cover the barrel with a lid, upon which one places a heavy stone, and let that ferment for forty days: then put everything into a copper kettle, and pour forty pounds of good old beer over it, and distill with the worm <term>a spiral cooling tube used in a condenser</term> until one-third remains in the kettle; then rectify <note>to purify a liquid by repeated distillation</note> in the [water] bath, and preserve it.
*It is strengthening in cases of fainting.*

## XXVII. *Another way.*

Crush your roses fine, put them in a pot, and place them in the cellar until they begin to turn sour, which happens within two or three months; then distill them in the water-bath, without any additions; then pour water over a portion of the crushed roses, and distill again as before; and do this until all the fermented roses have been distilled: finally, take all the distilled water, and re-distill it with a flask, and separate about the twelfth part from it; thus you have a burning *spirit* <note>original: *spiritus*; an alcoholic distillate</note> of roses.

# XXXIV. *On distilling Spirits, Oil of Myrrh, Galbanum, turpentine, tacamahac, etc., through a retort, and making colophony.*

Fill a glass or stone <term>retort</term> <note>a flask with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> with a third part of these gums or resins, and a good portion of sand; place it in the sand-bath, and heat with graduated degrees of fire; thus you obtain oil and **spirit** <note>the volatile, concentrated essence</note> which one can rectify <note>purify through repeated distillation</note>. In this way one also makes **oil of amber, caranna, mastic, turpentine, etc.**; that which remains behind from the turpentine is **colophony** <note>original: *colophonie*; the solid resin or rosin left over after distillation</note>.

# XXXV. *Oil of Cloves by descent.* <note>original: *per descensum*; a method of distillation where the heat is applied from above, causing the essence to melt and drip downward into a container.</note>

Take large glazed pots; cover them with cloths, and tie the same fast around the pot, but ensure that each cloth has a hollow [depression], in which one can place the powdered **cloves** <note>original: *nagelen*, literally "nails," referring to the shape of the spice</note>; then place upon each pot, in whose cloth the cloves are, a hollow tin plate; <term>lute</term> <note>to seal a joint with a paste made of clay, lime, or flour to make it airtight</note> their edges fast to the edges of the pot, so that no vapor escapes; then place ash or sand upon it, on which one places a little fire, and so the oil and **phlegm** <note>the watery, non-essential part of the distillate</note> runs through the cloth into the pot.

## XXXVII. *Oil of Myrrh by liquefaction,* <note>original: *Oleum Myrrhae per deliquium*; a process where a substance melts or dissolves by absorbing moisture from the air, typically in a damp environment like a cellar.</note>

Take hard-boiled eggs, peel them, and cut them in half; remove the yolks, then fill the cavities of both half-whites with finely pounded myrrh; tie them up neatly and hang them in the cellar, and thus an oil shall drip out, which is used for the sore nipples of nursing women.

## XXXVIII. *Oil of Camphor.* <note>original: *Oleum Camphorae*</note>

Take a good portion of pounded camphor; pour over it an equal amount of "strong water" <term>aq. fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> or spirit of nitre; let it stand in a warm place, and so the camphor melts into an oil, which is then separated and kept.

## XXXIX. *Flowers and Oil of Benzoin.* <note>original: *Flores en Oleum Benzoin*; in early chemistry, "flowers" refers to the powdery crystals formed through sublimation—the process where a solid turns directly into a gas and then back to a solid.</note>

Take a good portion of coarsely pounded benzoin and put it in a moderately tall flask or pot; place it in the sand-bath and light a gentle fire beneath it; place a paper cone <term>peperhuisjen</term> <note>literally "little pepper-house"; a conical paper cap used to catch the rising vapors</note> on top of it, and so the **flowers** <note>benzoic acid crystals</note> will fly upwards to the top, which one can wipe away every two or three hours. The remainder is then put into a

### XL. *Tincture of Benzoin.* <note>original: *Tinctura Benzoin*</note>

Take the flowers of benzoin <note>original: *flores benzoin*; these are the white needle-like crystals of benzoic acid produced through sublimation</note>, one ounce; pour upon it three ounces of spirit of wine <note>original: *alcohol vini*</note>; place it in a warm spot, so the flowers swell, and you have a tincture.

### XLI. *Spirit and Oil of Scurvy-grass.* <note>original: *Spiritus en Olie van de Cochlearia*</note>

Take a great quantity of scurvy-grass <term>lepelbladen</term> <note>literally "spoon-leaves"; a herb high in vitamin C traditionally used to treat scurvy</note>, crush them and put them in a vessel; then sprinkle powdered tartar <term>wijnsteen</term> <note>a salt found in wine barrels, used here to assist fermentation</note> in between them; cover the vessel well, and let it ferment thus gently; then put them into the cauldron and fire it gently so that they do not burn; thus you shall receive water, spirit, and oil: one can then separate the oil from it, and dephlegmate <term>dephlegmeren</term> <note>the process of removing the watery "phlegm" from a substance to concentrate its strength</note> the spirit through several rectifications <note>repeated distillations to increase purity</note>.

### XLII. *Another way.*

Take spirit of wine <note>original: *alcohol vini*</note>, one pint; drip a few drops of the oil of scurvy-grass into it, and thus you have a spirit immediately.

### XLIII. *Third way.*

Take a good quantity of scurvy-grass, put it in the cauldron; pour so much spirit of wine <note>original: *spir. vini*</note> over it that they are covered; by distilling, you obtain the spirit made from all kinds of "hot" <note>in the humoral sense, referring to herbs that stimulate or warm the body</note> herbs, seeds, roots, etc.

## **IV. Spirit, Oil, Volatile Salt, and Fixed Salt of Vipers.**

Take seventy-two vipers that have been dried and place them in a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note> made of earth or clay-coated glass. Place it in the <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects heat from the roof onto the vessel</note>, attach a wide receiver <note>the glass vessel that collects the distilled liquid</note>, seal all the joints tightly with <term>lute</term> <note>a paste used to make airtight seals</note>, and light a gentle fire beneath it so that the retort remains steadily warm. In this way, a moisture will gradually drip out. When no more comes out, increase the fire bit by bit; white clouds will then emerge, which will gradually fill the receiver. Finally, you will see a black oil come over, and at the same time, the **Volatile Salt** <term>Sal Volatile</term> <note>a salt that evaporates easily; in this era, usually ammonium carbonate derived from animal matter</note> will cling to the sides of the receiver. Keep the fire going until nothing more flows out.

When this is done, let everything cool down and detach the receiver. Shake the receiver slightly so that the salt hanging on the sides melts into the liquid. Then pour all the material into a long-necked <term>flask</term> <note>original: *kolf*</note>, place a **helm** <note>the cap or head of a still that directs vapors into the cooling area</note> on top, and attach a receiver, sealing everything together with a wet bladder. Place the flask in the sand <note>a sand bath, used to provide even, indirect heat</note>. Once the fire is lit beneath it, a **Volatile Salt** will <term>sublimate</term> <note>transform from a solid to vapor and back to solid without becoming liquid</note>, clinging to the helm and the upper part of the flask. Melt this and store it in a tightly sealed glass vessel.

Next, pour the remaining liquid that stayed in the funnel through unsized paper <note>absorbent paper used for filtering</note>; the **phlegm** <term>phlegma</term> <note>the watery, tasteless part of a distillation</note> will pass through it, while the oil remains in the funnel. The **phlegm** is then <term>rectified</term> <note>purified through repeated distillation</note> once or twice. The residue that remains in the retort can be <term>calcined</term> <note>burned to ash at very high heat</note> and leached with water to extract a **Fixed Salt** <term>Sal Fixum</term> <note>a stable salt that does not evaporate, usually potassium or sodium carbonate</note> from it.

### V. **Spirit**, **Oil**, **Volatile Salt**, and **Fixed Salt of Urine.**

**E**vaporate ten or twelve pints of healthy child's urine <note>In historical chemistry, the urine of children was often specified because it was considered more "pure" or "potent" due to their vitality</note> in a glass or stone flask over a sand fire <note>A sand bath, which provides even, indirect heat</note>, until a substance remains with the thickness of honey. Set a helm upon it and seal everything with a wet bladder; place the matrass <note>a round-bottomed glass flask</note> in the sand and heat with a gentle fire. In this way, all the **Volatile Salt** <term>Sal Volatile</term> will sublimate, just as was described regarding the **Salt of vipers**. Then separate this volatile salt and keep it tightly sealed in a vial.

It is a noble fever remedy for quartan <note>A fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note> and malignant fevers; it opens all obstructions and expels harmful humors <note>The "fluids" of the body (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) which were believed to cause illness when imbalanced</note> through sweating, and it also acts as a diuretic. It is administered in doses of six to sixteen grains in some suitable liquid.

### VI. **The Phosphorus of Helvetius from Urine.** <note>Adriaan Helvetius was a famous 17th-century Dutch-born physician known for his chemical remedies</note>

Take a good portion of urine, let it putrefy in a tub for a month long, until it becomes a dry black substance; then take one pound of this, and of **oil of tartar** <note>original: *olei tartari*; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note> or of **Hartshorn** <note>original: *C. C.* for *Cornu Cervi*; the antler of a deer, used as a source of ammonia</note>; otherwise take four ounces of green wax, mix the matter well together, place it in a Waldenburg retort <note>original: *retort van Walpurg*; high-quality heat-resistant earthenware from Waldenburg</note>, and set it in a wind-furnace <note>a furnace designed with a draft to reach the very high temperatures required for phosphorus production</note>. Heat first with a weak fire, and finally heat for 4 hours with a strong fire, so that in the receiver first shall come a **Volatile Salt** <note>original: *Sal volatile*</note>, thereafter a little oil, and finally the **Phosphorus** shall be sublimated in the dome of the receiver <note>original: *Capitolio*; the upper part of the vessel</note>, as yellow as wax. Let the receiver stand thus for one night, so that it becomes cold. Afterwards wash off the Phosphorus and the **Oil** <note>original: *Oleum*</note> with the **liquid** <note>original: *liquor*</note> which the retort has gathered at the bottom; mix it all well together, place it in a glass retort in a sand bath, and thus you shall find many chunks or grains of the Phosphorus, which you must keep under water in the receiver; that which remains is good for washing or greasing the hands.
