### VII. **Spirit and Oil of Honey.** <note>original: *Spiritus en Oleum Mellis*</note>

**P**ut four pounds of the best *Honey* into a wide stone flask; distill all the moisture from it with a gentle fire until the sour drops run out: then remove the fire from beneath it and preserve the water in a bottle; thus you will have twenty-five ounces.

It is good for making the hair grow, with which one daily wets the comb, or a sponge to moisten the roots of the hair.

The material that remains in the flask, put that into a stone or glass **luted retort** <note>original: *beleemde retort*; a distillation vessel coated with a layer of clay or "lute" to protect the glass and seal the heat</note>, but let two-thirds of the retort remain empty; then set it in a **reverberatory furnace** <note>original: *reverbereer oven*; a furnace designed to reflect heat back onto the vessel</note>, attach a large **receiver** <note>original: *recipient*; the vessel that collects the distilled liquid</note>, everything being well **luted** <note>sealed with clay to prevent the escape of vapors</note>; so begins the distillation with a gentle fire; stoke it for three hours so that the retort becomes warm, then increase the fire gradually; so shall the spirits fly out little by little with a small amount of black oil and fill the receiver with clouds; stoke until no more comes out. Everything having become cold, detach the receiver and pour the oil and the **Spirit** <note>the volatile liquid extract</note> through a piece of **filtering paper** <note>original: *klad-papier*</note>; thus the spirit can be separated from the stinking oil, but very little oil comes over; preserve it in a vial; you shall have twelve ounces of spirit.

It can be added to **syrups** <note>original: *suleppen*; related to "juleps," these were medicinal flavored syrups</note> to give a **tartness** <note>original: *rinsigheyt*; a pleasant acidity</note>.

The spirit can be **rectified** <note>purified and concentrated through a second distillation</note> in a sand bath.

The oil serves for **decay of the bone** <note>original: *Caries Ossis*; a historical term for bone rot or chronic infection of the bone</note>.

## VIII. Oil of Wax. <note>original: *Oleum Ceræ*</note>

**M**elt two pounds of wax in an earthen pan, then add to it three or four pounds of crushed potter's clay, or as much as is enough to make a dough and to form into small balls, which you shall place in a stone or glass **luted retort** <note>original: *beleemt*; a vessel coated with a protective layer of clay and sand to withstand high heat</note>, but let a third part remain empty; set the retort in the **reverberatory furnace** <note>a furnace designed to reflect heat back onto the vessel</note>, and attach a receiver to it; everything being well **luted** <note>sealed with airtight paste</note>, first stoke with a gentle fire, so there comes over a **phlegm** <note>original: *Phlegma*; a watery, inactive distillate</note> and after that the spirit: increase the fire gradually, which shall solidify in the receiver like a butter: continue the fire until nothing more comes out: then detach the receiver, and separate the spirit, which is mixed with its phlegm, from the butter. It is a very good **opening remedy** <note>a medicine used to clear blockages in the body's vessels or organs</note>; it is administered in doses of ten to twenty drops, with turnip water or any other appropriate liquid.

Some prefer to use the butter of wax rather than its oil to make swellings disappear, which we shall now describe.

Melt the butter of wax in an earthen pan, mix into it a good portion of potter's clay or **Bolus** <note>a type of medicinal clay</note> which has been crushed: set the retort in the sand [bath], and attach a receiver to it; everything being well luted, stoke with a slow fire at first, so much spirit mixed with phlegm shall come out; which having been driven out, increase the fire gradually so a clear and yellow oil shall come over; when about three ounces have passed over, then attach a new **receiver** <note>original: *recipient*</note>; that which passes over at the last is like butter,

A **chemical** <note>original: *chymischen*; relating to alchemy and early modern chemistry</note> furnace, which can be easily moved, and appears almost like the **tripod** <note>a three-legged stand; here Becher likens his invention to the sacred three-legged seat used by the Pythia, the priestess at the Oracle of Delphi</note> of **Apollo at Delphi**, being described, is made of three parts; the first of which shows the furnace—designed to perform all chemical operations at little cost and to finish firing in a short time—and with eight figures (the first two of which are described here) its construction is shown, consisting of its lid, hoop, the body itself, and the pedestal, as if made of four parts.

## VIII. *Water of Life that is made ready at hand.*
<note>original: *Aqua Vitæ dat men voor de vuyst vaardig maakt.* This recipe provides a shortcut for pharmacists or householders to create flavored spirits instantly without the need for a lengthy distillation process.</note>

->Take two ounces of well-rectified brandy.<-
<note>original: *wel gerectificeerde brandewyn unc. ij.*; "rectified" spirits have been distilled multiple times to achieve high purity and alcohol content.</note>
->Ten drops of oil of cinnamon.<-
<note>original: *Ol. cinamomi gutt. x.*</note>

Mix these together until the oil is well dissolved with the Spirit. Then add a good quantity of common brandy to it, and pour in a little candy syrup <note>sugar syrup used for sweetening and consistency</note>. In this way, you have a spirit as if it had been distilled.
Note:
1. This can be done with all kinds of distilled oils, such as cloves, nutmeg, mace, rosemary, juniper, etc.
2. If you wish to have them colored, take red sandalwood for a red color; for a yellow color, take turmeric <note>original: *curcuma*</note> or some saffron; then pour it off gently and preserve it.

It warms and dries, and serves as a liquid in which to mix other things for cold diseases. <note>In the humoral medical system of the time, "cold diseases" were ailments thought to be caused by an excess of phlegm or cold humors, such as certain respiratory or digestive issues.</note>

### X. Compound Distilled Water.
<note>original: *Aqua Composita Destillata.*</note>

->Take ten handfuls of **greater celandine.**<-
<note>original: *chelidonie man. x.*; Celandine was traditionally used to treat liver and eye ailments.</note>
->**Six handfuls of wild radish leaves.**<-
<note>original: *Fol. raphan. rust. man. vi.*; likely *Armoracia rusticana* or horseradish.</note>
->**Four handfuls of figwort.**<-
<note>original: *Scrophul. man. iv.*; *Scrophularia* was often used to treat "scrofula" or swollen lymph nodes.</note>
->**Dandelion.**<-
->**Three handfuls of each of the violets.**<-
<note>original: *Taraxici. Violar. ana man. iij.*; "ana" is a medical shorthand meaning "of each."</note>

After everything has been cut, place it into a copper kettle, and having poured a good quantity of water over it, let it digest <note>to soak or macerate in gentle heat to extract the properties of the herbs</note> for an entire night; then distill it with a cooling-vat according to the art. Distill until you have obtained eight or ten pounds of water.

It thins and resolves <note>medical terms for breaking up thick humors or blockages in the body</note>. It is useful for fevers and obstructions, especially if it is made somewhat more potent with some volatile salt <note>original: *vlug zout*; such as ammonium carbonate, used to stimulate the system</note>, or with something else.

### X. Extract of Asarabacca.
<note>original: *Coagulum Asari.* In this context, *coagulum* refers to a thickened, solid extract. *Asarum* is also known as wild ginger or Asarabacca.</note>

Take a good quantity of the leaves and roots of the **Asarum** that are fresh; crush them into pieces: then wring the juice through a cloth. Pour this juice back onto the finely cut leaves or those that have been pressed out, and digest them in a water-bath <note>a *bain-marie*, providing gentle, even heat</note> for a full day and night, even until it reaches a boil. Press out the juice again, as before, and then evaporate it until it reaches the thickness of pills; thus you have an extract of the roots and the leaves.

To preserve it from mold, one puts it into a small stoneware pot or a glass jar, and moistens it with rectified brandy <note>high-proof distilled spirit used here as a preservative</note>.

## XII. *Aerial Noctiluca of Boyle.*
<note>original: *Noctiluca Aerea*; Latin for "light-bringing thing of the air." This refers to Robert Boyle’s 1680 discovery of a method to produce phosphorus.</note>

This consists of human urine that has stood to putrefy for a long time, which is evaporated <note>original: *uitgerookt*; literally "smoked out," referring to boiling a liquid down to a concentrate</note> to the thickness of a thick syrup or a thin extract; this is then mixed with three times as much sand, which is then heated by degrees over an open fire, up to the very highest degree, until at the end of the distillation a substance boils that is heavier than the others and quickly sinks down into the liquid that was distilled first: then you have the substance that glows at night.

## XIII. *Phosphorus of Comierius.*
<note>Refers to Claude Comiers (d. 1693), a French provost and scholar who wrote on the "cold fire" of phosphorus.</note>

One allows a large quantity of urine to ferment and evaporates it to the thickness of honey; place this in a stone retort, so that all the water and the spirit are drawn off by placing a gentle fire beneath it; this is done until red drops of oil begin to follow, which must be caught immediately by hanging a receiver <note>original: *recipient*; the collecting vessel in a distillation apparatus</note> to it. Then increase the fire slightly so that all the oil comes out: at the bottom of the retort you will then find the <term>Caput Mortuum</term> <note>Latin for "dead head"; the useless solid residue remaining after distillation or chemical exhaustion</note>, the upper part of which will be black and spongy. This you shall add to another entirely similar substance, which in another vessel...

will remain, after you have separated all the moisture of the urine oil <note>original: *pis olie*</note> by a gentle fire, which was in the receiver. From the mixture of these two kinds of matter, you should have one **medicinal pound** <note>original: *Medicinaal pond*; a unit of weight used by apothecaries, approximately 375 grams</note>. Put this into a stone retort made of good earth, which can hold seven pounds of liquid; attach a large glass receiver <note>original: *recipient*; the vessel that collects the distilled substance</note> to it, sealing the openings properly. Then one heats with an open fire, increasing it gradually until the retort is glowing red; once this is done, one must increase the fire for eight or nine hours. Then white clouds appear in the receiver, followed by a yellowish substance, which, by subliming <note>the process of a substance turning from a solid to a gas and back to a solid without becoming liquid</note> inside the neck of the receiver, will be your **Phosphorus**. This can be removed the next day, after the receiver has been washed with cold water. You shall then place the entire mass in a glass over a gentle fire, and from the water an oily substance will rise, and there small particles of the **Phosphorus** will gather. Once everything has become quite cold, you gather the mass of the **Phosphorus**, which you shall put into a glass that must be filled with water, and one must stop the glass very well with a glass stopper. If the mouth should be a bit wide, one can put a cork on it and tie it with a pig's bladder.

### XIX. Spa Pills

**Dose:** From 6 to 12 **grains**.
They purge gently, removing **obstructions** <note>blockages of the internal organs, thought to cause many ailments</note>, especially in long-lasting illnesses.

## XX. Mosaic Gold <note>original: *Sol Musivum*; a shimmering gold-colored pigment, chemically known as stannic sulfide, used by artists and bookbinders</note>

**Tin** <note>represented by the alchemical symbol ♃ for the planet Jupiter</note>, the best English, 1 **ounce** <note>original: *unc. i.*</note>.
**Mercury**, washed of its blackness <note>purified until the dark oxides are removed</note>.
**Sulfur**.
**Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: *Sal. Armon.*; ammonium chloride, used here as a flux</note>, of each half an **ounce**.
**Make an amalgam.**

Amalgamate <note>blend the metals into a soft alloy</note> the **Tin** with the **Mercury**, and then rub those with the **Sulfur** and the **Sal Ammoniac** until they become a fine powder.

## XXI. Another method.

**Take:**
**Tin**, 1 **ounce**.
**Mercury**, 2 **ounces**.
**Sulfur**.
**Sal Ammoniac**, of each 1 **dram** <note>original: *dr. i.*</note>.
**Mix.**

Proceed with this as before.

## XXII. Another way.

**Take:**
**Golden Marcasite** <note>original: *Marcaf. auri*; a term often used for iron pyrites or other metallic minerals used to create gold-colored powders</note>.
**Mercury**,
**Sulfur**,
**Sal Ammoniac**, in equal parts.

**Sublimate** <note>heat until the substance vaporizes and then solidifies again</note> these from a **luted** glass flask <note>original: *beleemde glase kolf*; a glass retort coated with a mixture of clay and straw to protect it from breaking in the high heat of the furnace</note>.

## CHAPTER II.

### A certain operation with *Gold* and *Quicksilver*,
### by Lord Dandre.

Carefully make an *Amalgam* <term>Amalgam: a mixture of mercury with another metal, which creates a soft, paste-like alloy</term> of one ounce of *Calx of Gold* <term>Calx: the powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or "burnt"; essentially a metallic oxide</term> with seven or eight ounces of well-purified *Quicksilver*; then evaporate so much *Quicksilver* from it that only four ounces of *Quicksilver* remain, so you keep four ounces in your glass: add to this one ounce of *living Sulfur* <note>original: *levendige Swavel*; sulfur in its raw, natural state, often found near volcanoes</note>, the pieces of which are clear and transparent (which is found in *Italy*); rub these well together (for herein lies the greatest part of the *secret*, as one must rub for three or four hours at a time). Then put your substance into a matress <term>Matrass: a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck</term> and give it a gentle heat, without stopping the glass in any way, as the moisture and smoke must evaporate. Then let your fire go out, and when your matress has cooled, seal it in the manner of *Hermes* <term>Hermetic seal: making a vessel airtight by melting the glass of the neck until it is fused shut</term>, and let it with

## CHAPTER IV.

### *The secret of the Lord of Outer, Physician in Brussels, regarding Gold and Butter of Antimony.*

Take Mineral of Antimony <term>Antimony: a brittle, silvery-gray metalloid often used in alchemical processes to "purify" gold</term> and Sublimate of Quicksilver <note>original: *Sublimaat van Quiksilver*; refers to mercuric chloride</note>, an equal amount of each; add a little Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux or to help substances react</term> to it, and make a butter from it <note>original: *boter*; this refers to "Butter of Antimony" (antimony trichloride), a thick, oily substance</note>: then pour off the Spirit of the Butter, which you shall rectify <gloss>To purify a liquid by repeated distillation</gloss> again (note, that this Butter, being set in the air, draws out from it as much as it needs in the time of one hour, thereby increasing in quantity: that which it has drawn to itself is the hidden food of human life, and of all the beings that are in the world. This Butter is the true magnet, which in its purity draws [this substance] to itself). Then put this spirit in a glass flask <note>original: *kolf glas*</note> of a suitable size, set it in a suitable heat, with an alembic <term>Alembic: the top part of a still, used to direct vapors into a cooling tube</term> and a receiver <term>Receiver: the vessel used to collect the condensed liquid at the end of the distillation process</term>; seal <note>original: *luteert*; to "lute" is to seal the joints of alchemical apparatus with clay or paste to prevent vapors from escaping</note> all the openings well, then set it to putrefy <note>original: *te rotten*; in alchemy, the "rotting" or putrefaction stage was essential for the transformation of matter</note> in the ashes for two months. Thus, the substance shall become as red as blood, and thereafter black, hanging on the sides of the glass like a clammy soot; but the spirit of the air climbs up and descends into the receiver in the form of a spirit, and a body like a fusible salt, from which one must draw the spirit and separate it through distillation with a good, gentle fire.

When you then see a red and glistening fire upon your matter, that is a sign of ripeness, and that you have obtained the *Mercury of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Mercurius der Philosophen*; a legendary alchemical substance sought as a key ingredient for the Philosopher's Stone</note>, which is the true *universal solvent* <note>original: *universele dissolvent*</note>; then let it cool. Take six ounces of this *Menstruum* <term>Menstruum: a specialized solvent used to dissolve or extract essence from a solid substance</term>, and add it to one ounce of gold beaten into thin plates, so that it might melt all the more readily; thus it shall penetrate [the gold] entirely and become of the same nature. You must take great care that you lose none of the spirit: put it into a matrass <term>Matrass: a long-necked glass flask used for digestion and distillation</term> with a glass stopper upon it that fits snugly; then being well-closed and luted <gloss>Sealed with airtight paste or clay</gloss>, digest it by the flame of a lamp, and that with a gentle heat at the beginning.

After it has then stood in digestion for five days, you must penetrate and saturate your substance with the said *Menstruum*, of which you must have an abundance in order to multiply your work. As soon as you have then poured your said solvent therein, you must immediately stop it up again and seal it as before: digest again for five days, gradually increasing the heat; when the fire has then gone out, you must again penetrate your substance with the virginal milk <note>original: *virginale Melk*; a poetic alchemical term for a white, purified liquid or solvent used to "nourish" the matter</note>; adding a little more than before, continuing the digestion with a slightly hotter fire.

Repeat this imbibition <gloss>The process of soaking or saturating a solid with a liquid</gloss> up to seven times; thus your matter shall become powerful and be able, from time to time, to endure stronger nourishment or penetration, and to suffer greater heat; nevertheless, one must not be too hasty.

## CHAPTER V.

### A significant work with Gold and Mercury.

# IX CHAPTER.

## *A Great Secret of the aforementioned Mr. Snyder's Powder.*

Dissolve your **Gold** in the **Acid Salt** <note>original: *Sal Enixum*</note> <term>Acid Salt: potassium bisulfate, a byproduct of making nitric acid, used here as a solvent for noble metals</term>, and exalt it with **Sulfur of Antimony** <term>Sulfur of Antimony: a chemical compound of sulfur and antimony used to "purify" gold or provide it with a deeper red color</term>; place these in a **conical mold** <note>original: *conus*</note> until it becomes a very red **Salt**; (but take care that no coals fall into it.) Leave the **Salt** in the fire as long as it remains fluid: grind it fine, and let it melt in a **matrass** <term>Matrass: a long-necked glass flask used for heating and digesting substances in alchemical experiments</term>; add a grain or two of the **Powder** to it, and let it melt for twelve or twenty hours in a strong fire, so shall this **Powder** be increased; pour it out, melt, and filter it; add **Silver** and **Mercury** <note>original: *Quik-silver*</note> to it, and it shall transmute into fine **Gold**.

Or, precipitate the liquid with **Salt** into a **Sulfur of Gold**, which you then digest for a long time with **Antimony Butter** <note>original: *Boter van Antimonie*</note> <term>Antimony Butter: antimony trichloride, a thick, oily, and highly corrosive substance used to dissolve or react with metals</term>.

Or, preserve the **Sulfur**, and ferment it again with dissolved **Gold**, just as was said, with the **Acid Salt**, and in a matrass, until the **Powder** may be increased unto infinity.

# CHAPTER XXII.

## *A Mineral of Gold, Processed.*

Take half a pound of **live sulfur** <note>naturally occurring or unrefined sulfur; brimstone</note>, melt it in an earthenware pot; then add to it a pound of **Quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, stir it constantly, until no more Quicksilver is seen within the sulfur: let it then become cold, and rub it into a powder; then <term>digest</term> <note>to apply steady, gentle heat over a long period to mature a substance</note> it in a **matrass** <note>a glass flask with a round body and a long neck</note> for two days with a strong fire: then take it from the fire, and rub it fine again; add to it double the weight of **iron filings**; mix it well together, then put it in a **retort** <note>a glass vessel with a long neck pointing downward, used for distilling liquids or gases</note>, and distill all the Quicksilver from it: mix this Quicksilver again with new sulfur, and melt it as before, digest it as before in a matrass for two days in succession; then rub fine again the filings of steel (from which your **Mercury** was distilled), wash the same well from all impurities and blackness: dry it then, and rub again with sulfur and Quicksilver; distill then again as before in a retort. # CHAPTER XXII.

->The Fixation of Lead into Silver, with good profit.<- <note>"Fixation" refers to the process of making a volatile substance stable or turning a "base" liquid metal into a solid, "fixed" precious metal.</note>

MELT one pound of lead, add to it half an ounce of silver, along with some iron-scale <term>iron-scale</term> <note>original: *hamerslag*; the flaky crust of iron oxide that falls off during forging</note>, as well as a little red *arsenic*. Then take this material again and melt it with the same quantity of silver and new iron-scale; set it to melt again as before.

Repeat this operation ten or twelve times, until the lead has become very hard, being impregnated with the silver; then place it on the cupel <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *copel*; a shallow, porous dish used in assaying to separate lead and other base metals from precious gold and silver</note> with one ounce of silver for every pound of this mixture.

Then dissolve in four ounces of well-rectified **spirit of Vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol: a strong acid, usually sulfuric acid, distilled from green vitriol (iron sulfate)</term>, one ounce of **sulfur of Iron**, and two drachms of **sulfur of Gold**, which is made in the same way, except for the first solution of the **Gold**, which is performed with ***Aqua Regia*** <term>aqua regia: Latin for "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</term>, made from **Salt**, **Saltpeter**, and **Vitriol**.

Then mix these last two solutions together, and digest <term>digest: to apply a gentle, constant heat to a substance, often by placing the vessel in a warm medium</term> them in horse manure <note>Horse manure was used as a natural, steady heat source for slow chemical reactions</note>, and coagulate it gently; then dissolve it again with **spirit of Vitriol**, and coagulate anew: repeat this up to seven times, and if any *feces* <note>original: *faces*; refers to dregs or solid impurities that settle at the bottom</note> remain at the end, remove them.

Then test this **Medicine** on a hot Silver plate; if it then penetrates and thoroughly permeates through and through and remains fixed without smoke, it is a sign of perfection; but if it smokes, you must melt it again and gently coagulate.

Then melt one ounce of **Gold**, and throw into it, bit by bit, one drachma of the aforementioned **Medicine**; when it has been swallowed and incorporated by the **Gold**, then place it on the cupel <term>cupel: a shallow, porous dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</term>, and you shall have a substance as brittle as glass, as transparent as a dark garnet, and as meltable as **Lead**.

Then melt fine **Gold** and fine **Silver**, an equal amount of each, and throw some of this **Medicine** into it, and you shall obtain a pure **Gold**.

## *A Method to Fix <term>fix: to turn a volatile substance into a solid that can withstand heat without evaporating</term> one fourth of Silver into Gold.*

Take one ounce of silver filings and amalgamate <term>amalgamate: to blend a metal with mercury to form a soft paste</term> it with four ounces of **mercury** <note>original: *Quiksilver*</note>: put this **amalgam** into a retort <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-sloping neck used for distilling liquids or gases</term>, and distill the **mercury** off from it; then take the silver and amalgamate it once again with the distilled **mercury**, and distill as before: do this three or four times, and the silver will become an impalpably <note>Too fine to be felt as individual grains</note> fine powder.

Then take **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to "open" metals and aid in sublimation</term> and **cinnabar** <term>cinnabar: a bright red mineral (mercury sulfide) and the primary ore of mercury</term>, one and a half ounces of each; and a half ounce of ***mercury sublimate*** <term>mercury sublimate: also known as corrosive sublimate (mercuric chloride), a highly toxic white powder used to refine and "spiritualize" metals</term>; grind and mix everything thoroughly with the **silver**: then sublimate <term>sublimate: to heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again at the top of the vessel, used for purification</term> it with a gentle heat; then mix that which has sublimated with that which remains at the bottom, and sublimate as before.

Then take both the *dregs* <note>original: *fæces*</note> and the **sublimate**, and mix them with **sulfur of copper**, and ***crocus martis*** <term>crocus martis: "Saffron of Mars," a red iron oxide powder used as a pigment or alchemical reagent</term>, and with a **regulus** <term>regulus: the metallic mass found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term> made of **antimony**, **iron**, and **copper**, a half ounce of each; grind everything well together with a little **sal ammoniac**: sublimate it four times with a gentle heat, adding some **sal ammoniac** each time, through which the body of the **iron** and **copper** is opened <note>to "open" a metal meant to break down its physical structure to make it chemically reactive</note>.

# CHAPTER XXXIII.

## An excellent Smelting-salt.

Decrepitate <note>to heat a salt until it stops crackling</note> and reverberate <note>to heat in a furnace where the flame is deflected back onto the material</note> your <term>Salt</term>, then dissolve it in clean Water, filter and coagulate <note>to thicken or solidify a liquid, usually by evaporating the solvent</note> it: do this four or five times: when it is then entirely pure, dissolve it in spirit of <term>Vinegar</term>; filter and coagulate it: do this with the distilled <term>Vinegar</term> once more, so you shall have a perfect Smelting-salt.

# CHAPTER XXXIV

## *Another way to make a Smelting-salt.*

Dissolve your Salt in clean Water, filter and <term>coagulate</term> <note>original: "coaguleert"; to thicken or turn a liquid into a solid state, often through evaporation</note> it; when the Water has then all evaporated, and the Salt falls to the bottom, then take it out from there with a small wooden spatula a little at a time, until all the Water has steamed away.

Then rub this Salt fine, once it is first well dried, and <term>reverberate</term> <note>original: "reverbereert"; to heat a substance in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" down onto the material, usually without the fuel touching the material directly</note> it in an earthen, closed, and well-<term>luted</term> <note>sealed with "lute," a clay or paste used to make chemical apparatus airtight</note> pot; let the pot glow in the fire, but the Salt must not melt; as soon as you see the pot glowing, let it stand until the fire has gone out; then rub it fine, and reverberate as before; dissolve and coagulate also as before: repeat this so many times until it is a perfect <term>Smelting-salt</term> <note>original: "Smelt-sout"; a flux used to promote the melting of metals and help separate impurities</note>.

Note, that you must not <term>decrepitate</term> <note>original: "decrepiteren"; to heat a salt until it makes a crackling sound as it loses its "water of crystallization"</note> your Salt.

## CHAPTER 52.

### To extract the Quicksilver from Antimony, or from Lead.

Take mineral **antimony** (or **calx** <note>the powdery residue left after heating a metal</note> of lead) crushed into a fine powder; pour as much **spirit of salt** <note>original: "geest van Sout"; modern hydrochloric acid</note> onto it until it becomes as thick as porridge. **Digest** <note>heat gently to encourage chemical reaction</note> it for seven or eight days, or even longer; then distill the moisture from it until it is dry. Then change the **receiver**, filling the new one with water in which **Sal Armoniac** <note>original: "Sal Armoniac"; ammonium chloride, used in alchemy as a volatile salt and solvent</note> has been dissolved. Distill this according to the art with **degrees of fire** <note>the alchemical practice of gradually increasing heat from gentle to intense</note>, and thus you shall obtain **living quicksilver**.

## CHAPTER 53.

### Butter of Antimony without Sublimate, to make Mercury of Antimony.

Take one part *Antimony*, two parts decrepitated *Salt* <note>original: "Sout"; salt that has been heated until it stops crackling</note>, and four parts *Vitriol* <note>original: "Vitriool"; likely iron or copper sulfate</note> which have been calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove moisture</note> until they are white; bring them all to a fine powder, and mix them well together, and pour it bit by bit into a glowing retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</note>, through a hole that is at the top of the retort, just as *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for his improvements to laboratory equipment</note> says; distill that then in a glass retort, well luted <note>sealed with an airtight paste</note> in the open fire, and so you shall obtain the **Butter of Antimony** <note>original: "Boter van Antimonie"; antimony trichloride, a thick, oily substance used in alchemical processes</note>, just as if it were made with *Sublimate* <note>mercury(II) chloride, a common but toxic reagent</note>.

# CHAPTER LVII.

## *To make Mercury from Antimony.*

Take one pound of *Antimony*, crushed to a fine powder; boil it in lye, made from quicklime <note>original: "levende Kalk"; calcium oxide, used here for its caustic properties</note> and Potash; let it boil for two hours, and after it has settled, pour off the clear liquid, then pour more Lye onto the Antimony, and boil it as before; repeat this as many times until there is no more Sulfur <note>original: "Swavel"</note> left in the Antimony, which you can know by pouring distilled Vinegar into the decanted Lye, and no more *Sulfur* <note>original: "Sulphur"; the alchemical principle of combustibility</note> precipitates, or changes no further; then edulcorate <note>to wash a solid substance to remove acids or soluble salts</note> the remainder of the Antimony, and rub it with four ounces of Salt of Tartar <note>original: "Sout van Wijnsteen"; potassium carbonate, often derived from wine lees</note>, and as much Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Sal Armoniac"; ammonium chloride</note>, with eight ounces of Vitriol <note>a metal sulfate, likely iron or copper sulfate</note>; set these to sublimate <note>to heat a solid until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again in a cooler part of the apparatus</note> with a gentle heat at first, and thereafter with a strong fire for seven or eight hours, then everything shall be sublimated.

Then mix this Sublimate with an equal weight of quicklime; distill it in a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-sloping neck</note>, attach a receiver to it, which is filled with Water in which Sal Ammoniac has been dissolved <note>original: "gesmolten"; literally 'melted', but here meaning dissolved</note>, thus you shall obtain the living Quicksilver.

In the same manner, one makes Quicksilver from Lead, taking Calx <note>a powdery metallic oxide produced by heating</note> of Lead instead of Antimony.

# CHAPTER LXVI.

### *A special spirit of Saltpeter, or the Sharpest Vinegar.*

It is no common spirit of Saltpeter, but it is a spirit which, by cohobating and distilling many times, makes its own body volatile <note>original: "vlug"; meaning it can be evaporated or transformed into vapor</note> in the form of a snow, which melts at the slightest warmth and solidifies in the cold; this is the **Sharpest Vinegar** <note>original: "Acetum Acerrimum"; an alchemical term for a powerful acidic solvent, likely concentrated nitric acid or a highly purified acid</note>, which dissolves all metals and returns them to their first matter <note>the *prima materia*, or the original substance from which all things are made</note>: all perfect metals <note>referring to gold and silver</note> melt within it and coagulate again, and shall change into perfect fixed <term>In alchemy, "fixed" substances are stable under heat and do not evaporate, unlike "volatile" ones</term> substances, and all imperfect metals shall be changed into perfect ones through projection <note>the act of throwing a small amount of the alchemical medicine onto base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</note>.

Take **silver** and **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, as much as you wish, and make an **amalgam** <term>A mixture or alloy of mercury with another metal, often creating a soft paste</term> with one another: then mix this amalgam with half its weight of **sublimated mercury** <term>Also known as corrosive sublimate (mercury chloride), a white crystalline powder used as a powerful reagent</term>; put it in a retort, then pour our **sour spirit** upon it, and once the substance therein is well-melted, distill and cohobate <term>To pour a distilled liquid back onto the solid residue left in the vessel and re-distill it, often done repeatedly to concentrate or "purify" the substance</term> upon the remaining body as many times until all the matter is changed into a volatile spirit and nothing more remains at the bottom; for it must all ascend and become volatile: then melt this volatile substance again in our sour spirit: then distill and cohobate so many times upon the remainder until all the substance has become fixed, and the fixed matter volatile again, and the volatile fixed again, so shall you have a penetrating **Salt**.

# CHAPTER LXVI.

## A special spirit of saltpeter, or the *Sharpest Vinegar*.

It is no common spirit of saltpeter, but it is a spirit which, by repeatedly **cohobating** <term>to distill a liquid from its own residue multiple times to concentrate its power</term> and distilling, makes its own body volatile in the form of a snow, which melts at the slightest heat and solidifies in the cold; this is the *Sharpest Vinegar* <note>original: "Acetum Acerrimum"</note>, which dissolves all metals and turns them back into their first matter. All perfect metals <note>Gold and silver</note> melt within it and coagulate again, and shall change into perfect fixed [substances], and all imperfect metals shall be changed into perfect ones by **projection** <note>The alchemical process of casting a small amount of a transmuting substance onto a molten base metal to effect a change</note>.

Take silver and **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, as much as you wish, and make an **amalgam** <term>a soft paste made by blending mercury with another metal</term> with one another. Then mix this **amalgam** with half as much weight of **corrosive sublimate** <note>original: "Mercurius Sublimatus"; mercuric chloride, a potent chemical used in alchemical transformations</note>; place it in a **retort**, then pour our sour spirit upon it. Once the substance therein is well melted, distill and cohobate upon the remaining body so many times until all the matter is changed into a volatile spirit and nothing more remains on the bottom; for it must all ascend and become volatile. Then melt this volatile [substance] again in our sour spirit; then distill and cohobate as many times upon the remainder until all the substance has become fixed, and the fixed matter [made] volatile again, and the volatile fixed again; thus you shall have a penetrating salt.

->Chemical Theater.<-

You must then have the spirit of the natural **Casting-salt** <term>likely a reference to a fusible salt or saltpeter used in smelting</term>, which is the most principal part of all Metals, Plants, and Animals; this spirit, being purified and united with its bodies (which are also purified), makes its bodies **volatile** <term>capable of being evaporated or distilled</term>, and unites them inseparably; thus you obtain a volatile Casting-salt like a **Butter** <note>In alchemy, a "butter" refers to a substance with a thick, oily consistency, often a chloride of a metal</note>, which solidifies in the cold. This Butter dissolves all Metals, just as warm Water melts Ice; this is then the true matter for the **Great Work** <note>The "Magnum Opus," the process of creating the Philosophers' Stone</note>, and the Mercury of the *Philosophers*.

To prepare the universal spirit, which is the universal Salt, you must purify and **rectify** <term>to refine a substance by repeated distillation</term> [it] well; and by that means the fixed body becomes volatile (being thus purified). But to make the fixed volatile, the quantity of the volatile must exceed the fixed; but if one wishes to **fix** <term>to make a volatile substance solid and resistant to heat</term> and make the volatile solid, then the fixed must have the upper hand. However, long **digestion** <note>The process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat</note> fulfills the quantity of the fixed, for that which is naturally fixed is enclosed (although it is changed for the present) within the volatile. But the addition of Gold (which is dissolved and radically united) shortens the time and hastens the **fixation**, and then it is made fixed from volatile through a long digestion. When it is volatile, it passes through the **retort** <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> like an Oil, which shall **coagulate** <note>thicken or solidify</note> when it is cold, and melts in the heat: it is the seed of Metals. To fix [it] better and more effectively, it is best that one adds Gold to it, and then digests.

# CHAPTER LXVII.

## *An operation regarding* **Lead**; *the* **Philosophers'** *supplement.*

The Solution and Ablution <term>the process of washing or purifying a solid substance with a liquid</term> are one and the same thing; for through **calcination** <term>heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> the bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to solid metals or minerals</note> are divided into small parts; through **putrefaction** <note>a stage of chemical breakdown often likened to organic decay</note> they decompose; and when it is distilled, it is brought to its first matter, and remains dissolved.

The congelation <term>the solidification of a liquid</term> is a fixation, union, or coagulation of the volatile and the melted body. Through reduction and fixation, when the body has been **sublimated** <term>transformed from a solid directly into a vapor and back to solid</term>, it becomes fatty, and resolves, unites, and finally is perfectly coagulated. Thus, in these two solutions and coagulations are the ablution, reduction, and fixation.

**Ripley** <note>Referring to George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> acts in his *Viaticum* <note>original: "Viaticum"; a work by Ripley regarding the alchemical journey</note> in this manner: calcines the **Tin** into a very **subtle Lime** (for there is a pure Mercury in it, which has not been brought to its full perfection by nature) which easily hardens through the **Oil of Silver**; therefore, perform your work with **Tin** (until you are rich), for to work in this way is much easier and of small expense.

# CHAPTER LXXV.
## Of the Great Philosopher's Stone.

Take prepared **Salt**, **Saltpeter**, and **Roman Vitriol** <note>original: "Roomse Vitriool"; typically blue vitriol or copper sulfate, though sometimes used for iron sulfate</note>, two pounds of each; pound them all to a fine powder; mix them well together, and place them in a pot over a gentle fire; stir it so that it melts and dries a little.
   Take then **Mercury** drawn from mineral <note>original: "Mercurius uit Mineraal"; mercury obtained directly from its ore, cinnabar, rather than recycled from other chemical processes</note>, one pound, put it in a linen cloth, squeeze it out, and pour it onto the hot matter; stir it with an iron rod until the **Quicksilver** is no longer visible; incorporate the mass well until it is cool in a marble mortar; then dry it very gently in a pot, until it is so dry that a polished sword held over the pot is not affected by the moisture <note>This was a common test to ensure all water had evaporated: if steam remained, it would fog or rust the blade</note>: then set it to **sublime** <note>The process of heating a substance into a vapor so it collects as a solid on the upper, cooler part of the vessel</note> for twelve hours, and increase the fire, so that all the **Mercury** is well sublimated, and is as white as Snow: if the **Mercury** has lost nothing of its fine weight, then it is mixed with the *invisible Sulfur of Vitriol*, and purified from the Earth and fine blackness; and when you find that **conjunction** <note>original: "conjunctie"; the chemical and mystical marriage of two substances</note>, you can separate the **Sulfur of Vitriol** from the **Mercury** in this manner.

Take distilled **Vinegar**, as much as is sufficient, and quench a glowing piece of iron in it several times; let your **Sublimate** <note>The solid substance resulting from the heating process described on the previous page</note> stand in this every night, then let it be filtered three times; then set it over a gentle fire. # CHAPTER XCI.

## *To fix Sulfur for the aforementioned work.*

Take five ounces of <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: *levende Kalk*; calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance.</note>, place it in clean Water, then filter it after it has soaked for 24 hours, and place the [filtered] liquid in a kettle: then take eight ounces of <term>flowers of sulfur</term> <note>original: *Bloem van Swavel*; a fine powder produced by heating sulfur until it turns to vapor and then solidifies.</note>, bind it in a linen bag, and hang it in the Water that is in the kettle; let it boil for one hour, and thus you will have an incombustible <term>Sulfur</term> <note>original: *Sulphur*; in alchemy, sulfur represents the principle of combustibility and soul.</note>.

## CHAPTER III.
### Red Calx of Gold.

Take fine Gold (which has been purified by <term>Antimony</term> <note>A brittle, silvery-white metalloid used in alchemy to "purify" gold because it alloys with impurities, leaving the pure gold behind.</note>) in <term>Aqua Regia</term> <note>original: *Konings-water*; a highly corrosive mixture of acids, literally "royal water," capable of dissolving gold.</note>, then pour water over it, then add the <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurius*; quicksilver.</note> to it, so that everything becomes like a <term>liver</term> <note>original: *Hepar*; a Latin term used to describe a substance with a dark, reddish-brown color or liver-like consistency.</note> or liver; then wash this <term>amalgam</term> <note>original: *Amalgama*; a mixture of mercury with another metal.</note>, and rub it three times with very well-prepared Salt, and distill that in a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note>; then <term>edulcorate</term> <note>To wash away salts or acids to make a substance "sweet" or neutral.</note> the <term>Calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after a metal has been burned or calcined.</note>, and rub one ounce of it with three ounces of <term>Cinnabar</term> <note>A bright red mineral, the primary ore of mercury.</note>, and <term>reverberate</term> <note>To heat in a furnace where the flames are "reflected" or "thrown back" onto the substance.</note> then gently by degrees: this is done for two days; repeating this eleven or twelve times, and it is a very subtle Calx as red as <term>scarlet</term> <note>original: *scharlaken*.</note>.

## CHAPTER IV.
### An Elixir of Wine and Gold.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## Of the *Eagle’s Glue* or *Mercury of the Wise*, or the *Metallic <term>Solvent</term>*, with which and the *Lion’s Blood* the *Metallic Stone* is made.

for it will all fly away on the cupel <note>A "cupel" is a shallow, porous dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</note>; the same will happen if it is attracted by 
plates of **Copper**.

Note that this spirituous **Silver** is a potential and 
spiritual **Gold**, as you shall find if you unite it with its body 
on the cupel.

Note that the physical **Silver** which is added thereto 
retains everything of the nature of **Gold**, which it afterwards 
gives over into the parting-water <note>original: "scheiwater"; nitric acid, used by alchemists to "part" or separate gold from silver.</note>: therefore take these filtered 
solutions (which are yellow) and precipitate them entirely into a 
**Silver Sulfur** <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" often refers to the combustible or "soul" essence of a substance, rather than the chemical element.</note> of a golden color, adding thereto a good quantity 
of that which precipitates: then dry this **Silver-Golden Precipitate** 
gently, and mix it with as much **Calx of Tin** <note>original: "Kalk van Tin"; the powdered oxide remains after tin has been burned.</note>, made *by itself* <note>original: "per se"; Latin for "by itself," meaning without other additives.</note> 
in the fire; or if you desire, you can make the Butter <note>A "butter" refers to a thick, oily substance, likely Butter of Antimony (antimony trichloride).</note> or 
fiery Crystals with equal parts of **Antimony**, which melt in the

Stars <note>original: "Gesternten"; referring to the belief that celestial bodies influenced the properties of terrestrial chemicals.</note>, or the Water of Nature; then put this moisture in a 
glass flask with its helm <note>The "helm" or alembic is the cap of a still that directs vapors into the cooling neck.</note> on it and a receiver attached, and let

## CHAPTER XXIV.

### *Of the Stone of Metals by itself or its spiritual Silver.*

Take the preceding moisture and put it into a small glass flask; let it remain uncovered and evaporate it in the ash-bath with a gentle lamp-fire; this is so that if any moisture from the air were present, it may evaporate. There remains at the bottom of the flask the **Metallic Gum**, the **Silver Glue**, the **Azoth** <note>Azoth was considered by alchemists to be the "universal solvent" or the "first principle" of metals, often associated with Mercury.</note>, etc., which melts like butter with the slightest heat, and liquefies through the cold <note>The text refers to deliquescence, where a substance absorbs moisture from the air to become liquid.</note>. Put that **Gum** into a matrass <note>A long-necked glass bulb used for heating and digesting substances.</note> and seal it hermetically; digest it *by itself* <note>original: "per se"</note>, and it will turn black, and then white, and that is the **White Stone**; when you then increase the fire, it becomes yellow and red without any **Gold ferment**. And to shorten the work, add to this **Glue** a tenth part of **gold leaf** or **Sulfur of Salt** <note>original: "Sulphur Salis"</note>, made spiritual by the sulfurous **Sal Enixum** <note>A technical term for a neutral salt, usually potassium sulfate, often produced as a byproduct in alchemical distillations.</note>, and digest as before.

If **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> is digested therewith, it becomes **Silver**; and if one drops it upon a **Copper** plate, it penetrates the same and becomes **Silver**. It is an **eternal Magnet** that remains after the distillation of the **Silver**; and to effect this, dissolve it in the air, and proceed as before with a lamp; distill then the **Heavenly moisture** (which is impregnated with the **Silver soul**) into a receiver, and it will once again become a **Glue**; and this one can do unto infinity.

## CHAPTER XXV.

Repeat this twice, being three **cohobations** <note>A technique where the liquid that was just distilled is poured back onto the solid residue to be distilled again, concentrating its "virtue."</note> without the first distillation. Then take your black and fixed **Sulfur** and pulverize it finely, and let it reverberate <note>To heat a substance in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the material.</note> in a glass furnace for three weeks, so it becomes white, then yellow, and then brown-

# CHAPTER XXVII.

## The Seal of Hermes. <note>original: "Sigillum Hermetis"; though the term often refers to an airtight seal, here it describes a specific chemical preparation.</note>

Dissolve six drams <note>A dram is approximately 3.9 grams.</note> of Silver in the best **Strong-water** <note>original: "Sterk-water"; nitric acid, a powerful solvent for metals.</note>; after the solution, put into a flask an **amalgam** <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal.</note> of one dram of fine Gold and 2 ounces of **Mercury** <note>original: "Quik"</note>: from which a great movement arises: let the flask stand still upon a table, until everything is dissolved; meanwhile you shall perceive many different colors: after having stood for 50 days you shall find a sort of roughness upon the surface of the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, which daily shall sprout and grow more and more: in more than 20 days (60 in total) it shall shoot forth some little spears or needles and branches: when you now see that it grows or shoots forth no more, then pour off all the liquid, so the **Mercurial** substance shall immediately float upon it of its own accord. Take then these sprouted branches from the mass, which shall amount to about a dram or more, and rub that to a powder that shall be very white. Of this powder one gives 24 grains <note>A tiny unit of weight, about 65 milligrams.</note> or more, according to the **constitution** <note>original: "complexie"; the medical theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note> in a candied cherry or the yolk of an egg, very early in the morning, or when one goes to bed in the evening, or rather after the first sleep at three or four hours in the morning, and sleep upon it.
It cures **quartan fevers** <note>A recurring fever associated with malaria that peaks every four days.</note> and other fevers and desperate illnesses.

It heals cancer, wolf <note>original: "wolf"; a historical term for *lupus* or a "devouring" skin ulcer.</note>, fistulas, and all kinds of old, malignant, and corrosive sores, used externally.

## CHAPTER XXIX.
### *Mercury of Antimony.* <note>original: "Mercurius van Antimonie."</note>

**Calcinate** <note>To heat a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile parts or reduce it to a powder.</note> **Antimony** in a closed **reverberatory furnace** <note>original: "reverbereer-oven"; a furnace where the flame and heat are deflected (reverberated) from the roof onto the material.</note>, until it is gray; then **sublime** <note>original: "ſublimeert"; the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid, used for purification.</note> it in an earthen vessel; grind again that which has been sublimed, and sublime again as before. Repeat this up to three times, and when you find that the sublimed **Antimony** is hard and heavy, then the **Mercury of Antimony** is enclosed therein.

# CHAPTER XXXI.
## *Tincture of the Flowers of Antimony <note>original: "Tinctura Florum Antimonii"</note>.*

Take the high red **flowers of Antimony** <note>The powdery sublimate produced by heating antimony ore.</note>, digest and circulate with well-rectified **Spirit of Vitriol** <note>original: "Spiritus Vitrioli"; a concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>; being well united, then **abstract** <note>To remove a liquid by distillation.</note> the Spirit until it becomes an Oil; then pour over it **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: "Spir. Vini"; high-proof alcohol or ethanol.</note>; then digest and abstract again until it becomes an Oil.

It refreshes the heart, strengthens the stomach, cures fever, and opens all obstructions, given from 1, 3, to 4 drops.

# CHAPTER XXXIII.

## *Tincture of Antimony.* <note>original: "Tinctura Antimonii"</note>

Take **Salt of Tartar** <note>original: "Wijnsteen-sout"; potassium carbonate, often used as a flux or solvent.</note> and Antimony, of each an equal amount, melt them together in a crucible, let the same stand in fusion for half an hour; pour out the crucible, and bring it to a powder; then put it in a **matrass** <note>A long-necked glass flask.</note>, and pour upon it of the best rectified **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: "Spiritus Vini"; high-proof alcohol.</note>, enough so that it stands three fingers broad on top; then set the matrass in warm sand <note>A sand bath, used to provide even, controllable heat.</note>, in such a way that the Spirit of Wine boils a little, so you obtain a high red Tincture: decant it, and keep it for use.

It opens all **obstructions** <note>Blockages of the internal "vessels" or organs, thought to be the cause of many diseases.</note> of all the principal parts, such as liver, spleen, lungs, the womb, kidneys, bladder; cures **jaundice** <note>original: "geel-sugt"</note>, **green sickness** <note>original: "groene-sugt"; chlorosis, a type of anemia.</note>, scabies, **dropsy** <note>original: "water-sugt"; swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>, **shortness of breath** <note>original: "engborstigheid"</note>, pleurisy, melancholy, internal and external ulcers, **pocks** <note>original: "pokken"; can refer to smallpox or syphilis.</note> etc. given in doses of four to twelve drops.

<meta>catchword: NARE-</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the instructions for a Tincture of Corals and provides a detailed recipe for a Tincture of Antimony, a potent alchemical medicine used to treat a wide variety of systemic ailments and "obstructions."</summary>

# AFTERWORD.

*Concerning the true preparation of the Powder of Sympathy of Mr. Kenelm Digby, as he prepared it every year in his laboratory.* <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665) was an English courtier and diplomat famous for promoting this "sympathetic" cure, which was applied to the weapon or blood-stained clothing rather than the wound itself.</note>

Take as much good English vitriol <note>original: "Engelse vitriool"; iron(II) sulfate, commonly known as green vitriol or copperas.</note> as you please; dissolve it in warm water, but take no more water than is necessary for the dissolution, letting the most impure parts sink to the bottom: then the solution is filtered, then it is evaporated until one sees a skin <note>A thin film or pellicle that forms on the surface of a liquid when it becomes saturated.</note> appear on it; then set it in a cool place and let it stand still for two or three days; cover it only so that nothing falls into it; thus clear, green, and large crystals will form <note>original: "schieten"; literally "shoot," describing the rapid growth of crystals.</note> there, which are then removed, and placed outside in a large earthenware dish in the hot sun during the **Dog Days** <note>original: "Honds-dagen"; the hottest weeks of summer, typically July and August, named for the rising of the "Dog Star" Sirius.</note>, stirring them occasionally; thus they shall be **calcined** <note>Reduced to a dry, white powder through the heat of the sun, removing the water of crystallization.</note> white by the sun. When you see that it will get no whiter; then crush it coarsely and place it in the sun again, taking care that no rain falls: when it is now well calcined; then rub it fine and place the powder in the sun again, stirring it often: continue this until it is brought to a white powder; then put it in a glass; seal it well, and keep it in a dry place.

Regarding the virtues of this powder, I will only tell you that I have seen great experience of it in my time in the staunching <note>original: "stempen"; to stop the flow of blood.</note> of desperate nosebleeds, in the staunching of bleeding wounds, and in the curing of fresh wounds,

<summary>This page provides a detailed alchemical recipe for the "Powder of Sympathy," a famous 17th-century remedy attributed to Sir Kenelm Digby, focusing on the purification and solar calcination of green vitriol.</summary>
<keywords>Powder of Sympathy, Kenelm Digby, vitriol, crystallization, calcination, Dog Days, staunching blood, wound care</keywords>

--- Page 704 ---
<meta>This page continues from the description of calcining vitriol in the sun to create the Powder of Sympathy, concluding the preparation instructions and providing testimonials of its efficacy.</meta>

# AFTERWORD.

...when there are no broken bones involved, without any plaster or ointment <note>original: "pleister ofte smeering"; typical 17th-century medical treatments that often involved painful scrubbing or heavy bandages.</note> in five days' time.

A certain girl of twelve years bled without ceasing from the nose for two or three days in a row; her mother had used everything she could bring to bear, all in vain: she came to me, told me this, and said she had heard that I had such a **blood-stopping powder** <term>stemp-poeder</term><note>A styptic powder used to contract tissues and stop bleeding.</note>: she begged me to have a little of it, for she feared that her daughter would bleed to death: I gave her some of that powder, and told her to put a little of it in 3 or 4 spoonfuls of fresh water, and with a small cloth wet her nostrils with it, sticking it somewhat deep into the nostrils, which she did, and her bleeding was stopped immediately: the next day she bled a little again, and the same was used again, and the blood stilled at once, and she bled no more thereafter.

I have spoken with a famous **Surgeon** <term>Chirurgijn</term><note>In this era, surgeons were manual practitioners who treated wounds and performed operations, distinct from academic physicians.</note> named *Master Smith*, in *Augsburg* in *Germany*, who told me that he had great respect for the book of Mr. *Digby*, and that he made that powder every year, with which he performed the most difficult cures in all fresh wounds; with much greater ease for the **Patient**, than with ointments or plasters.

Should the reader desire to know more of the effects of this powder, and the reasons for it, I then direct him to the treatise concerning the healing of wounds by **sympathy** <term>sijmpathie</term><note>The "Cure by Sympathy" was a popular theory that a remedy could heal a wound by being applied to the blood of the victim on a cloth or weapon, rather than to the body itself.</note> described by Mr. *Digby* himself: in which he shall find complete satisfaction, and have pleasure regarding the reasoning of its effects.

->*End of the second Part of the continuation of*<-
->*Mr. K. Digby.*<-
